abstract: We present an application of back-propagation networks to hand(cid:173) written digit recognition. Minimal preprocessing of the data was required, but architecture of the network was highly constrained and specifically designed for the task. The input of the network consists of normalized images of isolated digits. The method has 1 % error rate and about a 9% reject rate on zipcode digits provided by the U.S. Postal Service.
originalAbstract: We present an application of back-propagation networks to hand(cid:173) written digit recognition. Minimal preprocessing of the data was required, but architecture of the network was highly constrained and specifically designed for the task. The input of the network consists of normalized images of isolated digits. The method has 1 % error rate and about a 9% reject rate on zipcode digits provided by the U.S. Postal Service.

paragraphs: The paper applies a network trained by backpropagation to recognizing handwritten digits. Its inputs are normalized images containing individual digits. This defines the recognition problem clearly: the network receives an already isolated digit image and must determine which digit it represents.

The system requires little preprocessing, but its network architecture is strongly constrained and designed specifically for the task. That pairing is the central design choice. Task knowledge enters through the organization of the network, while learning adjusts its parameters from examples. The result illustrates how a carefully chosen architecture can accompany relatively modest preparation of the image data.

On ZIP code digits supplied by the U.S. Postal Service, the method reports a one percent error rate and approximately a nine percent rejection rate. Rejection means some inputs are left without an accepted classification, so both figures matter when judging the result. The reported performance combines successful digit recognition with the option to decline a decision on part of the input set.
summary.tldr: A task-specific backpropagation network recognizes isolated postal digits with a reported one percent error rate and roughly nine percent rejection rate.

title: Handwritten Digit Recognition with a Back-Propagation Network

abstract: We compare two strategies for training connectionist (as well as non(cid:173) connectionist) models for statistical pattern recognition. The probabilistic strat(cid:173) egy is based on the notion that Bayesian discrimination (i.e .• optimal classifica(cid:173) tion) is achieved when the classifier learns the a posteriori class distributions of the random feature vector. The differential strategy is based on the notion that the identity of the largest class a posteriori probability of the feature vector is all that is needed to achieve Bayesian discrimination. Each strategy is directly linked to a family of objective functions that can be used in the supervised training procedure. We prove that the probabilistic strategy - linked with error measure objective functions such as mean-squared-error and cross-entropy - typically used to train classifiers necessarily requires larger training sets and more complex classifier architectures than those needed to approximate the Bayesian discrim(cid:173) linked inant function. In contrast. we prove that the differential strategy - with classificationfigure-of-merit objective functions (CF'MmoIlO) [3] - requires the minimum classifier functional complexity and the fewest training examples necessary to approximate the Bayesian discriminant function with specified pre(cid:173) cision (measured in probability of error). We present our proofs in the context of a game of chance in which an unfair C-sided die is tossed repeatedly. We show that this rigged game of dice is a paradigm at the root of all statistical pattern recognition tasks. and demonstrate how a simple extension of the concept leads us to a general information-theoretic model of sample complexity for statistical pattern recognition.

paragraphs: This paper compares two goals for training a classifier. The probabilistic strategy learns the posterior probability of every class. The differential strategy focuses on identifying the class with the largest posterior probability, because that identity determines the optimal classification decision. The distinction concerns how much information the learner must recover to make a decision.

The authors connect each strategy to a family of training objectives. Probabilistic learning includes mean-squared error and cross-entropy, while differential learning uses classification figure-of-merit objectives. They prove that learning posterior distributions requires larger training sets and more complex classifiers than approximating the Bayesian decision function itself. Their differential strategy achieves the stated minimum requirements for a specified error-based precision.

The proofs use repeated throws of an unfair die with multiple sides. This game provides a way to separate estimating all outcome probabilities from determining which outcome is most likely. The authors extend that reasoning into an information-theoretic model of sample complexity for statistical pattern recognition, linking the information demanded by an objective to the resources needed to learn it.
summary.tldr: The paper proves resource advantages for learning the optimal class decision directly instead of estimating every class's posterior probability.

title: Shooting Craps in Search of an Optimal Strategy for Training Connectionist Pattern Classifiers

abstract: Two projection based feedforward network learning methods for model(cid:173) free regression problems are studied and compared in this paper: one is the popular back-propagation learning (BPL); the other is the projection pursuit learning (PPL). Unlike the totally parametric BPL method, the PPL non-parametrically estimates unknown nonlinear functions sequen(cid:173) tially (neuron-by-neuron and layer-by-Iayer) at each iteration while jointly estimating the interconnection weights. In terms of learning efficiency, both methods have comparable training speed when based on a Gauss(cid:173) Newton optimization algorithm while the PPL is more parsimonious. In terms of learning robustness toward noise outliers, the BPL is more sensi(cid:173) tive to the outliers.
originalAbstract: Two projection based feedforward network learning methods for model(cid:173) free regression problems are studied and compared in this paper: one is the popular back-propagation learning (BPL); the other is the projection pursuit learning (PPL). Unlike the totally parametric BPL method, the PPL non-parametrically estimates unknown nonlinear functions sequen(cid:173) tially (neuron-by-neuron and layer-by-Iayer) at each iteration while jointly estimating the interconnection weights. In terms of learning efficiency, both methods have comparable training speed when based on a Gauss(cid:173) Newton optimization algorithm while the PPL is more parsimonious. In terms of learning robustness toward noise outliers, the BPL is more sensi(cid:173) tive to the outliers.

paragraphs: The paper compares two ways to train feedforward networks for regression, where the goal is to predict numerical outputs without starting from a prescribed model of the underlying relationship. Both approaches build predictions using projections of the inputs, but they differ in how they learn the nonlinear transformations applied within the network.

Backpropagation learning uses a fully parametric formulation. Projection pursuit learning instead estimates unknown nonlinear functions nonparametrically, proceeding through neurons and layers in sequence at each iteration while also estimating connection weights. This gives the second approach flexibility in the shapes of its learned functions, rather than restricting learning to the parameters of a completely specified functional form.

With Gauss–Newton optimization, the two methods have comparable training speeds, while projection pursuit produces a more economical model. The comparison also finds backpropagation more sensitive to noise outliers. Together, these findings separate three considerations that can otherwise be conflated: computational speed, model economy, and robustness to unusual observations. Similar training speed does not imply similar behavior on the other two.
summary.tldr: Projection pursuit matches backpropagation’s training speed under Gauss–Newton optimization while producing more economical models and showing less sensitivity to outliers.

title: A Comparison of Projection Pursuit and Neural Network Regression Modeling

abstract: In this paper, a tree based neural network viz. MARS (Friedman, 1991) for the modelling of the yield strength of a steel rolling plate mill is described. The inputs to the time series model are temperature, strain, strain rate, and interpass time and the output is the corresponding yield stress. It is found that the MARS-based model reveals which variable's functional dependence is nonlinear, and significant. The results are compared with those obta.ined by using a Kalman filter based online tuning method and other classification methods, e.g. CART, C4 .5, Bayesian classification. It is found that the MARS-based method consistently outperforms the other methods.

paragraphs: This paper models yield stress in a steel plate rolling mill using MARS, described in the abstract as a tree-based neural network method. The time-series model receives temperature, strain, strain rate, and interpass time as inputs. Its output is the corresponding yield stress, connecting processing conditions with the material's mechanical response.

The model also reveals which input relationships are significant and which have nonlinear functional dependence. This matters because a useful process model can do more than return a prediction: it can show where changes in an input have a relationship to the output that cannot be captured by a simple linear dependence.

The authors compare the MARS model with a Kalman-filter-based online tuning method and classification approaches including CART, C4.5, and Bayesian classification. They report that MARS consistently performs better in those comparisons. The stated contribution therefore combines predictive modeling of the rolling process with information about the form and significance of the input-output relationships.
summary.tldr: A MARS model predicts steel yield stress and identifies significant nonlinear relationships, outperforming the compared methods.

title: Application of Neural Network Methodology to the Modelling of the Yield Strength in a Steel Rolling Plate Mill

abstract: A number of hybrid multilayer perceptron (MLP)/hidden Markov model (HMM:) speech recognition systems have been developed in recent years (Morgan and Bourlard. 1990). In this paper. we present a new MLP architecture and training algorithm which allows the modeling of context-dependent phonetic classes in a hybrid MLP/HMM: framework. The new training procedure smooths MLPs trained at different degrees of context dependence in order to obtain a robust estimate of the cootext-dependent probabilities. Tests with the DARPA Resomce Management database have shown substantial advantages of the context-dependent MLPs over earlier cootext(cid:173) independent MLPs. and have shown substantial advantages of this hybrid approach over a pure HMM approach.
originalAbstract: A number of hybrid multilayer perceptron (MLP)/hidden Markov model (HMM:) speech recognition systems have been developed in recent years (Morgan and Bourlard. 1990). In this paper. we present a new MLP architecture and training algorithm which allows the modeling of context-dependent phonetic classes in a hybrid MLP/HMM: framework. The new training procedure smooths MLPs trained at different degrees of context dependence in order to obtain a robust estimate of the cootext-dependent probabilities. Tests with the DARPA Resomce Management database have shown substantial advantages of the context-dependent MLPs over earlier cootext(cid:173) independent MLPs. and have shown substantial advantages of this hybrid approach over a pure HMM approach.

paragraphs: This paper improves phonetic modeling in speech recognition systems that combine a multilayer perceptron with a hidden Markov model. The central goal is to make phonetic class probabilities depend on context. This lets the model distinguish a sound's context-dependent forms within the same hybrid recognition framework, rather than assigning probabilities using context-independent classes alone.

The authors introduce both an MLP architecture and a training procedure for this purpose. Training smooths MLPs learned at different degrees of context dependence to obtain robust probability estimates. The approach therefore combines estimates with different levels of contextual specificity, making the relationship between detailed context and reliable estimation part of the learning method.

Tests on the DARPA Resource Management database show substantial advantages over earlier context-independent MLPs. The hybrid system also shows substantial advantages over a pure HMM approach. These results support two connected choices in the proposed system: representing phonetic context in the neural component and using that component within a hybrid speech recognizer.
summary.tldr: Smoothing neural phonetic models across context levels improves probability estimation and recognition in a hybrid MLP/HMM system.

title: Context-Dependent Multiple Distribution Phonetic Modeling with MLPs

abstract: In this paper, we derive classifiers which are winner-take-all (WTA) approximations to a Bayes classifier with Gaussian mixtures for class conditional densities. The derived classifiers include clustering based algorithms like LVQ and k-Means. We propose a constrained rank Gaussian mixtures model and derive a WTA algorithm for it. Our experiments with two speech classification tasks indicate that the constrained rank model and the WTA approximations improve the performance over the unconstrained models.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we derive classifiers which are winner-take-all (WTA) approximations to a Bayes classifier with Gaussian mixtures for class conditional densities. The derived classifiers include clustering based algorithms like LVQ and k-Means. We propose a constrained rank Gaussian mixtures model and derive a WTA algorithm for it. Our experiments with two speech classification tasks indicate that the constrained rank model and the WTA approximations improve the performance over the unconstrained models.

paragraphs: The paper connects probabilistic classification with clustering-based decision rules. It starts from a Bayes classifier whose distribution for each class is represented by a mixture of Gaussians. The authors then derive winner-take-all approximations, which use a winning component in place of the fuller mixture calculation. This provides a probabilistic route to simpler classifiers.

The derived family includes clustering approaches such as learning vector quantization and k-means. Relating these methods through a common starting point helps explain how cluster-based decisions can approximate decisions based on class probability models. The authors also propose a Gaussian mixture model with a rank constraint and derive a corresponding winner-take-all algorithm.

Experiments on two speech classification tasks indicate that the constrained model and the winner-take-all approximations improve performance over unconstrained models. In these tests, simplifying the decision procedure and restricting the model do not merely make it different; they improve classification. The result supports examining model structure and approximation together when designing a classifier.
summary.tldr: Winner-take-all approximations connect Gaussian-mixture classification to clustering and improve results on two speech tasks alongside a constrained-rank model.

title: Classifying with Gaussian Mixtures and Clusters

abstract: Infants' manipulative exploratory behavior within the environment is a vehicle of cognitive stimulation[McCall 1974]. During this time, infants practice and perfect sensorimotor patterns that become be(cid:173) havioral modules which will be seriated and imbedded in more com(cid:173) plex actions. This paper explores the development of such primitive learning systems using an embodied light-weight hand which will be used for a humanoid being developed at the MIT Artificial In(cid:173) telligence Laboratory[Brooks and Stein 1993]. Primitive grasping procedures are learned from sensory inputs using a connectionist reinforcement algorithm while two submodules preprocess sensory data to recognize the hardness of objects and detect shear using competitive learning and back-propagation algorithm strategies, respectively. This system is not only consistent and quick dur(cid:173) ing the initial learning stage, but also adaptable to new situations after training is completed.

paragraphs: The paper explores how a robotic hand can learn basic manipulation behaviors through sensory experience. Its motivation comes from infant exploration, where practiced sensorimotor patterns become components of more complex actions. The system uses an embodied lightweight hand intended for a humanoid, giving the learning process a physical manipulation setting.

A neural reinforcement learning algorithm learns primitive grasping procedures from sensory inputs. Two additional modules prepare sensory information for this process. One uses competitive learning to recognize object hardness, while the other uses backpropagation to detect shear. The architecture therefore connects learned sensory interpretation with learning how to act.

The reported system learns consistently and quickly during its initial training and remains adaptable to new situations afterward. This matters because the primitive behaviors are intended to function as reusable components of more elaborate actions. The contribution demonstrates an approach in which grasp learning and sensory preprocessing work together, with continued adaptability forming part of the stated outcome rather than learning ending permanently after initial training.
summary.tldr: A robotic hand combines reinforcement learning with learned sensory preprocessing to acquire adaptable grasping behaviors.

title: Primitive Manipulation Learning with Connectionism

abstract: We describe the use of modern analytical techniques in solving the dynamics of symmetric and nonsymmetric recurrent neural net(cid:173) works near saturation. These explicitly take into account the cor(cid:173) relations between the post-synaptic potentials, and thereby allow for a reliable prediction of transients.
originalAbstract: We describe the use of modern analytical techniques in solving the dynamics of symmetric and nonsymmetric recurrent neural net(cid:173) works near saturation. These explicitly take into account the cor(cid:173) relations between the post-synaptic potentials, and thereby allow for a reliable prediction of transients.

paragraphs: The paper describes analytical methods for understanding how recurrent neural networks evolve over time near saturation. It covers both symmetric and nonsymmetric networks, so its scope includes different relationships between reciprocal connections. The object of analysis is the network's dynamics, including the activity that occurs as its state changes.

The central methodological feature is explicit treatment of correlations between postsynaptic potentials. These are the input potentials received by neurons through their connections. Accounting for correlations means that relationships among these inputs enter the analysis, rather than being discarded when describing the network's behavior. This is the detail the authors identify as enabling reliable predictions.

The stated payoff is prediction of transients: the time-dependent behavior that occurs during the network's evolution. Such predictions describe the course of activity, beyond specifying an eventual state. The contribution is therefore an analytical account in which correlated neuronal inputs help determine temporal behavior. Its stated setting is networks near saturation, and the claimed reliability concerns transient predictions within that setting.
summary.tldr: Explicitly accounting for correlated postsynaptic potentials enables reliable transient predictions for recurrent networks near saturation.

title: Modern Analytic Techniques to Solve the Dynamics of Recurrent Neural Networks

abstract: While it is generally agreed that neurons transmit information about their synaptic inputs through spike trains, the code by which this information is transmitted is not well understood. An upper bound on the information encoded is obtained by hypothesizing that the precise timing of each spike conveys information. Here we develop a general approach to quantifying the information carried by spike trains under this hypothesis, and apply it to the leaky integrate-and-fire (IF) model of neuronal dynamics. We formulate the problem in terms of the probability distribution peT) of interspike intervals (ISIs), assuming that spikes are detected with arbitrary but finite temporal resolution . In the absence of added noise, all the variability in the ISIs could encode information, and the information rate is simply the entropy of the lSI distribution, H (T) = (-p(T) log2 p(T)}, times the spike rate. H (T) thus provides an exact expression for the information rate . The methods developed here can be used to determine experimentally the information carried by spike trains, even when the lower bound of the information rate provided by the stimulus reconstruction method is not tight. In a preliminary series of experiments, we have used these methods to estimate information rates of hippocampal neurons in slice in response to somatic current injection. These pilot experiments suggest information rates as high as 6.3 bits/spike.

paragraphs: This paper asks how much information a neuron can transmit if the precise timing of each spike carries meaning. That hypothesis provides an upper-bound perspective on neural information coding. The authors develop a general way to quantify this information and apply it to a leaky integrate-and-fire model.

The calculation uses the distribution of intervals between spikes, assuming that spike times are measured with arbitrary but finite temporal resolution. Without added noise, all variation in those intervals can potentially carry information. Under that condition, the entropy of the interval distribution gives information per spike, and multiplying by the spike rate gives information per unit time.

The approach also supports experimental estimates where stimulus-reconstruction methods yield an uninformative lower bound. Preliminary recordings from hippocampal neurons in slices, driven by current injected into the cell body, suggest values as high as 6.3 bits per spike. These pilot findings concern information available under the timing-based hypothesis, making the treatment of timing and noise central to their interpretation.
summary.tldr: An interspike-interval framework quantifies timing-based neural information, with pilot recordings suggesting up to 6.3 bits per spike.

title: Information through a Spiking Neuron

abstract: We describe the implementation of a hidden Markov model state decoding system, a component for a wordspotting speech recogni(cid:173) tion system. The key specification for this state decoder design is microwatt power dissipation; this requirement led to a continuous(cid:173) time, analog circuit implementation. We characterize the operation of a 10-word (81 state) state decoder test chip.
originalAbstract: We describe the implementation of a hidden Markov model state decoding system, a component for a wordspotting speech recogni(cid:173) tion system. The key specification for this state decoder design is microwatt power dissipation; this requirement led to a continuous(cid:173) time, analog circuit implementation. We characterize the operation of a 10-word (81 state) state decoder test chip.

paragraphs: Wordspotting seeks to identify target words within speech, and this paper addresses one component of such a system: decoding the states of a hidden Markov model. The decoder handles the model's state-based representation of the speech sequence. The contribution concerns implementing that computation in hardware under a stringent electrical power requirement.

The central design specification is power dissipation on the scale of microwatts. This requirement motivates a continuous-time analog circuit implementation. The choice of computational medium is therefore part of the solution: the authors organize state decoding around circuit behavior that operates continuously, with the power target guiding the hardware architecture.

The paper characterizes a test chip containing a decoder for 10 words represented by 81 states. This provides a concrete implementation at a stated vocabulary and state count. Its significance lies in bringing a speech-recognition computation into a hardware design centered on very low power. The reported work concerns the state decoder as a component, so its scope is the operation of that chip within the broader wordspotting task.
summary.tldr: The paper implements and characterizes a 10-word, 81-state analog HMM decoder designed around microwatt power dissipation.

title: A Micropower Analog VLSI HMM State Decoder for Wordspotting

abstract: The limitations of using self-organizing maps (SaM) for either clustering/vector quantization (VQ) or multidimensional scaling (MDS) are being discussed by reviewing recent empirical findings and the relevant theory. SaM 's remaining ability of doing both VQ and MDS at the same time is challenged by a new combined tech(cid:173) nique of online K-means clustering plus Sammon mapping of the cluster centroids. SaM are shown to perform significantly worse in terms of quantization error , in recovering the structure of the clus(cid:173) ters and in preserving the topology in a comprehensive empirical study using a series of multivariate normal clustering problems.
originalAbstract: The limitations of using self-organizing maps (SaM) for either clustering/vector quantization (VQ) or multidimensional scaling (MDS) are being discussed by reviewing recent empirical findings and the relevant theory. SaM 's remaining ability of doing both VQ and MDS at the same time is challenged by a new combined tech(cid:173) nique of online K-means clustering plus Sammon mapping of the cluster centroids. SaM are shown to perform significantly worse in terms of quantization error , in recovering the structure of the clus(cid:173) ters and in preserving the topology in a comprehensive empirical study using a series of multivariate normal clustering problems.

paragraphs: This paper examines self-organizing maps as tools for two related tasks: representing data through clusters or representative vectors, and arranging data to display its structure. It reviews empirical findings and relevant theory about their limitations. The broader question is whether one map performs both jobs well enough to justify combining them in a single method.

The authors introduce an alternative that pairs online K-means clustering with Sammon mapping of the cluster centers. This separates the construction of representative groups from the arrangement of those representatives. The combined technique directly challenges the argument that self-organizing maps retain a special advantage because they perform vector quantization and multidimensional scaling together.

A comprehensive empirical study uses a series of clustering problems based on multivariate normal distributions. In those comparisons, self-organizing maps perform significantly worse in quantization error, recovery of cluster structure, and preservation of topology. The results concern both accurate representation and faithful organization of the data. They support the proposed combination as a stronger approach on the studied problems.
summary.tldr: Online K-means followed by Sammon mapping outperforms self-organizing maps on the studied clustering and structure-preservation tasks.

title: Limitations of Self-organizing Maps for Vector Quantization and Multidimensional Scaling

abstract: The generalization ability of a neural network can sometimes be improved dramatically by regularization. To analyze the improve(cid:173) ment one needs more refined results than the asymptotic distri(cid:173) bution of the weight vector. Here we study the simple case of one-dimensional linear regression under quadratic regularization, i.e., ridge regression. We study the random design, misspecified case, where we derive expansions for the optimal regularization pa(cid:173) rameter and the ensuing improvement. It is possible to construct examples where it is best to use no regularization.

To analyze the improve(cid:173) ment one needs more refined results than the asymptotic distri(cid:173) bution of the weight vector. Here we study the simple case of one-dimensional linear regression under quadratic regularization, i.e., ridge regression. We study the random design, misspecified case, where we derive expansions for the optimal regularization pa(cid:173) rameter and the ensuing improvement. It is possible to construct examples where it is best to use no regularization.

paragraphs: Regularization discourages large fitted weights and can improve predictions on unseen data. This paper asks how to analyze that improvement precisely, using one-dimensional linear regression with a quadratic penalty, also called ridge regression. The deliberately simple setting makes it possible to study the strength of the penalty and its consequences mathematically.

The analysis treats the inputs as random and allows the fitted linear model to be misspecified, meaning that the underlying relationship need not belong to the chosen model family. The authors derive asymptotic expansions for the optimal regularization parameter and the improvement it produces. Such expansions describe behavior as the amount of data grows, retaining detail needed to distinguish regularized from unregularized fitting.

The paper argues that the asymptotic distribution of the fitted weight alone is insufficient for assessing these benefits. It also constructs examples in which the best choice is no regularization. The result makes the value of regularization a question about the statistical setting, rather than an automatic consequence of adding a penalty.
summary.tldr: A refined analysis of one-dimensional ridge regression characterizes optimal regularization and shows that no penalty can sometimes be best.

title: Asymptotic Theory for Regularization: One-Dimensional Linear Case

abstract: We study the approximation of functions by two-layer feedforward neural networks, focusing on incremental algorithms which greedily add units, estimating single unit parameters at each stage . As opposed to standard algorithms for fixed architectures, the optimization at each stage is performed over a small number of parameters, mitigating many of the difficult numerical problems inherent in high-dimensional non-linear optimization. We establish upper bounds on the error incurred by the algorithm, when approximating functions from the Sobolev class, thereby extending previous results which only provided rates of convergence for functions in certain convex hulls of functional spaces. By comparing our results to recently derived lower bounds, we show that the greedy algorithms are nearly optimal. Combined with estimation error results for greedy algorithms, a strong case can be made for this type of approach.
originalAbstract: We study the approximation of functions by two-layer feedforward neural networks, focusing on incremental algorithms which greedily add units, estimating single unit parameters at each stage . As opposed to standard algorithms for fixed architectures, the optimization at each stage is performed over a small number of parameters, mitigating many of the difficult numerical problems inherent in high-dimensional non-linear optimization. We establish upper bounds on the error incurred by the algorithm, when approximating functions from the Sobolev class, thereby extending previous results which only provided rates of convergence for functions in certain convex hulls of functional spaces. By comparing our results to recently derived lower bounds, we show that the greedy algorithms are nearly optimal. Combined with estimation error results for greedy algorithms, a strong case can be made for this type of approach.

paragraphs: The paper studies how well two-layer feedforward networks approximate functions when built incrementally. The algorithms greedily add units, estimating the parameters of one unit at each stage. Each optimization therefore involves relatively few parameters, mitigating numerical difficulties that arise when optimizing a large fixed architecture through a high-dimensional nonlinear problem.

The authors establish upper bounds on approximation error for functions in a Sobolev class. This extends earlier convergence-rate results that applied to functions in certain convex hulls of function spaces. The bounds quantify the accuracy obtainable through the incremental procedure for the function class under study, giving theoretical support to a computationally simpler construction strategy.

Comparing these upper bounds with recently derived lower bounds shows that the greedy algorithms are nearly optimal in the analyzed setting. The claim concerns approximation performance relative to those bounds, with the function-class qualification remaining essential. Together with estimation-error results for greedy algorithms, the analysis makes a strong case for incremental network construction as an approach that combines manageable optimization steps with favorable theoretical accuracy.
summary.tldr: Error bounds show that greedy unit-by-unit construction of two-layer networks is nearly optimal for the analyzed Sobolev function class.

title: On the Optimality of Incremental Neural Network Algorithms

abstract: In the analysis of data recorded by optical imaging from intrinsic signals (measurement of changes of light reflectance from cortical tissue) the re(cid:173) moval of noise and artifacts such as blood vessel patterns is a serious problem. Often bandpass filtering is used, but the underlying assumption that a spatial frequency exists, which separates the mapping component from other components (especially the global signal), is questionable. Here we propose alternative ways of processing optical imaging data, us(cid:173) ing blind source separation techniques based on the spatial decorre1ation of the data. We first perform benchmarks on artificial data in order to select the way of processing, which is most robust with respect to sen(cid:173) sor noise. We then apply it to recordings of optical imaging experiments from macaque primary visual cortex. We show that our BSS technique is able to extract ocular dominance and orientation preference maps from single condition stacks, for data, where standard post-processing pro(cid:173) cedures fail. Artifacts, especially blood vessel patterns, can often be completely removed from the maps. In summary, our method for blind source separation using extended spatial decorrelation is a superior tech(cid:173) nique for the analysis of optical recording data.

Often bandpass filtering is used, but the underlying assumption that a spatial frequency exists, which separates the mapping component from other components (especially the global signal), is questionable. Here we propose alternative ways of processing optical imaging data, us(cid:173) ing blind source separation techniques based on the spatial decorre1ation of the data. We first perform benchmarks on artificial data in order to select the way of processing, which is most robust with respect to sen(cid:173) sor noise. We then apply it to recordings of optical imaging experiments from macaque primary visual cortex. We show that our BSS technique is able to extract ocular dominance and orientation preference maps from single condition stacks, for data, where standard post-processing pro(cid:173) cedures fail. Artifacts, especially blood vessel patterns, can often be completely removed from the maps. In summary, our method for blind source separation using extended spatial decorrelation is a superior tech(cid:173) nique for the analysis of optical recording data.

paragraphs: Optical recordings of brain activity measure changes in light reflected from cortical tissue, but useful spatial maps can be obscured by noise, global signals, and blood vessel patterns. This paper questions the assumption behind ordinary bandpass filtering: that a spatial frequency boundary can separate the desired mapping signal from other components.

The authors instead investigate blind source separation based on spatial decorrelation. They first compare processing approaches on artificial data to select one that is most robust to sensor noise. They then apply the selected approach to optical recordings from macaque primary visual cortex, moving from a controlled comparison to actual brain imaging data.

The method extracts ocular dominance and orientation preference maps from single-condition stacks in cases where standard post-processing fails. Blood vessel patterns and other artifacts can often be removed completely from the resulting maps. These findings support the authors' claim that extended spatial decorrelation offers an improved analysis technique for the recordings studied, without making complete artifact removal a universal outcome.
summary.tldr: Spatial-decorrelation-based source separation recovers cortical maps from optical recordings where standard processing fails and often removes vessel artifacts.

title: Application of Blind Separation of Sources to Optical Recording of Brain Activity

abstract: We introduce an information theoretic method for nonparametric, nonlinear dimensionality reduction, based on the infinite cluster limit of rate distortion theory. By constraining the information available to manifold coordinates, a natural probabilistic map emerges that assigns original data to corresponding points on a lower dimensional manifold. With only the information-distortion trade off as a parameter, our method determines the shape of the manifold, its dimensionality, the probabilistic map and the prior that provide optimal description of the data.
originalAbstract: We introduce an information theoretic method for nonparametric, nonlinear dimensionality reduction, based on the infinite cluster limit of rate distortion theory. By constraining the information available to manifold coordinates, a natural probabilistic map emerges that assigns original data to corresponding points on a lower dimensional manifold. With only the information-distortion trade off as a parameter, our method determines the shape of the manifold, its dimensionality, the probabilistic map and the prior that provide optimal description of the data.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a method for describing data on a lower-dimensional manifold using an information-theoretic objective. The dimensionality reduction is nonlinear and nonparametric. Its foundation is the infinite-cluster limit of rate-distortion theory, which frames representation as a tradeoff between the information retained and the distortion introduced.

The method constrains how much information is available to the manifold coordinates. Under that constraint, a probabilistic mapping emerges from the original data to points on the lower-dimensional manifold. The mapping is therefore part of the optimized description, and assignments to the manifold are expressed probabilistically.

The information-distortion tradeoff is the method's only parameter. Within that formulation, the method determines the manifold's shape and dimensionality, the probabilistic map, and the prior that together give an optimal description of the data. The significance is that these choices are coupled by one objective. Optimality refers to this information-theoretic description, tying the chosen representation to an explicit balance between information and distortion.
summary.tldr: An information-distortion objective jointly determines a nonlinear manifold, its dimensionality, and a probabilistic mapping of data onto it.

title: Optimal Manifold Representation of Data: An Information Theoretic Approach

abstract: Many neural areas, notably, the hippocampus, show structured, dynamical, population behavior such as coordinated oscillations. It has long been observed that such oscillations provide a substrate for representing analog information in the firing phases of neurons relative to the underlying population rhythm. However, it has become increasingly clear that it is essential for neural populations to represent uncertainty about the information they capture, and the substantial recent work on neural codes for uncertainty has omitted any analysis of oscillatory systems. Here, we observe that, since neurons in an oscillatory network need not only fire once in each cycle (or even at all), uncertainty about the analog quantities each neuron represents by its firing phase might naturally be reported through the degree of concentration of the spikes that it fires. We apply this theory to memory in a model of oscillatory associative recall in hippocampal area CA3. Although it is not well treated in the literature, representing and manipulating uncertainty is fundamental to competent memory; our theory enables us to view CA3 as an effective uncertainty-aware, retrieval system.

paragraphs: Coordinated neural oscillations provide a timing reference against which a neuron's firing phase can represent an analog quantity. This paper asks how such a representation could also express uncertainty. A remembered value is more useful when a system can distinguish a precise estimate from one supported only weakly.

The proposed idea uses the fact that a neuron need not fire exactly once during each oscillation cycle: it can fire several times or remain silent. The degree to which its spikes concentrate around a phase could report uncertainty about the represented quantity. This links information in spike timing to a possible representation of confidence within the same oscillatory system.

The authors apply the theory to a model of oscillatory associative memory recall in hippocampal area CA3. Within that model, the theory supports viewing retrieval as a process that represents and manipulates uncertainty as well as recalling content. The contribution is a proposed coding account and its application to a memory model; the abstract presents phase concentration as a possible mechanism rather than an established biological measurement rule.
summary.tldr: A theory proposes that spike-phase concentration could encode uncertainty during oscillatory hippocampal memory recall.

title: Uncertainty, phase and oscillatory hippocampal recall

abstract: Many researchers have suggested that the psychological complexity of a concept is related to the length of its representation in a language of thought. As yet, however, there are few concrete proposals about the nature of this language. This paper makes one such proposal: the language of thought allows first order quantification (quantification over objects) more readily than second-order quantification (quantification over features). To support this proposal we present behavioral results from a concept learning study inspired by the work of Shepard, Hovland and Jenkins."

This paper makes one such proposal: the language of thought allows first order quantification (quantification over objects) more readily than second-order quantification (quantification over features). To support this proposal we present behavioral results from a concept learning study inspired by the work of Shepard, Hovland and Jenkins."

paragraphs: One proposal in cognitive science connects the difficulty of a concept with the length of its internal description. For that proposal to explain learning, however, the mental language in which descriptions are written must have some specified structure. This paper offers a concrete hypothesis about one aspect of that language.

The proposed distinction concerns quantification. First-order quantification ranges over objects, whereas second-order quantification ranges over features. The authors suggest that the language of thought supports the first kind more readily than the second. This is a claim about relative accessibility in mental representation, not a claim that people cannot reason about features.

The authors present behavioral evidence from a concept-learning study to support the proposal. Its importance lies in making the description-length view more specific: the ease of expressing a concept depends on which representational operations are readily available, as well as on description length. The study therefore supplies evidence for a particular property of the proposed mental language rather than a complete characterization of that language.
summary.tldr: A concept-learning study supports the proposal that mental representations permit quantification over objects more readily than over features.

title: Quantification and the language of thought

abstract: Recently, Mahoney and Orecchia demonstrated that popular diffusion-based procedures to compute a quick approximation to the first nontrivial eigenvector of a data graph Laplacian exactly solve certain regularized Semi-Definite Programs (SDPs). In this paper, we extend that result by providing a statistical interpretation of their approximation procedure. Our interpretation will be analogous to the manner in which l2-regularized or l1-regularized l2 regression (often called Ridge regression and Lasso regression, respectively) can be interpreted in terms of a Gaussian prior or a Laplace prior, respectively, on the coefficient vector of the regression problem. Our framework will imply that the solutions to the Mahoney-Orecchia regularized SDP can be interpreted as regularized estimates of the pseudoinverse of the graph Laplacian. Conversely, it will imply that the solution to this regularized estimation problem can be computed very quickly by running, e.g., the fast diffusion-based PageRank procedure for computing an approximation to the first nontrivial eigenvector of the graph Laplacian. Empirical results are also provided to illustrate the manner in which approximate eigenvector computation implicitly performs statistical regularization, relative to running the corresponding exact algorithm.

paragraphs: Fast diffusion procedures can approximate a graph Laplacian's first nontrivial eigenvector. Earlier work showed that certain such approximations exactly solve regularized semidefinite programs. This paper gives that connection a statistical interpretation, asking what kind of estimation the fast numerical procedure is implicitly performing.

The interpretation parallels the connection between regression penalties and probability priors: Ridge and Lasso can be understood through Gaussian and Laplace priors. Here, solutions of the regularized semidefinite program become regularized estimates of the graph Laplacian's pseudoinverse. This links an approximate spectral computation to a statistical estimation target.

The connection also works computationally in the other direction. The corresponding regularized estimation problem can be solved quickly using diffusion procedures such as PageRank. Empirical results illustrate how approximate eigenvector computation introduces statistical regularization relative to the corresponding exact algorithm. The contribution is thus an explanation of the statistical effect of approximation, together with a fast route to the associated estimation problem.
summary.tldr: Fast diffusion-based eigenvector approximations can be interpreted as regularized statistical estimates of a graph Laplacian's pseudoinverse.

title: Regularized Laplacian Estimation and Fast Eigenvector Approximation

abstract: Modelling natural images with sparse coding (SC) has faced two main challenges: ﬂexibly representing varying pixel intensities and realistically representing low- level image components. This paper proposes a novel multiple-cause generative model of low-level image statistics that generalizes the standard SC model in two crucial points: (1) it uses a spike-and-slab prior distribution for a more realistic representation of component absence/intensity, and (2) the model uses the highly nonlinear combination rule of maximal causes analysis (MCA) instead of a lin- ear combination. The major challenge is parameter optimization because a model with either (1) or (2) results in strongly multimodal posteriors. We show for the ﬁrst time that a model combining both improvements can be trained efﬁciently while retaining the rich structure of the posteriors. We design an exact piece- wise Gibbs sampling method and combine this with a variational method based on preselection of latent dimensions. This combined training scheme tackles both analytical and computational intractability and enables application of the model to a large number of observed and hidden dimensions. Applying the model to image patches we study the optimal encoding of images by simple cells in V1 and compare the model’s predictions with in vivo neural recordings. In contrast to standard SC, we ﬁnd that the optimal prior favors asymmetric and bimodal ac- tivity of simple cells. Testing our model for consistency we ﬁnd that the average posterior is approximately equal to the prior. Furthermore, we ﬁnd that the model predicts a high percentage of globular receptive ﬁelds alongside Gabor-like ﬁelds. Similarly high percentages are observed in vivo. Our results thus argue in favor of improvements of the standard sparse coding model for simple cells by using ﬂexible priors and nonlinear combinations.

paragraphs: This paper modifies sparse coding to represent both the absence and intensity of image components more flexibly. It combines a spike-and-slab prior with the nonlinear combination rule of maximal causes analysis. These changes address how individual components are represented and how multiple components jointly generate an image.

Combining the changes creates difficult, strongly multimodal posterior distributions. The authors develop an exact piecewise Gibbs sampler and combine it with a variational method that preselects latent dimensions. This training scheme addresses analytical and computational difficulties while retaining rich posterior structure, enabling models with many observed and hidden dimensions.

summary.tldr: Efficient inference enables a nonlinear spike-and-slab image model whose predicted activity and receptive fields support a richer sparse-coding account of V1.

title: Why MCA? Nonlinear sparse coding with spike-and-slab prior for neurally plausible image encoding

abstract: Cross-region dynamic connectivity, which describes spatio-temporal dependence of neural activity among multiple brain regions of interest (ROIs), can provide important information for understanding cognition. For estimating such connectivity, magnetoencephalography (MEG) and electroencephalography (EEG) are well-suited tools because of their millisecond temporal resolution. However, localizing source activity in the brain requires solving an under-determined linear problem. In typical two-step approaches, researchers first solve the linear problem with general priors assuming independence across ROIs, and secondly quantify cross-region connectivity. In this work, we propose a one-step state-space model to improve estimation of dynamic connectivity. The model treats the mean activity in individual ROIs as the state variable, and describes non-stationary dynamic dependence across ROIs using time-varying auto-regression. Compared with a two-step method, which first obtains the commonly used minimum-norm estimates of source activity, and then fits the auto-regressive model, our state-space model yielded smaller estimation errors on simulated data where the model assumptions held. When applied on empirical MEG data from one participant in a scene-processing experiment, our state-space model also demonstrated intriguing preliminary results, indicating leading and lagged linear dependence between the early visual cortex and a higher-level scene-sensitive region, which could reflect feed-forward and feedback information flow within the visual cortex during scene processing.

paragraphs: MEG and EEG measure brain activity with millisecond timing, making them useful for studying how brain regions interact over time. However, reconstructing activity inside the brain from these measurements is underdetermined: the observations do not uniquely specify the underlying sources. A common approach first estimates each region's activity using independence assumptions, then analyzes relationships between the reconstructed signals.

This paper combines those stages in a state-space model. Average activity within each region becomes an internal state, while time-varying autoregression describes how regional activities depend on earlier activity across regions. This lets source estimation and changing connectivity participate in the same model, rather than estimating sources under assumptions that separate the regions before examining their dependence.

In simulations satisfying its assumptions, the model produced smaller estimation errors than minimum-norm source reconstruction followed by autoregression. Results from one participant's scene-processing MEG data were preliminary: they suggested leading and lagged linear relationships between early visual cortex and a scene-sensitive region. Those relationships could reflect forward and feedback information flow, rather than establishing that interpretation conclusively.
summary.tldr: A joint state-space model improves connectivity estimates in simulations satisfying its assumptions and offers preliminary evidence of changing visual-region dependencies.

title: A state-space model of cross-region dynamic connectivity in MEG/EEG

abstract: We consider the problem of optimization from samples of monotone submodular functions with bounded curvature. In numerous applications, the function optimized is not known a priori, but instead learned from data. What are the guarantees we have when optimizing functions from sampled data? In this paper we show that for any monotone submodular function with curvature c there is a (1 - c)/(1 + c - c^2) approximation algorithm for maximization under cardinality constraints when polynomially-many samples are drawn from the uniform distribution over feasible sets. Moreover, we show that this algorithm is optimal. That is, for any c < 1, there exists a submodular function with curvature c for which no algorithm can achieve a better approximation. The curvature assumption is crucial as for general monotone submodular functions no algorithm can obtain a constant-factor approximation for maximization under a cardinality constraint when observing polynomially-many samples drawn from any distribution over feasible sets, even when the function is statistically learnable.

In numerous applications, the function optimized is not known a priori, but instead learned from data. What are the guarantees we have when optimizing functions from sampled data? In this paper we show that for any monotone submodular function with curvature c there is a (1 - c)/(1 + c - c^2) approximation algorithm for maximization under cardinality constraints when polynomially-many samples are drawn from the uniform distribution over feasible sets. Moreover, we show that this algorithm is optimal. That is, for any c < 1, there exists a submodular function with curvature c for which no algorithm can achieve a better approximation. The curvature assumption is crucial as for general monotone submodular functions no algorithm can obtain a constant-factor approximation for maximization under a cardinality constraint when observing polynomially-many samples drawn from any distribution over feasible sets, even when the function is statistically learnable.

paragraphs: This paper studies optimization when the objective function is available through sampled data. The setting involves monotone submodular functions, a limit on the number of selected elements, and a curvature parameter c. The question is how closely an algorithm can approach the best feasible value using only polynomially many samples.

For samples drawn uniformly from feasible sets, the authors give an approximation ratio of (1−c)/(1+c−c²). They also prove a matching impossibility result: for every c below one, some function with that curvature prevents any algorithm from obtaining a better approximation. Thus, the guarantee captures an optimal worst-case tradeoff for the stated sampling setting.

The curvature assumption is decisive. For general monotone submodular functions, polynomially many samples cannot guarantee a constant-factor approximation under a cardinality constraint, even when samples may come from any distribution over feasible sets. This remains true even when the function is statistically learnable. The result separates learning a function from having enough information to optimize it: success at the former does not necessarily deliver the latter.
summary.tldr: Bounded curvature enables an optimal approximation guarantee for submodular optimization from samples, while statistical learnability alone does not ensure useful optimization.

title: The Power of Optimization from Samples

abstract: Low-rank matrix approximation (LRMA) methods have achieved excellent accuracy among today's collaborative filtering (CF) methods. In existing LRMA methods, the rank of user/item feature matrices is typically fixed, i.e., the same rank is adopted to describe all users/items. However, our studies show that submatrices with different ranks could coexist in the same user-item rating matrix, so that approximations with fixed ranks cannot perfectly describe the internal structures of the rating matrix, therefore leading to inferior recommendation accuracy. In this paper, a mixture-rank matrix approximation (MRMA) method is proposed, in which user-item ratings can be characterized by a mixture of LRMA models with different ranks. Meanwhile, a learning algorithm capitalizing on iterated condition modes is proposed to tackle the non-convex optimization problem pertaining to MRMA. Experimental studies on MovieLens and Netflix datasets demonstrate that MRMA can outperform six state-of-the-art LRMA-based CF methods in terms of recommendation accuracy.

paragraphs: Collaborative filtering often approximates a user-item rating matrix with low-rank models, representing users and items through a limited number of features. Standard approaches typically use the same rank throughout. The authors' studies indicate that different submatrices can have different ranks, suggesting that a single shared rank may miss important internal structure.

The proposed mixture-rank matrix approximation represents ratings using a mixture of low-rank models with different ranks. This gives the overall model a way to express multiple levels of structural complexity within one rating matrix. To fit it, the authors develop a learning algorithm based on iterated condition modes for the resulting nonconvex optimization problem.

Experiments on MovieLens and Netflix show that the proposed method can exceed the recommendation accuracy of six state-of-the-art low-rank collaborative filtering methods. The finding supports adapting representation complexity to variation within the ratings. It provides empirical evidence for the mixture approach on these datasets, rather than establishing that every rating matrix requires models of multiple ranks.
summary.tldr: Mixing matrix models of different ranks improves recommendation accuracy by accommodating varying structure within user-item ratings.

title: Mixture-Rank Matrix Approximation for Collaborative Filtering

abstract: The sparse matrix estimation problem consists of estimating the distribution of an $n\times n$ matrix $Y$, from a sparsely observed single instance of this matrix where the entries of $Y$ are independent random variables. This captures a wide array of problems; special instances include matrix completion in the context of recommendation systems, graphon estimation, and community detection in (mixed membership) stochastic block models. Inspired by classical collaborative filtering for recommendation systems, we propose a novel iterative, collaborative filtering-style algorithm for matrix estimation in this generic setting. We show that the mean squared error (MSE) of our estimator converges to $0$ at the rate of $O(d^2 (pn)^{-2/5})$ as long as $\omega(d^5 n)$ random entries from a total of $n^2$ entries of $Y$ are observed (uniformly sampled), $\E[Y]$ has rank $d$, and the entries of $Y$ have bounded support. The maximum squared error across all entries converges to $0$ with high probability as long as we observe a little more, $\Omega(d^5 n \ln^5(n))$ entries. Our results are the best known sample complexity results in this generality.

This captures a wide array of problems; special instances include matrix completion in the context of recommendation systems, graphon estimation, and community detection in (mixed membership) stochastic block models. Inspired by classical collaborative filtering for recommendation systems, we propose a novel iterative, collaborative filtering-style algorithm for matrix estimation in this generic setting. We show that the mean squared error (MSE) of our estimator converges to $0$ at the rate of $O(d^2 (pn)^{-2/5})$ as long as $\omega(d^5 n)$ random entries from a total of $n^2$ entries of $Y$ are observed (uniformly sampled), $\E[Y]$ has rank $d$, and the entries of $Y$ have bounded support. paragraphs: The paper considers estimating a random matrix’s distribution from a single, sparsely observed realization. Its framework includes recommendation-system matrix completion, graphon estimation, and community detection. The authors propose an iterative algorithm inspired by collaborative filtering, applying that style of estimation across this broader collection of matrix problems.

The guarantees assume independent, bounded entries, uniformly sampled observations, and an expected matrix of rank d. Under these assumptions, mean squared error decreases at rate O(d²(pn)^(-2/5)), provided the observation count grows faster than d⁵n. The result links estimation accuracy to sparsity and the rank of the expected matrix, rather than requiring all n² entries to be observed.

A stronger requirement addresses the largest squared error among individual entries. With Ω(d⁵n ln⁵(n)) observations, that maximum error converges to zero with high probability. This separates average accuracy from a guarantee protecting every entry, with the latter requiring more observations. The authors describe their sample-complexity results as the best known at this level of generality, encompassing the different applications within one analysis.
summary.tldr: An iterative collaborative-filtering estimator achieves vanishing matrix-estimation error from sparse observations under stated rank, sampling, and boundedness assumptions.

title: Thy Friend is My Friend: Iterative Collaborative Filtering for Sparse Matrix Estimation

abstract: We propose a new technique, Singular Vector Canonical Correlation Analysis (SVCCA), a tool for quickly comparing two representations in a way that is both invariant to affine transform (allowing comparison between different layers and networks) and fast to compute (allowing more comparisons to be calculated than with previous methods). We deploy this tool to measure the intrinsic dimensionality of layers, showing in some cases needless over-parameterization; to probe learning dynamics throughout training, finding that networks converge to final representations from the bottom up; to show where class-specific information in networks is formed; and to suggest new training regimes that simultaneously save computation and overfit less.

We deploy this tool to measure the intrinsic dimensionality of layers, showing in some cases needless over-parameterization; to probe learning dynamics throughout training, finding that networks converge to final representations from the bottom up; to show where class-specific information in networks is formed; and to suggest new training regimes that simultaneously save computation and overfit less.

paragraphs: Understanding a neural network requires comparing the representations it learns across layers, networks, or stages of training. SVCCA provides a fast way to make those comparisons while remaining invariant to affine transformations. This allows representations to be compared even when their coordinate descriptions differ, making similarity less dependent on the particular form of their encoding.

The authors use the method to estimate the intrinsic dimensionality of layers and find unnecessary over-parameterization in some cases. They also track representation changes during training, observing that convergence toward final representations proceeds from lower layers upward. Another application examines where information specific to individual classes emerges within a network.

These analyses suggest training regimes that save computation and reduce overfitting. The paper's contribution combines a comparison tool with examples of what such comparisons can reveal about learning. Its speed permits more comparisons than previous methods, while its invariance makes comparisons across different layers and networks meaningful. The reported findings connect representation analysis to both interpretation and changes in training practice.
summary.tldr: SVCCA efficiently compares neural representations, revealing excess dimensionality, bottom-up convergence, and opportunities to improve training.

title: SVCCA: Singular Vector Canonical Correlation Analysis for Deep Learning Dynamics and Interpretability

abstract: Recent work has developed methods for learning deep network classifiers that are \emph{provably} robust to norm-bounded adversarial perturbation; however, these methods are currently only possible for relatively small feedforward networks. In this paper, in an effort to scale these approaches to substantially larger models, we extend previous work in three main directly. First, we present a technique for extending these training procedures to much more general networks, with skip connections (such as ResNets) and general nonlinearities; the approach is fully modular, and can be implemented automatically analogously to automatic differentiation. Second, in the specific case of $\ell_\infty$ adversarial perturbations and networks with ReLU nonlinearities, we adopt a nonlinear random projection for training, which scales \emph{linearly} in the number of hidden units (previous approached scaled quadratically). Third, we show how to further improve robust error through cascade models. On both MNIST and CIFAR data sets, we train classifiers that improve substantially on the state of the art in provable robust adversarial error bounds: from 5.8% to 3.1% on MNIST (with $\ell_\infty$ perturbations of $\epsilon=0.1$), and from 80% to 36.4% on CIFAR (with $\ell_\infty$ perturbations of $\epsilon=2/255$).

In this paper, in an effort to scale these approaches to substantially larger models, we extend previous work in three main directly. First, we present a technique for extending these training procedures to much more general networks, with skip connections (such as ResNets) and general nonlinearities; the approach is fully modular, and can be implemented automatically analogously to automatic differentiation. Second, in the specific case of $\ell_\infty$ adversarial perturbations and networks with ReLU nonlinearities, we adopt a nonlinear random projection for training, which scales \emph{linearly} in the number of hidden units (previous approached scaled quadratically). Third, we show how to further improve robust error through cascade models. On both MNIST and CIFAR data sets, we train classifiers that improve substantially on the state of the art in provable robust adversarial error bounds: from 5.8% to 3.1% on MNIST (with $\ell_\infty$ perturbations of $\epsilon=0.1$), and from 80% to 36.4% on CIFAR (with $\ell_\infty$ perturbations of $\epsilon=2/255$).

It first extends existing procedures to architectures with skip connections and general nonlinearities through a modular construction that can be automated similarly to automatic differentiation.

For ReLU networks under perturbations bounded in the infinity norm, the authors introduce a nonlinear random projection used during training. Its scaling is linear in the number of hidden units, improving on the previous quadratic scaling. They also use cascade models to further reduce robust error, combining architectural flexibility, computational improvements, and stronger reported bounds.

On MNIST, the reported provable robust error bound improves from 5.8% to 3.1% at a perturbation budget of 0.1. On CIFAR, it improves from 80% to 36.4% at a budget of 2/255. These are guarantees for the specified infinity-norm settings. The results show substantial improvements in certified performance while extending the training approach toward larger and more general networks.
summary.tldr: Modular robustness training, random projections, and cascades scale provable defenses and improve certified error bounds on MNIST and CIFAR.

title: Scaling provable adversarial defenses

abstract: Various 3D semantic attributes such as segmentation masks, geometric features, keypoints, and materials can be encoded as per-point probe functions on 3D geometries. Given a collection of related 3D shapes, we consider how to jointly analyze such probe functions over different shapes, and how to discover common latent structures using a neural network — even in the absence of any correspondence information. Our network is trained on point cloud representations of shape geometry and associated semantic functions on that point cloud. These functions express a shared semantic understanding of the shapes but are not coordinated in any way. For example, in a segmentation task, the functions can be indicator functions of arbitrary sets of shape parts, with the particular combination involved not known to the network. Our network is able to produce a small dictionary of basis functions for each shape, a dictionary whose span includes the semantic functions provided for that shape. Even though our shapes have independent discretizations and no functional correspondences are provided, the network is able to generate latent bases, in a consistent order, that reflect the shared semantic structure among the shapes. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our technique in various segmentation and keypoint selection applications.

The paper asks whether a neural network can discover shared semantic structure across related shapes when their points and supplied functions have no provided correspondence.

The network receives point clouds together with semantic functions defined on them. Those functions share meaning across the collection but need not use coordinated annotations. For example, a function can mark an arbitrary collection of shape parts without telling the network which combination it represents. The network produces a compact dictionary of basis functions whose combinations can represent the supplied functions.

The striking result is that the learned bases appear in a consistent order across shapes despite their independent point representations. This makes the dictionaries a shared semantic representation without requiring explicit matching information during training. Applications to segmentation and keypoint selection demonstrate that the recovered structure can support concrete shape-analysis tasks.
summary.tldr: A neural network learns consistently ordered semantic dictionaries across 3D shapes without supplied correspondences.

title: Deep Functional Dictionaries: Learning Consistent Semantic Structures on 3D Models from Functions

abstract: Deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are powerful tools for a wide range of vision tasks, but the enormous amount of memory and compute resources required by CNNs poses a challenge in deploying them on constrained devices. Existing compression techniques, while excelling at reducing model sizes, struggle to be computationally friendly. In this paper, we attend to the statistical properties of sparse CNNs and present focused quantization, a novel quantization strategy based on power-of-two values, which exploits the weight distributions after fine-grained pruning. The proposed method dynamically discovers the most effective numerical representation for weights in layers with varying sparsities, significantly reducing model sizes. Multiplications in quantized CNNs are replaced with much cheaper bit-shift operations for efficient inference. Coupled with lossless encoding, we build a compression pipeline that provides CNNs with high compression ratios (CR), low computation cost and minimal loss in accuracies. In ResNet-50, we achieved a 18.08x CR with only 0.24% loss in top-5 accuracy, outperforming existing compression methods. We fully compress a ResNet-18 and found that it is not only higher in CR and top-5 accuracy, but also more hardware efficient as it requires fewer logic gates to implement when compared to other state-of-the-art quantization methods assuming the same throughput.

This paper addresses both storage and arithmetic by examining the weight distributions that remain after fine-grained pruning. Its focused quantization strategy adapts the numerical representation of weights to layers with different levels of sparsity, using power-of-two values.

Power-of-two weights allow multiplication to be replaced by cheaper bit shifts. The authors combine this quantization with lossless encoding to form a compression pipeline intended to reduce model size and inference cost while keeping accuracy losses small. The approach connects the statistical structure of pruned weights with the operations needed to execute the compressed network.

For ResNet-50, the paper reports an 18.08-fold compression ratio with a 0.24% loss in top-5 accuracy, outperforming existing compression methods. A fully compressed ResNet-18 also improves compression ratio and top-5 accuracy over compared quantization methods. Its hardware comparison reports fewer required logic gates at equal throughput, providing evidence that the representation offers implementation benefits as well as a smaller stored model.
summary.tldr: Focused quantization adapts power-of-two weight representations to pruned CNNs, reducing storage and arithmetic costs with small reported accuracy losses.

title: Focused Quantization for Sparse CNNs

abstract: Neural models for text generation require a softmax layer with proper token embeddings during the decoding phase. Most existing approaches adopt single point embedding for each token. However, a word may have multiple senses according to different context, some of which might be distinct. In this paper, we propose KerBS, a novel approach for learning better embeddings for text generation. KerBS embodies two advantages: (a) it employs a Bayesian composition of embeddings for words with multiple senses; (b) it is adaptive to semantic variances of words and robust to rare sentence context by imposing learned kernels to capture the closeness of words (senses) in the embedding space. Empirical studies show that KerBS significantly boosts the performance of several text generation tasks.

paragraphs: Text generation models use a softmax layer during decoding to assign probabilities to possible tokens. Many approaches represent each token with a single embedding. The paper argues that this representation is restrictive because a word can have several meanings, and those meanings can differ substantially depending on the surrounding context.

KerBS changes how word embeddings are represented and compared within this output mechanism. It uses a Bayesian composition of embeddings to accommodate multiple senses. It also learns kernels that capture closeness between words or senses in embedding space. These kernels let the method adapt to variation in meaning and are intended to provide robustness for rare sentence contexts.

Empirical studies report significant performance improvements across several text generation tasks. The findings support giving the decoder a richer representation of word meaning, rather than relying solely on one fixed point per token. The two components address related needs: representing distinct senses and learning how their semantic proximity should influence the generation process.
summary.tldr: KerBS combines multiple word-sense embeddings with learned similarity kernels to improve text generation.

title: Kernelized Bayesian Softmax for Text Generation

abstract: SATNet is an award-winning MAXSAT solver that can be used to infer logical rules and integrated as a differentiable layer in a deep neural network. It had been shown to solve Sudoku puzzles visually from examples of puzzle digit images, and was heralded as an impressive achievement towards the longstanding AI goal of combining pattern recognition with logical reasoning. In this paper, we clarify SATNet's capabilities by showing that in the absence of intermediate labels that identify individual Sudoku digit images with their logical representations, SATNet completely fails at visual Sudoku (0% test accuracy). More generally, the failure can be pinpointed to its inability to learn to assign symbols to perceptual phenomena, also known as the symbol grounding problem, which has long been thought to be a prerequisite for intelligent agents to perform real-world logical reasoning. We propose an MNIST based test as an easy instance of the symbol grounding problem that can serve as a sanity check for differentiable symbolic solvers in general. Naive applications of SATNet on this test lead to performance worse than that of models without logical reasoning capabilities. We report on the causes of SATNet’s failure and how to prevent them.
