paragraphs: SATNet combines a logical solver with a differentiable neural-network layer, allowing logical reasoning to participate in learning. Its reported success on visual Sudoku suggested progress toward systems that connect image recognition with symbolic reasoning. This paper investigates whether that success also demonstrates learning the connection between visual inputs and the symbols used by the solver.

The authors remove intermediate labels that identify digit images with their logical representations. Under that condition, SATNet achieves zero test accuracy on visual Sudoku. They attribute the failure to symbol grounding: learning which perceptual patterns correspond to which symbols. This experiment distinguishes solving a logical problem with supplied symbol associations from learning those associations as part of the task.

The paper also proposes a simpler MNIST-based grounding test as a sanity check for differentiable symbolic solvers. Naive uses of SATNet perform worse on this test than models without logical reasoning capabilities. The authors investigate causes and ways to prevent the failures. The findings clarify which capability the earlier visual Sudoku result established and why evaluating the perceptual-to-symbolic connection separately matters.
summary.tldr: SATNet fails visual Sudoku without intermediate digit-to-symbol labels, motivating a simpler test of symbol grounding.

title: Assessing SATNet's Ability to Solve the Symbol Grounding Problem

abstract: Boolean tensor has been broadly utilized in representing high dimensional logical data collected on spatial, temporal and/or other relational domains. Boolean Tensor Decomposition (BTD) factorizes a binary tensor into the Boolean sum of multiple rank-1 tensors, which is an NP-hard problem. Existing BTD methods have been limited by their high computational cost, in applications to large scale or higher order tensors. In this work, we presented a computationally efficient BTD algorithm, namely Geometric Expansion for all-order Tensor Factorization (GETF), that sequentially identifies the rank-1 basis components for a tensor from a geometric perspective. We conducted rigorous theoretical analysis on the validity as well as algorithemic efficiency of GETF in decomposing all-order tensor. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world data demonstrated that GETF has significantly improved performance in reconstruction accuracy, extraction of latent structures and it is an order of magnitude faster than other state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Boolean tensors organize binary information across multiple dimensions, such as space, time, and other relationships. Boolean tensor decomposition represents this information as a Boolean combination of simpler rank-one components. Although this can expose underlying structure, finding a decomposition is NP-hard, and existing methods can be costly for large tensors or tensors with many dimensions.

The paper introduces Geometric Expansion for all-order Tensor Factorization, or GETF. It approaches decomposition geometrically and identifies the rank-one basis components sequentially. This gives a way to build the representation component by component across tensor orders. The authors provide theoretical analysis of both the method’s validity and its algorithmic efficiency.

Experiments on synthetic and real data report better reconstruction accuracy and better recovery of latent structures than other leading methods, together with an order-of-magnitude speed advantage. These outcomes matter because they connect faster computation with the quality of the extracted representation. GETF’s contribution is therefore an efficient decomposition approach backed by analysis and empirical results, within a problem class whose general computational difficulty remains part of the motivation.
summary.tldr: GETF sequentially extracts Boolean tensor components geometrically, improving reconstruction and latent-structure recovery while running substantially faster in experiments.

title: Geometric All-way Boolean Tensor Decomposition

abstract: Adversarial data augmentation has shown promise for training robust deep neural networks against unforeseen data shifts or corruptions. However, it is difficult to define heuristics to generate effective fictitious target distributions containing "hard" adversarial perturbations that are largely different from the source distribution. In this paper, we propose a novel and effective regularization term for adversarial data augmentation. We theoretically derive it from the information bottleneck principle, which results in a maximum-entropy formulation. Intuitively, this regularization term encourages perturbing the underlying source distribution to enlarge predictive uncertainty of the current model, so that the generated "hard" adversarial perturbations can improve the model robustness during training. Experimental results on three standard benchmarks demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms the existing state of the art by a statistically significant margin.

paragraphs: Adversarial data augmentation trains a model using deliberately challenging variations of its training data. The difficulty is deciding how to generate useful variations that differ substantially from the source distribution. This paper introduces a regularization term that gives this process a principled objective instead of relying entirely on manually chosen perturbation heuristics.

The authors derive the regularizer from the information bottleneck principle, obtaining a maximum-entropy formulation. Its intuitive effect is to encourage changes to the source distribution that increase the current model’s predictive uncertainty. Those uncertain examples provide challenging training inputs, with the aim of improving robustness to unforeseen distribution shifts or corruptions.

Experiments on three standard benchmarks show statistically significant improvements over the existing state of the art. The findings support uncertainty as a useful signal for constructing adversarial training distributions in the evaluated settings. The contribution links a theoretical derivation to a practical augmentation mechanism: make the current model less certain when generating examples, then use those examples to strengthen its training.
summary.tldr: A maximum-entropy regularizer generates adversarial training examples that increase predictive uncertainty, improving robustness and generalization on three benchmarks.

title: Maximum-Entropy Adversarial Data Augmentation for Improved Generalization and Robustness

abstract: Probabilistic neural networks are typically modeled with independent weight priors, which do not capture weight correlations in the prior and do not provide a parsimonious interface to express properties in function space. A desirable class of priors would represent weights compactly, capture correlations between weights, facilitate calibrated reasoning about uncertainty, and allow inclusion of prior knowledge about the function space such as periodicity or dependence on contexts such as inputs. To this end, this paper introduces two innovations: (i) a Gaussian process-based hierarchical model for network weights based on unit priors that can flexibly encode correlated weight structures, and (ii) input-dependent versions of these weight priors that can provide convenient ways to regularize the function space through the use of kernels defined on contextual inputs. We show these models provide desirable test-time uncertainty estimates on out-of-distribution data and demonstrate cases of modeling inductive biases for neural networks with kernels which help both interpolation and extrapolation from training data.

Such priors do not express correlations among weights and provide a limited interface for specifying desired behavior of the resulting function. This paper seeks a more structured way to encode relationships among weights and knowledge such as periodicity or dependence on the input context.

The first contribution is a hierarchical model that uses Gaussian processes and unit priors to represent correlated weight structures. The second extends these weight priors to depend on inputs. Kernels defined over contextual inputs then offer a way to regularize the functions represented by the network, connecting assumptions about behavior to the probability model over weights.

The authors demonstrate desirable uncertainty estimates on out-of-distribution test data. They also present cases where kernel-based inductive biases help both interpolation within the training-data region and extrapolation beyond it. These findings support structured priors as a practical interface for expressing functional assumptions, while the reported benefits remain demonstrations in particular cases rather than universal guarantees of calibrated uncertainty.
summary.tldr: Hierarchical Gaussian process priors encode correlated and input-dependent neural network weights to express functional assumptions and improve demonstrated uncertainty behavior.

title: Hierarchical Gaussian Process Priors for Bayesian Neural Network Weights

abstract: We propose a new randomized algorithm for solving L2-regularized least-squares problems based on sketching. We consider two of the most popular random embeddings, namely, Gaussian embeddings and the Subsampled Randomized Hadamard Transform (SRHT). While current randomized solvers for least-squares optimization prescribe an embedding dimension at least greater than the data dimension, we show that the embedding dimension can be reduced to the effective dimension of the optimization problem, and still preserve high-probability convergence guarantees. In this regard, we derive sharp matrix deviation inequalities over ellipsoids for both Gaussian and SRHT embeddings. Specifically, we improve on the constant of a classical Gaussian concentration bound whereas, for SRHT embeddings, our deviation inequality involves a novel technical approach. Leveraging these bounds, we are able to design a practical and adaptive algorithm which does not require to know the effective dimension beforehand. Our method starts with an initial embedding dimension equal to 1 and, over iterations, increases the embedding dimension up to the effective one at most. Hence, our algorithm improves the state-of-the-art computational complexity for solving regularized least-squares problems. Further, we show numerically that it outperforms standard iterative solvers such as the conjugate gradient method and its pre-conditioned version on several standard machine learning datasets.

This paper shows that L2-regularized least-squares problems can instead use their effective dimension while retaining convergence guarantees that hold with high probability.

Adaptation matters because it makes the theoretical reduction usable without knowing its target size beforehand.
summary.tldr: An adaptive sketching solver uses effective dimension to reduce regularized least-squares computation while preserving high-probability convergence guarantees.

title: Effective Dimension Adaptive Sketching Methods for Faster Regularized Least-Squares Optimization

abstract: Meta-Learning promises to enable more data-efficient inference by harnessing previous experience from related learning tasks. While existing meta-learning methods help us to improve the accuracy of our predictions in face of data scarcity, they fail to supply reliable uncertainty estimates, often being grossly overconfident in their predictions. Addressing these shortcomings, we introduce a novel meta-learning framework, called F-PACOH, that treats meta-learned priors as stochastic processes and performs meta-level regularization directly in the function space. This allows us to directly steer the probabilistic predictions of the meta-learner towards high epistemic uncertainty in regions of insufficient meta-training data and, thus, obtain well-calibrated uncertainty estimates. Finally, we showcase how our approach can be integrated with sequential decision making, where reliable uncertainty quantification is imperative. In our benchmark study on meta-learning for Bayesian Optimization (BO), F-PACOH significantly outperforms all other meta-learners and standard baselines. Even in a challenging lifelong BO setting, where optimization tasks arrive one at a time and the meta-learner needs to build up informative prior knowledge incrementally, our proposed method demonstrates strong positive transfer.

paragraphs: Meta-learning uses experience from related tasks to improve learning when new data are scarce. However, better prediction accuracy can coexist with unreliable confidence: a learner may be overly certain where its experience offers little support. F-PACOH addresses this problem by changing how it represents and regularizes the prior knowledge learned across tasks.

The framework treats learned priors as stochastic processes and applies regularization directly in function space. This lets the training procedure steer probabilistic predictions toward greater epistemic uncertainty in regions with insufficient meta-training data. The purpose is to retain useful shared knowledge while making uncertainty reflect where that knowledge is weak.

The authors apply the framework to sequential decision-making through Bayesian optimization, where uncertainty influences which evaluations to perform. In their benchmark study, F-PACOH significantly outperforms the other meta-learners and standard baselines. It also shows strong positive transfer in a lifelong setting where tasks arrive individually and prior knowledge must accumulate incrementally. These findings connect reliable uncertainty estimates with effective reuse of experience.
summary.tldr: F-PACOH regularizes meta-learned priors in function space to improve uncertainty calibration and support effective transfer in Bayesian optimization.

title: Meta-Learning Reliable Priors in the Function Space

abstract: Minimizing a sum of simple submodular functions of limited support is a special case of general submodular function minimization that has seen numerous applications in machine learning. We develop faster techniques for instances where components in the sum are cardinality-based, meaning they depend only on the size of the input set. This variant is one of the most widely applied in practice, encompassing, e.g., common energy functions arising in image segmentation and recent generalized hypergraph cut functions. We develop the first approximation algorithms for this problem, where the approximations can be quickly computed via reduction to a sparse graph cut problem, with graph sparsity controlled by the desired approximation factor. Our method relies on a new connection between sparse graph reduction techniques and piecewise linear approximations to concave functions. Our sparse reduction technique leads to significant improvements in theoretical runtimes, as well as substantial practical gains in problems ranging from benchmark image segmentation tasks to hypergraph clustering problems.

paragraphs: The paper addresses optimization problems whose objective is a sum of simpler submodular functions, each involving only a limited subset of the variables. It focuses on components determined by how many elements are selected, rather than their identities. This structure appears in applications including image segmentation and generalized cuts in hypergraphs.

The authors develop the first approximation algorithms for this particular problem. Their approach converts the objective into a sparse graph cut problem that can be computed quickly. The requested approximation factor controls the sparsity of the resulting graph, connecting the quality of the approximation to the size of the computational representation.

The central technical insight links sparse graph constructions with piecewise linear approximations of concave functions. This connection makes it possible to exploit the cardinality structure systematically. The resulting reductions improve theoretical running times and deliver substantial practical gains on image segmentation and hypergraph clustering tasks. The contribution is specifically an approximation approach for cardinality-based components, rather than a claim of faster exact minimization for every submodular objective.
summary.tldr: The paper accelerates approximate minimization of cardinality-based submodular sums by reducing them to sparse graph cut problems.

title: Approximate Decomposable Submodular Function Minimization for Cardinality-Based Components

abstract: Modern machine learning systems such as deep neural networks are often highly over-parameterized so that they can fit the noisy training data exactly, yet they can still achieve small test errors in practice. In this paper, we study this "benign overfitting" phenomenon of the maximum margin classifier for linear classification problems. Specifically, we consider data generated from sub-Gaussian mixtures, and provide a tight risk bound for the maximum margin linear classifier in the over-parameterized setting. Our results precisely characterize the condition under which benign overfitting can occur in linear classification problems, and improve on previous work. They also have direct implications for over-parameterized logistic regression.

paragraphs: A model can fit noisy training data exactly and still make few errors on new examples. This phenomenon, called benign overfitting, challenges the intuition that fitting noise must always destroy generalization. The paper studies it in linear classification, focusing on the maximum margin classifier in an over-parameterized setting.

The analysis assumes that data come from sub-Gaussian mixtures. Within that model, the authors derive a tight bound on the classifier's risk, meaning its prediction error on new data. The bound precisely characterizes conditions under which benign overfitting can occur and improves on previous theoretical results. Its conclusions are therefore tied to a specified distributional setting and classifier.

The findings also have direct implications for over-parameterized logistic regression. Their significance is a sharper account of when interpolation and small test error can coexist in classification. Rather than treating exact training fit as sufficient evidence of either success or failure, the analysis connects generalization to conditions within the data model. The contribution is theoretical clarification of the phenomenon in this linear setting.
summary.tldr: Tight risk bounds characterize when over-parameterized maximum margin classifiers can benignly overfit data from sub-Gaussian mixtures.

title: Risk Bounds for Over-parameterized Maximum Margin Classification on Sub-Gaussian Mixtures

abstract: Neural responses are variable: even under identical experimental conditions, single neuron and population responses typically differ from trial to trial and across time. Recent work has demonstrated that this variability has predictable structure, can be modulated by sensory input and behaviour, and bears critical signatures of the underlying network dynamics and computations. However, current methods for characterising neural variability are primarily geared towards sensory coding in the laboratory: they require trials with repeatable experimental stimuli and behavioural covariates. In addition, they make strong assumptions about the parametric form of variability, rely on assumption-free but data-inefficient histogram-based approaches, or are altogether ill-suited for capturing variability modulation by covariates. Here we present a universal probabilistic spike count model that eliminates these shortcomings. Our method builds on sparse Gaussian processes and can model arbitrary spike count distributions (SCDs) with flexible dependence on observed as well as latent covariates, using scalable variational inference to jointly infer the covariate-to-SCD mappings and latent trajectories in a data efficient way. Without requiring repeatable trials, it can flexibly capture covariate-dependent joint SCDs, and provide interpretable latent causes underlying the statistical dependencies between neurons. We apply the model to recordings from a canonical non-sensory neural population: head direction cells in the mouse. We find that variability in these cells defies a simple parametric relationship with mean spike count as assumed in standard models, its modulation by external covariates can be comparably strong to that of the mean firing rate, and slow low-dimensional latent factors explain away neural correlations. Our approach paves the way to understanding the mechanisms and computations underlying neural variability under naturalistic conditions, beyond the realm of sensory coding with repeatable stimuli.

title: A universal probabilistic spike count model reveals ongoing modulation of neural variability

abstract: We study a class of computer vision settings wherein one can modify the design of the objects being recognized. We develop a framework that leverages this capability---and deep networks' unusual sensitivity to input perturbations---to design ``robust objects,'' i.e., objects that are explicitly optimized to be confidently classified. Our framework yields improved performance on standard benchmarks, a simulated robotics environment, and physical-world experiments.

Our framework yields improved performance on standard benchmarks, a simulated robotics environment, and physical-world experiments.

paragraphs: This paper studies recognition settings in which the objects themselves can be redesigned. That capability changes the available solution space: object design becomes something that can be optimized for machine perception. The authors develop a framework for creating objects that a deep vision system is intended to classify confidently.

The approach uses deep networks’ unusual sensitivity to changes in their inputs as a design opportunity. Object modifications are optimized to support recognition, producing what the paper calls robust objects. The relevant assumption is concrete: the application must permit changes to the design of what is being recognized. Within that setting, the framework makes recognizability an explicit design objective.

The authors report improved performance on standard benchmarks, in a simulated robotics environment, and in physical-world experiments. These results demonstrate the approach across multiple evaluation settings, including actual physical objects. The contribution is a way to incorporate the vision model into object design, using its response to input changes to guide modifications that improve recognition in the tested settings.
summary.tldr: Optimizing object designs for confident recognition improves vision performance in benchmark, simulated robotics, and physical-world experiments.

title: Unadversarial Examples: Designing Objects for Robust Vision

abstract: Despite a series of recent successes in reinforcement learning (RL), many RL algorithms remain sensitive to hyperparameters. As such, there has recently been interest in the field of AutoRL, which seeks to automate design decisions to create more general algorithms. Recent work suggests that population based approaches may be effective AutoRL algorithms, by learning hyperparameter schedules on the fly. In particular, the PB2 algorithm is able to achieve strong performance in RL tasks by formulating online hyperparameter optimization as time varying GP-bandit problem, while also providing theoretical guarantees. However, PB2 is only designed to work for \emph{continuous} hyperparameters, which severely limits its utility in practice. In this paper we introduce a new (provably) efficient hierarchical approach for optimizing \emph{both continuous and categorical} variables, using a new time-varying bandit algorithm specifically designed for the population based training regime. We evaluate our approach on the challenging Procgen benchmark, where we show that explicitly modelling dependence between data augmentation and other hyperparameters improves generalization.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning performance can depend strongly on hyperparameter choices. Population-based AutoRL tries to automate these choices by adjusting hyperparameters during training, producing schedules rather than relying on one fixed configuration. This paper addresses the need to tune both numerical settings and categorical choices within that process.

The starting point is PB2, which models online hyperparameter optimization as a time-varying Gaussian-process bandit problem but supports only continuous variables. The authors introduce a hierarchical approach for mixed continuous and categorical inputs. A new time-varying bandit algorithm is designed specifically for population-based training, and the approach comes with a provable efficiency result.

Evaluation on Procgen shows that explicitly modeling the dependence between data augmentation and other hyperparameters improves generalization. This matters because selecting an augmentation and tuning other settings are not necessarily separable decisions. The paper extends the range of choices that population-based optimization can handle while providing empirical evidence that accounting for their interactions benefits reinforcement learning in the tested benchmark.
summary.tldr: A provably efficient hierarchical bandit approach jointly tunes continuous and categorical hyperparameters during population-based reinforcement learning.

title: Tuning Mixed Input Hyperparameters on the Fly for Efficient Population Based AutoRL

abstract: There have been many recent advances in representation learning; however, unsupervised representation learning can still struggle with model identification issues related to rotations of the latent space. Variational Auto-Encoders (VAEs) and their extensions such as $\beta$-VAEs have been shown to improve local alignment of latent variables with PCA directions, which can help to improve model disentanglement under some conditions. Borrowing inspiration from Independent Component Analysis (ICA) and sparse coding, we propose applying an $L_1$ loss to the VAE's generative Jacobian during training to encourage local latent variable alignment with independent factors of variation in images of multiple objects or images with multiple parts. We demonstrate our results on a variety of datasets, giving qualitative and quantitative results using information theoretic and modularity measures that show our added $L_1$ cost encourages local axis alignment of the latent representation with individual factors of variation.

paragraphs: Unsupervised representations can suffer from ambiguity about how their latent coordinates should be oriented. A rotation of the latent space can change what each coordinate represents. This paper focuses on local disentanglement: encouraging individual latent directions to align with independent factors of variation in images containing multiple objects or parts.

The authors note that variational autoencoders and related models can align latent variables locally with principal-component directions, which can help disentanglement under some conditions. Inspired by independent component analysis and sparse coding, they add an L1 penalty to the generative Jacobian during training. This Jacobian describes how small latent changes affect the generated image, so the penalty acts directly on those local relationships.

Across several datasets, qualitative examples and quantitative information-theoretic and modularity measures show that the added penalty encourages local axis alignment with individual factors of variation. The contribution is a targeted modification to VAE training that shapes the local relationship between latent coordinates and image changes. The stated outcome is improved local alignment, preserving the paper’s focus rather than implying complete global identification of all underlying factors.
summary.tldr: An L1 penalty on a VAE’s generative Jacobian encourages local alignment between latent coordinates and individual image factors.

title: Local Disentanglement in Variational Auto-Encoders Using Jacobian $L_1$ Regularization

abstract: The liquid state machine (LSM) combines low training complexity and biological plausibility, which has made it an attractive machine learning framework for edge and neuromorphic computing paradigms. Originally proposed as a model of brain computation, the LSM tunes its internal weights without backpropagation of gradients, which results in lower performance compared to multi-layer neural networks. Recent findings in neuroscience suggest that astrocytes, a long-neglected non-neuronal brain cell, modulate synaptic plasticity and brain dynamics, tuning brain networks to the vicinity of the computationally optimal critical phase transition between order and chaos. Inspired by this disruptive understanding of how brain networks self-tune, we propose the neuron-astrocyte liquid state machine (NALSM) that addresses under-performance through self-organized near-critical dynamics. Similar to its biological counterpart, the astrocyte model integrates neuronal activity and provides global feedback to spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP), which self-organizes NALSM dynamics around a critical branching factor that is associated with the edge-of-chaos. We demonstrate that NALSM achieves state-of-the-art accuracy versus comparable LSM methods, without the need for data-specific hand-tuning. With a top accuracy of $97.61\%$ on MNIST, $97.51\%$ on N-MNIST, and $85.84\%$ on Fashion-MNIST, NALSM achieved comparable performance to current fully-connected multi-layer spiking neural networks trained via backpropagation. Our findings suggest that the further development of brain-inspired machine learning methods has the potential to reach the performance of deep learning, with the added benefits of supporting robust and energy-efficient neuromorphic computing on the edge.

title: Increasing Liquid State Machine Performance with Edge-of-Chaos Dynamics Organized by Astrocyte-modulated Plasticity

abstract: Existing semi-supervised learning (SSL) studies typically assume that unlabeled and test data are drawn from the same distribution as labeled data. However, in many real-world applications, it is desirable to have SSL algorithms that not only classify the samples drawn from the same distribution of labeled data but also detect out-of-distribution (OOD) samples drawn from an unknown distribution. In this paper, we study a setting called semi-supervised OOD detection. Two main challenges compared with previous OOD detection settings are i) the lack of labeled data and in-distribution data; ii) OOD samples could be unseen during training. Efforts on this direction remain limited. In this paper, we present an approach STEP significantly improving OOD detection performance by introducing a new technique: Structure-Keep Unzipping. It learns a new representation space in which OOD samples could be separated well. An efficient optimization algorithm is derived to solve the objective. Comprehensive experiments across various OOD detection benchmarks clearly show that our STEP approach outperforms other methods by a large margin and achieves remarkable detection performance on several benchmarks.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning often assumes that labeled, unlabeled, and test examples come from the same distribution. The paper considers a broader requirement: a learner should classify familiar inputs while also recognizing inputs from an unknown distribution. This becomes especially challenging when labeled and in-distribution data are scarce and unfamiliar inputs may not appear during training.

The proposed approach, STEP, introduces a technique called Structure-Keep Unzipping. It learns a representation space in which out-of-distribution examples could be separated more effectively. This places the emphasis on how inputs are represented, so that detecting unfamiliar samples becomes easier in the learned space. The authors also derive an efficient algorithm for optimizing the objective.

Experiments across multiple out-of-distribution detection benchmarks show large improvements over the compared methods. These results support the effectiveness of the learned representation for the semi-supervised detection setting studied. The contribution directly addresses the combination of limited familiar data and potentially unseen unfamiliar examples, rather than relying on the usual assumption that all available data share one distribution.
summary.tldr: STEP learns representations that improve out-of-distribution detection when labeled in-distribution data are limited and unfamiliar samples may be absent during training.

title: STEP: Out-of-Distribution Detection in the Presence of Limited In-Distribution Labeled Data

abstract: Symbolic music generation aims to generate music scores automatically. A recent trend is to use Transformer or its variants in music generation, which is, however, suboptimal, because the full attention cannot efficiently model the typically long music sequences (e.g., over 10,000 tokens), and the existing models have shortcomings in generating musical repetition structures. In this paper, we propose Museformer, a Transformer with a novel fine- and coarse-grained attention for music generation. Specifically, with the fine-grained attention, a token of a specific bar directly attends to all the tokens of the bars that are most relevant to music structures (e.g., the previous 1st, 2nd, 4th and 8th bars, selected via similarity statistics); with the coarse-grained attention, a token only attends to the summarization of the other bars rather than each token of them so as to reduce the computational cost. The advantages are two-fold. First, it can capture both music structure-related correlations via the fine-grained attention, and other contextual information via the coarse-grained attention. Second, it is efficient and can model over 3X longer music sequences compared to its full-attention counterpart. Both objective and subjective experimental results demonstrate its ability to generate long music sequences with high quality and better structures.

paragraphs: Generating symbolic music requires handling long sequences while preserving patterns such as repetition across bars. Full Transformer attention becomes expensive for these sequences, and existing models can struggle with musical structure. Museformer addresses both issues by varying how much detail its attention assigns to different bars.

Fine-grained attention reads every token in selected earlier bars that are especially relevant to musical structure. Similarity statistics guide those selections, with examples including bars one, two, four, and eight positions earlier. For the remaining bars, coarse-grained attention reads summaries. This keeps broader context available while reserving detailed attention for relationships considered particularly useful.

The authors report that Museformer can model sequences more than three times longer than its full-attention counterpart. Objective and subjective evaluations also support its ability to produce long music with high quality and improved structure. The findings suggest that selective detail can serve both musical organization and computational efficiency: the model retains direct access to structurally relevant material without processing every past token at the same level.
summary.tldr: Museformer combines detailed attention to structurally relevant bars with summaries of other bars to generate longer, better-structured music efficiently.

title: Museformer: Transformer with Fine- and Coarse-Grained Attention for Music Generation

abstract: Artificial lights commonly leave strong lens flare artifacts on images captured at night. Nighttime flare not only affects the visual quality but also degrades the performance of vision algorithms. Existing flare removal methods mainly focus on removing daytime flares and fail in nighttime. Nighttime flare removal is challenging because of the unique luminance and spectrum of artificial lights and the diverse patterns and image degradation of the flares captured at night. The scarcity of nighttime flare removal datasets limits the research on this crucial task. In this paper, we introduce, Flare7K, the first nighttime flare removal dataset, which is generated based on the observation and statistics of real-world nighttime lens flares. It offers 5,000 scattering and 2,000 reflective flare images, consisting of 25 types of scattering flares and 10 types of reflective flares. The 7,000 flare patterns can be randomly added to flare-free images, forming the flare-corrupted and flare-free image pairs. With the paired data, we can train deep models to restore flare-corrupted images taken in the real world effectively. Apart from abundant flare patterns, we also provide rich annotations, including the labeling of light source, glare with shimmer, reflective flare, and streak, which are commonly absent from existing datasets. Hence, our dataset can facilitate new work in nighttime flare removal and more fine-grained analysis of flare patterns. Extensive experiments show that our dataset adds diversity to existing flare datasets and pushes the frontier of nighttime flare removal.

Those labels support closer analysis of individual flare components alongside overall restoration quality. The reported experiments show that the dataset broadens the diversity of existing flare data and advances nighttime removal performance, with paired synthetic training data supporting effective restoration of real-world images.
summary.tldr: Flare7K supplies diverse, annotated nighttime flare patterns that can generate paired training data for restoring real photographs.

title: Flare7K: A Phenomenological Nighttime Flare Removal Dataset

abstract: We address the consistency of a kernel ridge regression estimate of the conditional mean embedding (CME), which is an embedding of the conditional distribution of $Y$ given $X$ into a target reproducing kernel Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}_Y$. The CME allows us to take conditional expectations of target RKHS functions, and has been employed in nonparametric causal and Bayesian inference.We address the misspecified setting, where the target CME isin the space of Hilbert-Schmidt operators acting from an input interpolation space between $\mathcal{H}_X$ and $L_2$, to $\mathcal{H}_Y$. This space of operators is shown to be isomorphic to a newly defined vector-valued interpolation space. Using this isomorphism, we derive a novel and adaptive statistical learning rate for the empirical CME estimator under the misspecified setting. Our analysis reveals that our rates match the optimal $O(\log n / n)$ rates without assuming $\mathcal{H}_Y$ to be finite dimensional. We further establish a lower bound on the learning rate, which shows that the obtained upper bound is optimal.

paragraphs: A conditional mean embedding represents the conditional distribution of an outcome given an input inside a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. It supports computing conditional expectations of functions in that space and has applications in nonparametric causal and Bayesian inference. This paper studies the consistency and learning rate of an estimator based on kernel ridge regression.

The analysis covers a misspecified setting in which the target embedding is a Hilbert–Schmidt operator from an input interpolation space into the target Hilbert space. The input space lies between the input kernel space and L2. The authors show that this operator space is equivalent, through an isomorphism, to a newly defined vector-valued interpolation space.

That connection enables an adaptive statistical learning rate for the empirical estimator. The analysis matches the optimal O(log n / n) rate without requiring the target Hilbert space to have finite dimension. A lower bound establishes optimality of the obtained upper bound. The contribution therefore gives both an error guarantee and evidence that its rate cannot generally be improved within the analyzed setting.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes optimal learning rates for regularized conditional mean embeddings in a misspecified setting without requiring a finite-dimensional target space.

title: Optimal Rates for Regularized Conditional Mean Embedding Learning

abstract: We study the fundamental task of outlier-robust mean estimation for heavy-tailed distributions in the presence of sparsity. Specifically, given a small number of corrupted samples from a high-dimensional heavy-tailed distribution whose mean $\mu$ is guaranteed to be sparse, the goal is to efficiently compute a hypothesis that accurately approximates $\mu$ with high probability. Prior work had obtained efficient algorithms for robust sparse mean estimation of light-tailed distributions. In this work, we give the first sample-efficient and polynomial-time robust sparse mean estimator for heavy-tailed distributions under mild moment assumptions. Our algorithm achieves the optimal asymptotic error using a number of samples scaling logarithmically with the ambient dimension. Importantly, the sample complexity of our method is optimal as a function of the failure probability $\tau$, having an {\em additive} $\log(1/\tau)$ dependence. Our algorithm leverages the stability-based approach from the algorithmic robust statistics literature, with crucial (and necessary) adaptations required in our setting. Our analysis may be of independent interest, involving the delicate design of a (non-spectral) decomposition for positive semi-definite matrices satisfying certain sparsity properties.

paragraphs: Estimating an average becomes difficult when observations are high-dimensional, some are corrupted, and the underlying distribution has heavy tails. This paper assumes that the true mean is sparse, meaning only a small number of its coordinates are nonzero. The goal is to exploit that structure while remaining robust to corrupted samples.

The authors give a polynomial-time estimator that is sample-efficient under mild moment assumptions. It achieves optimal asymptotic error, with sample requirements growing logarithmically in the ambient dimension. Its dependence on the desired failure probability is also optimal: requiring greater confidence adds a term proportional to the logarithm of the inverse failure probability.

The algorithm adapts a stability-based approach from robust statistics to the combined challenges of sparsity and heavy tails. Its analysis includes a specially designed non-spectral decomposition of positive semidefinite matrices with sparsity properties. The result extends efficient robust sparse mean estimation beyond previously handled light-tailed settings, while tying the guarantee to explicit distributional and sparsity assumptions.
summary.tldr: Under mild moment assumptions, the paper gives an efficient outlier-robust estimator for sparse means of heavy-tailed distributions with optimal asymptotic error.

title: Outlier-Robust Sparse Mean Estimation for Heavy-Tailed Distributions

abstract: Training deep neural network classifiers that are certifiably robust against adversarial attacks is critical to ensuring the security and reliability of AI-controlled systems. Although numerous state-of-the-art certified training methods have been developed, they are computationally expensive and scale poorly with respect to both dataset and network complexity. Widespread usage of certified training is further hindered by the fact that periodic retraining is necessary to incorporate new data and network improvements. In this paper, we propose Certified Robustness Transfer (CRT), a general-purpose framework for reducing the computational overhead of any certifiably robust training method through knowledge transfer. Given a robust teacher, our framework uses a novel training loss to transfer the teacher’s robustness to the student. We provide theoretical and empirical validation of CRT. Our experiments on CIFAR-10 show that CRT speeds up certified robustness training by 8× on average across three different architecture generations while achieving comparable robustness to state-of-the-art methods. We also show that CRT can scale to large-scale datasets like ImageNet.

Repeated training adds another burden when new data arrive or architectures improve. This paper asks whether robustness already learned by one network can reduce the cost of training another.

The proposed framework, Certified Robustness Transfer, starts with a robust teacher model and trains a student using a loss designed to transfer the teacher's robustness. The central idea is to reuse this property through knowledge transfer. The authors present the framework as applicable across certified training methods and provide both theoretical and empirical support.

On CIFAR-10, the experiments report an average eightfold training speedup across three architecture generations while retaining robustness comparable to state-of-the-art methods. The authors also demonstrate scaling to ImageNet. These findings support robustness transfer as a way to make subsequent certified training less expensive, with an existing robust teacher serving as the starting resource.
summary.tldr: Certified Robustness Transfer uses a robust teacher to accelerate student training, reporting an average eightfold speedup on CIFAR-10 with comparable robustness.

title: Accelerating Certified Robustness Training via Knowledge Transfer

abstract: Federated learning provides an effective paradigm to jointly optimize a model benefited from rich distributed data while protecting data privacy. Nonetheless, the heterogeneity nature of distributed data, especially in the non-IID setting, makes it challenging to define and ensure fairness among local agents. For instance, it is intuitively ``unfair" for agents with data of high quality to sacrifice their performance due to other agents with low quality data. Currently popular egalitarian and weighted equity-based fairness measures suffer from the aforementioned pitfall. In this work, we aim to formally represent this problem and address these fairness issues using concepts from co-operative game theory and social choice theory. We model the task of learning a shared predictor in the federated setting as a fair public decision making problem, and then define the notion of core-stable fairness: Given $N$ agents, there is no subset of agents $S$ that can benefit significantly by forming a coalition among themselves based on their utilities $U_N$ and $U_S$ (i.e., $ (|S|/ N) U_S \geq U_N$). Core-stable predictors are robust to low quality local data from some agents, and additionally they satisfy Proportionality (each agent gets at least $1/n$ fraction of the best utility that she can get from any predictor) and Pareto-optimality (there exists no model that can increase the utility of an agent without decreasing the utility of another), two well sought-after fairness and efficiency notions within social choice. We then propose an efficient federated learning protocol CoreFed to optimize a core stable predictor. CoreFed determines a core-stable predictor when the loss functions of the agents are convex. CoreFed also determines approximate core-stable predictors when the loss functions are not convex, like smooth neural networks. We further show the existence of core-stable predictors in more general settings using Kakutani's fixed point theorem. Finally, we empirically validate our analysis on two real-world datasets, and we show that CoreFed achieves higher core-stability fairness than FedAvg while maintaining similar accuracy.

This paper frames shared-model learning as a public decision problem and uses cooperative game theory to define fairness through core stability.

Under this definition, no subset of participants should gain sufficiently by forming its own coalition, with the comparison accounting for the coalition’s share of all participants. summary.tldr: CoreFed promotes federated-learning fairness by seeking shared models that participants cannot substantially improve upon by forming smaller coalitions.

title: Fairness in Federated Learning via Core-Stability

abstract: Contrastive learning (CL) pretrains feature embeddings to scatter instances in the feature space so that the training data can be well discriminated. Most existing CL techniques usually encourage learning such feature embeddings in the highdimensional space to maximize the instance discrimination. However, this practice may lead to undesired results where the scattering instances are sparsely distributed in the high-dimensional feature space, making it difficult to capture the underlying similarity between pairwise instances. To this end, we propose a novel framework called contrastive learning with low-dimensional reconstruction (CLLR), which adopts a regularized projection layer to reduce the dimensionality of the feature embedding. In CLLR, we build the sparse / low-rank regularizer to adaptively reconstruct a low-dimensional projection space while preserving the basic objective for instance discrimination, and thus successfully learning contrastive embeddings that alleviate the above issue. Theoretically, we prove a tighter error bound for CLLR; empirically, the superiority of CLLR is demonstrated across multiple domains. Both theoretical and experimental results emphasize the significance of learning low-dimensional contrastive embeddings.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning builds representations that distinguish individual examples. Many methods use high-dimensional spaces to make that separation easier. This paper highlights a possible drawback: examples can become so sparsely scattered that meaningful similarities between them are difficult to capture. Separating instances well does not by itself ensure that their relationships remain easy to recognize.

The proposed framework, contrastive learning with low-dimensional reconstruction, or CLLR, adds a regularized projection layer that reduces representation dimensionality. Sparse or low-rank regularization helps adaptively reconstruct the lower-dimensional projection space. The method retains the objective of distinguishing instances while changing the space in which their representations are organized.

The authors prove a tighter error bound for CLLR and report empirical advantages across multiple domains. These findings support low-dimensional contrastive embeddings as a useful design choice for addressing the sparse-scattering issue. The contribution is a way to combine instance discrimination with a more compact representation, backed by both theoretical analysis and experiments, rather than simply maximizing separation in a large feature space.
summary.tldr: CLLR uses a regularized low-dimensional projection to preserve instance discrimination while better capturing relationships between contrastive embeddings.

title: Learning Contrastive Embedding in Low-Dimensional Space

abstract: Hidden semi-Markov Models (HSMM's) - while broadly in use - are restricted to a discrete and uniform time grid. They are thus not well suited to explain often irregularly spaced discrete event data from continuous-time phenomena. We show that non-sampling-based latent state inference used in HSMM's can be generalized to latent Continuous-Time semi-Markov Chains (CTSMC's). We formulate integro-differential forward and backward equations adjusted to the observation likelihood and introduce an exact integral equation for the Bayesian posterior marginals and a scalable Viterbi-type algorithm for posterior path estimates. The presented equations can be efficiently solved using well-known numerical methods. As a practical tool, variable-step HSMM's are introduced. We evaluate our approaches in latent state inference scenarios in comparison to classical HSMM's.

paragraphs: Hidden semi-Markov models infer an unobserved state process from observations, but their usual formulation relies on a uniform discrete time grid. That creates a mismatch for continuous-time phenomena observed through irregularly spaced events. This paper extends non-sampling inference techniques to hidden continuous-time semi-Markov chains, allowing inference to be formulated around continuous time.

The authors derive forward and backward integro-differential equations that account for the observation likelihood. They also introduce an exact integral equation for posterior marginals, which describe uncertainty about the hidden state at individual times. A scalable Viterbi-type algorithm addresses a complementary task: estimating a hidden state path rather than only separate state probabilities.

The equations can be solved efficiently using established numerical methods. The paper additionally introduces variable-step hidden semi-Markov models as a practical tool and evaluates the approaches against classical models in latent-state inference scenarios. The contribution brings both uncertainty estimation and path estimation into the continuous-time setting. Exactness applies to the stated posterior equation, while its computational solution uses numerical methods.
summary.tldr: The paper extends forward-backward hidden-state inference to continuous-time semi-Markov chains for irregularly timed observations.

title: Forward-Backward Latent State Inference for Hidden Continuous-Time semi-Markov Chains

abstract: Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) with large-scale unlabelled datasets enables learning useful representations for multiple downstream tasks. However, assessing the quality of such representations efficiently poses nontrivial challenges. Existing approaches train linear probes (with frozen features) to evaluate performance on a given task. This is expensive both computationally, since it requires retraining a new prediction head for each downstream task, and statistically, requires task-specific labels for multiple tasks. This poses a natural question, how do we efficiently determine the "goodness" of representations learned with SSL across a wide range of potential downstream tasks? In particular, a task-agnostic statistical measure of representation quality, that predicts generalization without explicit downstream task evaluation, would be highly desirable. In this work, we analyze characteristics of learned representations $\mathbf{f_\theta}$, in well-trained neural networks with canonical architectures \& across SSL objectives. We observe that the eigenspectrum of the empirical feature covariance $\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{f_\theta}$) can be well approximated with the family of power-law distribution. We analytically and empirically (using multiple datasets, e.g. CIFAR, STL10, MIT67, ImageNet) demonstrate that the decay coefficient $\alpha$ serves as a measure of representation quality for tasks that are solvable with a linear readout, i.e. there exist well-defined intervals for $\alpha$ where models exhibit excellent downstream generalization. Furthermore, our experiments suggest that key design parameters in SSL algorithms, such as BarlowTwins, implicitly modulate the decay coefficient of the eigenspectrum ($\alpha$). As $\alpha$ depends only on the features themselves, this measure for model selection with hyperparameter tuning for BarlowTwins enables search with less compute.

paragraphs: Evaluating a self-supervised representation commonly requires training a separate prediction head for each downstream task. That consumes computation and task-specific labels. This paper investigates whether the learned features themselves contain a useful signal of representation quality, allowing model selection without repeatedly carrying out those downstream evaluations.

The authors examine the eigenvalues of the empirical feature covariance, which describe how feature variation is distributed across directions. Across the architectures and self-supervised objectives studied, these eigenvalues are well approximated by a power law. Its decay coefficient, alpha, summarizes how quickly their magnitudes fall. Analytical and empirical results identify intervals of alpha associated with excellent generalization for tasks solvable through a linear readout.

Experiments also suggest that design choices in self-supervised algorithms implicitly influence this decay coefficient. For BarlowTwins, using alpha during hyperparameter selection enables a search with less computation. The result offers a feature-based evaluation signal with a clearly stated scope: its quality claims concern downstream tasks that a linear readout can solve.
summary.tldr: The decay of feature-covariance eigenvalues provides a task-agnostic quality signal for representations used with linear readouts.

title: $\alpha$-ReQ : Assessing Representation Quality in Self-Supervised Learning by measuring eigenspectrum decay

abstract: Hypergraph neural networks can model multi-way connections among nodes of the graphs, which are common in real-world applications such as genetic medicine. In particular, genetic pathways or gene sets encode molecular functions driven by multiple genes, naturally represented as hyperedges. Thus, hypergraph-guided embedding can capture functional relations in learned representations. Existing hypergraph neural network models often focus on node-level or graph-level inference. There is an unmet need in learning powerful representations of subgraphs of hypergraphs in real-world applications. For example, a cancer patient can be viewed as a subgraph of genes harboring mutations in the patient, while all the genes are connected by hyperedges that correspond to pathways representing specific molecular functions. For accurate inductive subgraph prediction, we propose SubHypergraph Inductive Neural nEtwork (SHINE). SHINE uses informative genetic pathways that encode molecular functions as hyperedges to connect genes as nodes. SHINE jointly optimizes the objectives of end-to-end subgraph classification and hypergraph nodes' similarity regularization. SHINE simultaneously learns representations for both genes and pathways using strongly dual attention message passing. The learned representations are aggregated via a subgraph attention layer and used to train a multilayer perceptron for subgraph inferencing. We evaluated SHINE against a wide array of state-of-the-art (hyper)graph neural networks, XGBoost, NMF and polygenic risk score models, using large scale NGS and curated datasets. SHINE outperformed all comparison models significantly, and yielded interpretable disease models with functional insights.

paragraphs: A hypergraph can represent relationships involving multiple genes at once, making genetic pathways natural hyperedges. This paper focuses on predicting properties of subgraphs within such a structure. For example, a patient can be represented by the subset of genes carrying mutations, embedded within a broader network of functional pathways.

SHINE learns representations for both genes and pathways through dual attention message passing. It jointly optimizes subgraph classification and a regularization objective concerning similarities between hypergraph nodes. A subgraph attention layer then aggregates the learned representations, and a multilayer perceptron makes the prediction. This architecture links the patient's selected genes to the functional relationships encoded by pathways.

The authors evaluate SHINE on large-scale sequencing and curated datasets against graph and hypergraph neural networks, XGBoost, nonnegative matrix factorization, and polygenic risk score models. They report significant improvements over every comparison model and disease models offering interpretable functional insights. The contribution extends hypergraph representation learning toward subgraph-level inference, where the object being classified is a biologically meaningful subset of the overall structure.
summary.tldr: SHINE combines gene and pathway representations to classify patient-related subgraphs, improving prediction and providing functional insights in the reported evaluations.

title: SHINE: SubHypergraph Inductive Neural nEtwork

abstract: Recent years have witnessed significant success in Gradient Boosting Decision Trees (GBDT) for a wide range of machine learning applications. Generally, a consensus about GBDT's training algorithms is gradients and statistics are computed based on high-precision floating points. In this paper, we investigate an essentially important question which has been largely ignored by the previous literature - how many bits are needed for representing gradients in training GBDT? To solve this mystery, we propose to quantize all the high-precision gradients in a very simple yet effective way in the GBDT's training algorithm. Surprisingly, both our theoretical analysis and empirical studies show that the necessary precisions of gradients without hurting any performance can be quite low, e.g., 2 or 3 bits. With low-precision gradients, most arithmetic operations in GBDT training can be replaced by integer operations of 8, 16, or 32 bits. Promisingly, these findings may pave the way for much more efficient training of GBDT from several aspects: (1) speeding up the computation of gradient statistics in histograms; (2) compressing the communication cost of high-precision statistical information during distributed training; (3) the inspiration of utilization and development of hardware architectures which well support low-precision computation for GBDT training. Benchmarked on CPUs, GPUs, and distributed clusters, we observe up to 2$\times$ speedup of our simple quantization strategy compared with SOTA GBDT systems on extensive datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness and potential of the low-precision training of GBDT. The code will be released to the official repository of LightGBM.

paragraphs: Gradient boosting decision tree training commonly represents gradients and related statistics with high-precision floating-point numbers. This paper asks how much precision those gradients actually need. The authors introduce a simple quantization method that replaces high-precision gradient representations with much lower-precision values during training.

Their theoretical analysis and experiments show that gradients can require as few as two or three bits without reducing performance in the studied settings. With these representations, most arithmetic operations can use 8-, 16-, or 32-bit integers. This creates opportunities to accelerate histogram statistics and reduce the communication required to exchange statistical information during distributed training.

Benchmarks on CPUs, GPUs, and distributed clusters show speedups of up to twofold over leading gradient boosting systems across the evaluated datasets. The authors also identify low-precision hardware as a potential avenue for further efficiency. The observed speedups establish a practical benefit of the quantization strategy, while the hardware discussion points to possible future gains rather than additional measured results.
summary.tldr: Very low-precision gradients can preserve gradient boosting performance in studied settings while enabling reported training speedups of up to twofold.

title: Quantized Training of Gradient Boosting Decision Trees

abstract: $\ell_0$ constrained optimization is prevalent in machine learning, particularly for high-dimensional problems, because it is a fundamental approach to achieve sparse learning. Hard-thresholding gradient descent is a dominant technique to solve this problem. However, first-order gradients of the objective function may be either unavailable or expensive to calculate in a lot of real-world problems, where zeroth-order (ZO) gradients could be a good surrogate. Unfortunately, whether ZO gradients can work with the hard-thresholding operator is still an unsolved problem.To solve this puzzle, in this paper, we focus on the $\ell_0$ constrained black-box stochastic optimization problems, and propose a new stochastic zeroth-order gradient hard-thresholding (SZOHT) algorithm with a general ZO gradient estimator powered by a novel random support sampling. We provide the convergence analysis of SZOHT under standard assumptions. Importantly, we reveal a conflict between the deviation of ZO estimators and the expansivity of the hard-thresholding operator, and provide a theoretical minimal value of the number of random directions in ZO gradients. In addition, we find that the query complexity of SZOHT is independent or weakly dependent on the dimensionality under different settings. Finally, we illustrate the utility of our method on a portfolio optimization problem as well as black-box adversarial attacks.

paragraphs: Sparse optimization restricts how many components of a solution can be nonzero. Hard-thresholding gradient descent enforces this restriction, but its gradient information may be unavailable or expensive in black-box problems. This paper investigates whether estimates obtained from function evaluations can work reliably with the hard-thresholding step in stochastic optimization.

The proposed SZOHT algorithm combines stochastic zeroth-order gradient estimation with hard thresholding. Its estimator uses a new random support-sampling mechanism. Under standard assumptions, the authors provide a convergence analysis and identify a central tension: errors in the gradient estimate interact with the thresholding operator’s tendency to expand differences.

That analysis yields a theoretical minimum number of random directions for the gradient estimates. It also shows that query complexity is independent of dimension or only weakly dependent on it, depending on the setting. Applications to portfolio optimization and black-box adversarial attacks illustrate the method’s utility. The contribution explains a mathematical obstacle to combining approximate gradients with sparsity enforcement and provides an algorithm analyzed around that obstacle.
summary.tldr: SZOHT combines black-box gradient estimates with hard thresholding, with convergence analysis explaining the sampling needed to manage amplified estimation errors.

title: Zeroth-Order Hard-Thresholding: Gradient Error vs. Expansivity

abstract: Collaborative inference leverages diverse features provided by different agents (e.g., sensors) for more accurate inference. A common setup is where each agent sends its embedded features instead of the raw data to the Fusion Center (FC) for joint prediction. In this setting, we consider the inference-time attacks when a small fraction of agents are compromised. The compromised agent either does not send embedded features to the FC, or sends arbitrarily embedded features. To address this, we propose a certifiably robust COllaborative inference framework via feature PURification (CoPur), by leveraging the block-sparse nature of adversarial perturbations on the feature vector, as well as exploring the underlying redundancy across the embedded features (by assuming the overall features lie on an underlying lower dimensional manifold). We theoretically show that the proposed feature purification method can robustly recover the true feature vector, despite adversarial corruptions and/or incomplete observations. We also propose and test an untargeted distributed feature-flipping attack, which is agnostic to the model, training data, label, as well as the features held by other agents, and is shown to be effective in attacking state-of-the-art defenses. Experiments on ExtraSensory and NUS-WIDE datasets show that CoPur significantly outperforms existing defenses in terms of robustness against targeted and untargeted adversarial attacks.

paragraphs: Collaborative inference combines information from multiple agents, such as sensors, to make a prediction. Often each agent sends an embedded feature representation to a central fusion system. The paper considers attacks during inference in which a small fraction of agents either withhold these features or send arbitrary replacements.

CoPur attempts to repair the combined feature vector before prediction. It uses two properties: compromised agents affect blocks of features, and features from different agents contain redundancy. The latter is expressed through an assumption that the overall feature vector lies on a lower-dimensional manifold. Within this framework, the authors theoretically establish robust recovery despite corrupted features, missing observations, or both.

The paper also introduces a distributed feature-flipping attack that does not require access to the model, training data, labels, or other agents’ features. It is effective against existing leading defenses. Experiments on ExtraSensory and NUS-WIDE show that CoPur substantially improves robustness over existing defenses against both targeted and untargeted attacks, supporting feature purification as a defense for this collaborative setting.
summary.tldr: CoPur uses structured corruption and redundancy across agents’ features to recover information and improve collaborative inference robustness.

title: CoPur: Certifiably Robust Collaborative Inference via Feature Purification

abstract: Uncertainty quantification has received increasing attention in machine learning in the recent past. In particular, a distinction between aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty has been found useful in this regard. The latter refers to the learner's (lack of) knowledge and appears to be especially difficult to measure and quantify. In this paper, we analyse a recent proposal based on the idea of a second-order learner, which yields predictions in the form of distributions over probability distributions. While standard (first-order) learners can be trained to predict accurate probabilities, namely by minimising suitable loss functions on sample data, we show that loss minimisation does not work for second-order predictors: The loss functions proposed for inducing such predictors do not incentivise the learner to represent its epistemic uncertainty in a faithful way.

paragraphs: Epistemic uncertainty concerns what a learner does not know. Measuring it requires more than producing a probability for an outcome: the learner must also represent uncertainty about its own predictive beliefs. This paper examines a proposed second-order approach in which predictions are distributions over probability distributions.

Ordinary first-order learners can be trained to predict accurate probabilities by minimizing suitable losses on observed examples. The authors investigate whether the same idea works for the second-order proposal. Their analysis shows that the proposed losses fail to give the learner an incentive to represent epistemic uncertainty faithfully. Optimizing those objectives therefore does not establish that the additional uncertainty information has the intended meaning.

The result separates expressive output structure from a training objective that supports its interpretation. A model may produce a distribution over distributions without being rewarded for accurately describing its lack of knowledge. The paper's criticism concerns the analyzed loss-based proposal and its objectives, exposing a problem in the connection between optimization and faithful epistemic uncertainty.
summary.tldr: The analyzed losses for second-order predictors do not incentivize faithful representations of epistemic uncertainty.

title: Pitfalls of Epistemic Uncertainty Quantification through Loss Minimisation

abstract: Spatial-wise dynamic convolution has become a promising approach to improving the inference efficiency of deep networks. By allocating more computation to the most informative pixels, such an adaptive inference paradigm reduces the spatial redundancy in image features and saves a considerable amount of unnecessary computation. However, the theoretical efficiency achieved by previous methods can hardly translate into a realistic speedup, especially on the multi-core processors (e.g. GPUs). The key challenge is that the existing literature has only focused on designing algorithms with minimal computation, ignoring the fact that the practical latency can also be influenced by scheduling strategies and hardware properties. To bridge the gap between theoretical computation and practical efficiency, we propose a latency-aware spatial-wise dynamic network (LASNet), which performs coarse-grained spatially adaptive inference under the guidance of a novel latency prediction model. The latency prediction model can efficiently estimate the inference latency of dynamic networks by simultaneously considering algorithms, scheduling strategies, and hardware properties. We use the latency predictor to guide both the algorithm design and the scheduling optimization on various hardware platforms. Experiments on image classification, object detection and instance segmentation demonstrate that the proposed framework significantly improves the practical inference efficiency of deep networks. For example, the average latency of a ResNet-101 on the ImageNet validation set could be reduced by 36% and 46% on a server GPU (Nvidia Tesla-V100) and an edge device (Nvidia Jetson TX2 GPU) respectively without sacrificing the accuracy. Code is available at https://github.com/LeapLabTHU/LASNet.

title: Latency-aware Spatial-wise Dynamic Networks

abstract: Large-scale video-language pre-training has shown significant improvement in video-language understanding tasks. Previous studies of video-language pretraining mainly focus on short-form videos (i.e., within 30 seconds) and sentences, leaving long-form video-language pre-training rarely explored. Directly learning representation from long-form videos and language may benefit many long-formvideo-language understanding tasks. However, it is challenging due to the difficulty of modeling long-range relationships and the heavy computational burden caused by more frames. In this paper, we introduce a Long-Form VIdeo-LAnguage pre-training model (LF-VILA) and train it on a large-scale long-form video and paragraph dataset constructed from an existing public dataset. To effectively capturethe rich temporal dynamics and to better align video and language in an efficient end-to-end manner, we introduce two novel designs in our LF-VILA model. We first propose a Multimodal Temporal Contrastive (MTC) loss to learn the temporal relation across different modalities by encouraging fine-grained alignment between long-form videos and paragraphs. Second, we propose a Hierarchical Temporal Window Attention (HTWA) mechanism to effectively capture long-range dependency while reducing computational cost in Transformer. We fine-tune the pre-trained LF-VILA model on seven downstream long-form video-language understanding tasks of paragraph-to-video retrieval and long-form video question-answering, and achieve new state-of-the-art performances. Specifically, our model achieves 16.1% relative improvement on ActivityNet paragraph-to-video retrieval task and 2.4% on How2QA task, respectively. We release our code, dataset, and pre-trained models at https://github.com/microsoft/XPretrain.

title: Long-Form Video-Language Pre-Training with Multimodal Temporal Contrastive Learning

abstract: In this paper, we study a class of stochastic bilevel optimization problems, also known as stochastic simple bilevel optimization, where we minimize a smooth stochastic objective function over the optimal solution set of another stochastic convex optimization problem. We introduce novel stochastic bilevel optimization methods that locally approximate the solution set of the lower-level problem via a stochastic cutting plane, and then run a conditional gradient update with variance reduction techniques to control the error induced by using stochastic gradients. For the case that the upper-level function is convex, our method requires $\mathcal{O}(\max\\{1/\epsilon_f^{2},1/\epsilon_g^{2}\\}) $ stochastic oracle queries to obtain a solution that is $\epsilon_f$-optimal for the upper-level and $\epsilon_g$-optimal for the lower-level. This guarantee improves the previous best-known complexity of $\mathcal{O}(\max\\{1/\epsilon_f^{4},1/\epsilon_g^{4}\\})$. Moreover, for the case that the upper-level function is non-convex, our method requires at most $\mathcal{O}(\max\\{1/\epsilon_f^{3},1/\epsilon_g^{3}\\}) $ stochastic oracle queries to find an $(\epsilon_f, \epsilon_g)$-stationary point. In the finite-sum setting, we show that the number of stochastic oracle calls required by our method are $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{n}/\epsilon)$ and $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{n}/\epsilon^{2})$ for the convex and non-convex settings, respectively, where $\epsilon=\min \\{\epsilon_f,\epsilon_g\\}$.

paragraphs: The paper studies optimization problems in which a smooth stochastic objective must be minimized among solutions that also minimize another, convex stochastic objective. This creates two accuracy requirements: the answer must perform well on the upper-level objective while remaining close to optimal for the lower-level problem.

The proposed methods locally approximate the lower-level solution set with a stochastic cutting plane. They then take a conditional-gradient step, avoiding a projection operation. Variance reduction controls the error introduced by noisy gradient estimates, allowing the method to combine an approximate feasible region with stochastic updates.

When the upper objective is convex, the oracle complexity improves from fourth-power to second-power dependence on the inverse accuracy targets: O(max{epsilon_f^-2, epsilon_g^-2}). For a nonconvex upper objective, the method reaches an appropriately defined stationary point with cubic inverse-accuracy dependence. In finite-sum problems, the reported complexities are O(sqrt(n)/epsilon) and O(sqrt(n)/epsilon²), respectively. These guarantees distinguish global objective accuracy in the convex case from stationarity in the nonconvex case.
summary.tldr: Stochastic cutting planes and variance-reduced conditional gradients improve oracle guarantees for simple bilevel optimization with a convex lower-level problem.

title: Projection-Free Methods for Stochastic Simple Bilevel Optimization with Convex Lower-level Problem

abstract: In convex optimization, first-order optimization methods efficiently minimizing function values have been a central subject study since Nesterov's seminal work of 1983. Recently, however, Kim and Fessler's OGM-G and Lee et al.'s FISTA-G have been presented as alternatives that efficiently minimize the gradient magnitude instead. In this paper, we present H-duality, which represents a surprising one-to-one correspondence between methods efficiently minimizing function values and methods efficiently minimizing gradient magnitude. In continuous-time formulations, H-duality corresponds to reversing the time dependence of the dissipation/friction term. To the best of our knowledge, H-duality is different from Lagrange/Fenchel duality and is distinct from any previously known duality or symmetry relations. Using H-duality, we obtain a clearer understanding of the symmetry between Nesterov's method and OGM-G, derive a new class of methods efficiently reducing gradient magnitudes of smooth convex functions, and find a new composite minimization method that is simpler and faster than FISTA-G.
