paragraphs: First-order optimization methods can target different measures of progress: reducing the function value or reducing the gradient magnitude. This paper introduces H-duality, a one-to-one correspondence between methods that efficiently pursue these two objectives. It offers a way to understand relationships among algorithms whose performance is usually assessed using different criteria.

In a continuous-time description, the correspondence arises by reversing the time dependence of the dissipation, or friction, term. This gives the algorithmic relationship a dynamical interpretation. The authors distinguish H-duality from Lagrange and Fenchel duality and, to their knowledge, from previously established duality or symmetry relations.

The framework clarifies the symmetry between Nesterov's method and OGM-G. It also leads to a new family of methods that efficiently reduce gradient magnitudes for smooth convex functions. For composite minimization, the authors derive a method described as simpler and faster than FISTA-G. Thus, the contribution both explains existing algorithms and supplies a route to new ones, with the stated results situated in convex optimization.
summary.tldr: H-duality links efficient function-value and gradient-magnitude minimization methods through time reversal of dissipation.

title: Time-Reversed Dissipation Induces Duality Between Minimizing Gradient Norm and Function Value

abstract: Large-scale text-to-image generative models have been a ground-breaking development in generative AI, with diffusion models showing their astounding ability to synthesize convincing images following an input text prompt. The goal of image editing research is to give users control over the generated images by modifying the text prompt. Current image editing techniques are susceptible to unintended modifications of regions outside the targeted area, such as on the background or on distractor objects which have some semantic or visual relationship with the targeted object. According to our experimental findings, inaccurate cross-attention maps are at the root of this problem. Based on this observation, we propose $\textit{Dynamic Prompt Learning}$ ($DPL$) to force cross-attention maps to focus on correct $\textit{noun}$ words in the text prompt. By updating the dynamic tokens for nouns in the textual input with the proposed leakage repairment losses, we achieve fine-grained image editing over particular objects while preventing undesired changes to other image regions. Our method $DPL$, based on the publicly available $\textit{Stable Diffusion}$, is extensively evaluated on a wide range of images, and consistently obtains superior results both quantitatively (CLIP score, Structure-Dist) and qualitatively (on user-evaluation). We show improved prompt editing results for Word-Swap, Prompt Refinement, and Attention Re-weighting, especially for complex multi-object scenes.

The authors’ experiments identify inaccurate cross-attention maps as the source of this problem. These maps connect parts of the text prompt with image regions, so incorrect associations can spread an edit beyond its intended area.

Dynamic Prompt Learning addresses this leakage by updating the representations of noun tokens in the prompt. Its repair losses guide cross-attention toward the correct noun-object associations. Built on Stable Diffusion, the approach aims to make edits more selective by improving the internal connection between the named object and the region being changed.

Across a wide range of evaluated images, the authors report consistently stronger quantitative results using CLIP score and Structure-Dist, alongside favorable user evaluations. Improvements cover word replacement, prompt refinement, and attention reweighting, with particular benefits in complex scenes containing multiple objects. The findings support targeted attention repair as a useful mechanism for finer editing control.
summary.tldr: Dynamic Prompt Learning updates noun representations to repair cross-attention leakage and make text-driven image edits more selective.

title: Dynamic Prompt Learning: Addressing Cross-Attention Leakage for Text-Based Image Editing

abstract: Human actions in egocentric videos often feature hand-object interactions composed of a verb (performed by the hand) applied to an object. Despite their extensive scaling up, egocentric datasets still face two limitations — sparsity of action compositions and a closed set of interacting objects. This paper proposes a novel open vocabulary action recognition task. Given a set of verbs and objects observed during training, the goal is to generalize the verbs to an open vocabulary of actions with seen and novel objects. To this end, we decouple the verb and object predictions via an object-agnostic _verb encoder_ and a prompt-based _object encoder_. The prompting leverages CLIP representations to predict an open vocabulary of interacting objects. We create open vocabulary benchmarks on the EPIC-KITCHENS-100 and Assembly101 datasets; whereas closed-action methods fail to generalize, our proposed method is effective. In addition, our object encoder significantly outperforms existing open-vocabulary visual recognition methods in recognizing novel interacting objects.

paragraphs: Actions in first-person video often combine a hand movement with an object. Even large datasets cover only a sparse set of these combinations and a limited set of objects. This paper introduces an open-vocabulary action-recognition task in which verbs learned during training must generalize to actions involving both previously seen and novel objects.

The method separates verb prediction from object prediction. An object-agnostic verb encoder models the action component, while a prompt-based object encoder uses CLIP representations to recognize an open vocabulary of interacting objects. This separation directly addresses the need to reuse a learned verb when the object involved changes, including when that object was absent from the training vocabulary.

The authors create benchmarks from EPIC-KITCHENS-100 and Assembly101. In these evaluations, closed-action methods fail to generalize, while the proposed method is effective. Its object encoder also significantly outperforms existing open-vocabulary visual-recognition methods on novel interacting objects. The results support treating action and object recognition separately for this specific generalization challenge.
summary.tldr: Separating verb and object prediction helps first-person action recognition generalize learned verbs to previously unseen interacting objects.

title: Opening the Vocabulary of Egocentric Actions

abstract: Unsupervised node representations learnt using contrastive learning-based methods have shown good performance on downstream tasks. However, these methods rely on augmentations that mimic low-pass filters, limiting their performance on tasks requiring different eigen-spectrum parts. This paper presents a simple filter-based augmentation method to capture different parts of the eigen-spectrum. We show significant improvements using these augmentations. Further, we show that sharing the same weights across these different filter augmentations is possible, reducing the computational load. In addition, previous works have shown that good performance on downstream tasks requires high dimensional representations. Working with high dimensions increases the computations, especially when multiple augmentations are involved. We mitigate this problem and recover good performance through lower dimensional embeddings using simple random Fourier feature projections. Our method, FiGURe, achieves an average gain of up to 4.4\%, compared to the state-of-the-art unsupervised models, across all datasets in consideration, both homophilic and heterophilic. Our code can be found at: https://github.com/Microsoft/figure.

paragraphs: Contrastive methods learn graph-node representations by comparing augmented views of the graph. The paper identifies a restriction in common augmentations: they behave like low-pass filters, emphasizing only part of the graph's eigen-spectrum. Tasks that depend on other spectral components can therefore receive less useful representations, even when the overall learning approach performs well elsewhere.

FiGURe introduces filter-based augmentations that capture different spectral components. The authors show that the same model weights can be shared across these augmentations, reducing computation. They also address the expense of high-dimensional node representations by using random Fourier feature projections, recovering good performance with lower-dimensional embeddings.

Across the datasets considered, FiGURe reports an average gain of up to 4.4% over state-of-the-art unsupervised models. The evaluation includes both homophilic and heterophilic graphs, covering different relationships between connected nodes. The findings support broadening the information exposed through augmentation while controlling the cost of processing multiple views and storing large representations.
summary.tldr: FiGURe improves unsupervised graph representations with diverse spectral filters, shared weights, and efficient lower-dimensional embeddings.

title: FiGURe: Simple and Efficient Unsupervised Node Representations with Filter Augmentations

abstract: As quantum chemical properties have a dependence on their geometries, graph neural networks (GNNs) using 3D geometric information have achieved high prediction accuracy in many tasks. However, they often require 3D geometries obtained from high-level quantum mechanical calculations, which are practically infeasible, limiting their applicability to real-world problems. To tackle this, we propose a new training framework, GeoTMI, that employs denoising process to predict properties accurately using easy-to-obtain geometries (corrupted versions of correct geometries, such as those obtained from low-level calculations). Our starting point was the idea that the correct geometry is the best description of the target property. Hence, to incorporate information of the correct, GeoTMI aims to maximize mutual information between three variables: the correct and the corrupted geometries and the property. GeoTMI also explicitly updates the corrupted input to approach the correct geometry as it passes through the GNN layers, contributing to more effective denoising. We investigated the performance of the proposed method using 3D GNNs for three prediction tasks: molecular properties, a chemical reaction property, and relaxed energy in a heterogeneous catalytic system. Our results showed consistent improvements in accuracy across various tasks, demonstrating the effectiveness and robustness of GeoTMI.

However, obtaining the accurate geometries used by many prediction models can require expensive quantum mechanical calculations. GeoTMI addresses this practical obstacle by training models to work with easier-to-obtain geometries, including those produced by lower-level calculations.

The framework treats these cheaper geometries as corrupted versions of the correct geometry. Starting from the idea that correct geometry best describes the target property, its training objective seeks to maximize mutual information among the correct geometry, corrupted geometry, and property. The authors evaluate GeoTMI with three-dimensional graph neural networks on molecular properties, a chemical reaction property, and relaxed energy in a heterogeneous catalytic system. They report consistent accuracy improvements across these tasks, supporting the usefulness of learning from more accessible geometric inputs.
summary.tldr: GeoTMI improves quantum chemical property prediction from accessible geometries by learning to denoise positions while preserving property-relevant information.

title: GeoTMI: Predicting Quantum Chemical Property with Easy-to-Obtain Geometry via Positional Denoising

abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved remarkable success in solving complex tasks through its integration with deep neural networks (DNNs) as function approximators. However, the reliance on DNNs has introduced a new challenge called primacy bias, whereby these function approximators tend to prioritize early experiences, leading to overfitting. To alleviate this bias, a reset method has been proposed, which involves periodic resets of a portion or the entirety of a deep RL agent while preserving the replay buffer. However, the use of this method can result in performance collapses after executing the reset, raising concerns from the perspective of safe RL and regret minimization. In this paper, we propose a novel reset-based method that leverages deep ensemble learning to address the limitations of the vanilla reset method and enhance sample efficiency. The effectiveness of the proposed method is validated through various experiments including those in the domain of safe RL. Numerical results demonstrate its potential for real-world applications requiring high sample efficiency and safety considerations.

Numerical results demonstrate its potential for real-world applications requiring high sample efficiency and safety considerations.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement learning agents can give disproportionate weight to early experiences, a problem called primacy bias. Their neural networks may overfit to those experiences even as more data becomes available. One proposed remedy periodically resets some or all of an agent while retaining its replay buffer of previously collected experience.

Resets introduce their own difficulty: performance can collapse immediately afterward. That instability matters when evaluating both safety and the cost of poor decisions during learning. This paper proposes a reset-based method using deep ensemble learning to address the shortcomings of ordinary resets while improving how efficiently the agent learns from collected samples.

The authors evaluate the method in several experiments, including safe reinforcement learning settings, and report evidence supporting its effectiveness. The findings suggest that combining ensembles with resets can help manage the tension between escaping early-experience bias and preserving useful behavior during training. The numerical results indicate potential for applications where sample efficiency and safety matter, rather than establishing a universal safety guarantee for deployed agents.
summary.tldr: A reset-based ensemble method addresses early-experience bias and post-reset performance collapse, with experiments supporting improved sample efficiency and safety-related performance.

title: Sample-Efficient and Safe Deep Reinforcement Learning via Reset Deep Ensemble Agents

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have notably accelerated progress towards artificial general intelligence (AGI), with their impressive zero-shot capacity for user-tailored tasks, endowing them with immense potential across a range of applications. However, in the field of computer vision, despite the availability of numerous powerful vision foundation models (VFMs), they are still restricted to tasks in a pre-defined form, struggling to match the open-ended task capabilities of LLMs. In this work, we present an LLM-based framework for vision-centric tasks, termed VisionLLM. This framework provides a unified perspective for vision and language tasks by treating images as a foreign language and aligning vision-centric tasks with language tasks that can be flexibly defined and managed using language instructions. An LLM-based decoder can then make appropriate predictions based on these instructions for open-ended tasks. Extensive experiments show that the proposed VisionLLM can achieve different levels of task customization through language instructions, from fine-grained object-level to coarse-grained task-level customization, all with good results. It's noteworthy that, with a generalist LLM-based framework, our model can achieve over 60% mAP on COCO, on par with detection-specific models. We hope this model can set a new baseline for generalist vision and language models. The code shall be released.

It uses a language-model-based framework in which the task definition can be expressed and adjusted through language.

The framework treats images as another language and aligns vision tasks with language tasks. An LLM-based decoder then produces predictions according to the supplied instructions. The authors investigate customization at different scales, from instructions concerning particular objects to instructions defining a broader task. This makes the instruction part of specifying what the model should predict.

Experiments show good results across these levels of customization. The model also exceeds 60% mean average precision on COCO, placing its reported detection performance on par with detection-specific models despite using a generalist framework. That result links flexibility with a concrete vision benchmark: the paper demonstrates that an instruction-driven LLM decoder can support task customization while retaining competitive detection performance in the evaluated setting.
summary.tldr: VisionLLM uses a language-model decoder for instruction-customizable vision tasks while reporting detection performance comparable to specialized models.

title: VisionLLM: Large Language Model is also an Open-Ended Decoder for Vision-Centric Tasks

abstract: Recent years have seen a growing interest in accelerating optimization algorithms with machine-learned predictions. Sakaue and Oki (NeurIPS 2022) have developed a general framework that warm-starts the *L-convex function minimization* method with predictions, revealing the idea's usefulness for various discrete optimization problems. In this paper, we present a framework for using predictions to accelerate *M-convex function minimization*, thus complementing previous research and extending the range of discrete optimization algorithms that can benefit from predictions. Our framework is particularly effective for an important subclass called *laminar convex minimization*, which appears in many operations research applications. Our methods can improve time complexity bounds upon the best worst-case results by using predictions and even have potential to go beyond a lower-bound result.

paragraphs: Machine-learned predictions can provide useful guidance to optimization algorithms before they begin their search. This paper studies that idea for M-convex function minimization, a class of discrete optimization problems. Its aim is to improve computational efficiency by giving an algorithm predictive information in addition to the optimization problem itself.

Earlier work established a framework for using predictions to warm-start L-convex minimization. The authors develop a corresponding framework for M-convex minimization, extending the range of discrete problems that can benefit from this approach. They identify laminar convex minimization, an important subclass appearing in operations research, as a particularly effective setting for their methods.

The theoretical results show that predictions can improve time-complexity bounds relative to the best existing worst-case results. The authors also describe potential to surpass a lower-bound result using this additional information. These are claims about what prediction-assisted algorithms can achieve; the abstract does not claim that every prediction accelerates every instance. The contribution broadens the theoretical foundation for combining learned guidance with structured optimization.
summary.tldr: The paper develops prediction-assisted algorithms that can accelerate M-convex minimization, particularly its laminar subclass.

title: Faster Discrete Convex Function Minimization with Predictions: The M-Convex Case

abstract: We present the HOH (Human-Object-Human) Handover Dataset, a large object count dataset with 136 objects, to accelerate data-driven research on handover studies, human-robot handover implementation, and artificial intelligence (AI) on handover parameter estimation from 2D and 3D data of two-person interactions. HOH contains multi-view RGB and depth data, skeletons, fused point clouds, grasp type and handedness labels, object, giver hand, and receiver hand 2D and 3D segmentations, giver and receiver comfort ratings, and paired object metadata and aligned 3D models for 2,720 handover interactions spanning 136 objects and 20 giver-receiver pairs—40 with role-reversal—organized from 40 participants. We also show experimental results of neural networks trained using HOH to perform grasp, orientation, and trajectory prediction. As the only fully markerless handover capture dataset, HOH represents natural human-human handover interactions, overcoming challenges with markered datasets that require specific suiting for body tracking, and lack high-resolution hand tracking. To date, HOH is the largest handover dataset in terms of object count, participant count, pairs with role reversal accounted for, and total interactions captured.

paragraphs: Human-object-human handovers require coordinated grasping, movement, and timing. The HOH dataset captures these interactions without body-tracking markers, aiming to preserve natural behavior while supporting research on handover prediction and eventual human-robot interaction.

It contains 2,720 interactions involving 136 objects and 40 participants, organized into 20 giver-receiver pairs or 40 with role reversal. Data include multiview color and depth, skeletons, fused point clouds, grasp and handedness labels, hand and object segmentations, comfort ratings, object metadata, and aligned three-dimensional models.

The authors train networks for grasp, orientation, and trajectory prediction to demonstrate uses of the resource. The abstract does not provide those models’ numerical performance or claim a deployed robot-handover system. Its primary contribution is the breadth of markerless interaction capture and annotation, with model experiments showing how the data can support several related prediction tasks.
summary.tldr: HOH records markerless human handovers with rich multimodal annotations across 136 objects.

title: HOH: Markerless Multimodal Human-Object-Human Handover Dataset with Large Object Count

abstract: Most work on the formal verification of neural networks has focused on bounding the set of outputs that correspond to a given set of inputs (for example, bounded perturbations of a nominal input). However, many use cases of neural network verification require solving the inverse problem, or over-approximating the set of inputs that lead to certain outputs. We present the INVPROP algorithm for verifying properties over the preimage of a linearly constrained output set, which can be combined with branch-and-bound to increase precision. Contrary to other approaches, our efficient algorithm is GPU-accelerated and does not require a linear programming solver. We demonstrate our algorithm for identifying safe control regions for a dynamical system via backward reachability analysis, verifying adversarial robustness, and detecting out-of-distribution inputs to a neural network. Our results show that in certain settings, we find over-approximations over $2500\times$ tighter than prior work while being $2.5\times$ faster. By strengthening robustness verification with output constraints, we consistently verify more properties than the previous state-of-the-art on multiple benchmarks, including a large model with 167k neurons in VNN-COMP 2023. Our algorithm has been incorporated into the $\alpha,\beta$-CROWN verifier, available at https://abcrown.org.

paragraphs: Neural-network verification often starts with a set of inputs and bounds the possible outputs. Many applications need the reverse: which inputs could produce outputs satisfying certain conditions? This paper introduces INVPROP to bound that preimage, focusing on output sets described by linear constraints.

INVPROP computes an over-approximation, an enclosing set for the relevant inputs. It can be combined with branch-and-bound to improve precision. The algorithm runs on GPUs and avoids requiring a linear-programming solver. The authors demonstrate uses in backward reachability for safe control regions, adversarial-robustness verification, and detection of out-of-distribution inputs.

In certain settings, the resulting over-approximations are more than 2,500 times tighter than those from prior work while computation is 2.5 times faster. Those ratios are specific to the reported settings. Using output constraints also lets the method consistently verify more robustness properties across multiple benchmarks, including a model with 167,000 neurons. Its integration into the α,β-CROWN verifier connects the inverse-analysis capability to an existing verification system.
summary.tldr: INVPROP efficiently bounds which inputs can produce constrained outputs, improving preimage precision and robustness verification in the reported evaluations.

title: Provably Bounding Neural Network Preimages

abstract: Combining test statistics from independent trials or experiments is a popular method of meta-analysis. However, there is very limited theoretical understanding of the power of the combined test, especially in high-dimensional models considering composite hypotheses tests. We derive a mathematical framework to study standard {meta-analysis} testing approaches in the context of the many normal means model, which serves as the platform to investigate more complex models.We introduce a natural and mild restriction on the meta-level combination functions of the local trials. This allows us to mathematically quantify the cost of compressing $m$ trials into real-valued test statistics and combining these. We then derive minimax lower and matching upper bounds for the separation rates of standard combination methods for e.g. p-values and e-values, quantifying the loss relative to using the full, pooled data. We observe an elbow effect, revealing that in certain cases combining the locally optimal tests in each trial results in a sub-optimal {meta-analysis} method and develop approaches to achieve the global optima. We also explore the possible gains of allowing limited coordination between the trial designs. Our results connect meta-analysis with bandwidth constraint distributed inference and build on recent information theoretic developments in the latter field.

paragraphs: Meta-analysis often combines a single statistical summary from each independent study instead of pooling all observations. This paper asks how much ability to detect a signal is lost through that compression. It develops a theoretical framework in the many normal means model, with particular attention to high-dimensional testing and hypotheses that contain multiple possibilities.

Under a stated mild restriction on how study summaries are combined, the authors derive matching lower and upper bounds on separation rates. These rates describe the signal strength needed for reliable detection. The results cover standard combinations of quantities such as p-values and e-values, making the information loss relative to pooled data mathematically explicit.

A central finding is an elbow effect: in some regimes, combining tests that are individually optimal does not produce an optimal overall test. The authors develop approaches that attain global optima and investigate possible benefits from limited coordination between study designs. This links meta-analysis to distributed inference under communication constraints, where the choice of information to transmit can matter as much as local statistical quality.
summary.tldr: The paper quantifies information lost when combining study-level tests and shows that locally optimal tests can yield suboptimal meta-analysis.

title: Optimal testing using combined test statistics across independent studies

abstract: Existing full text datasets of U.S. public domain newspapers do not recognize the often complex layouts of newspaper scans, and as a result the digitized content scrambles texts from articles, headlines, captions, advertisements, and other layout regions. OCR quality can also be low. This study develops a novel, deep learning pipeline for extracting full article texts from newspaper images and applies it to the nearly 20 million scans in Library of Congress's public domain Chronicling America collection. The pipeline includes layout detection, legibility classification, custom OCR, and association of article texts spanning multiple bounding boxes. To achieve high scalability, it is built with efficient architectures designed for mobile phones. The resulting American Stories dataset provides high quality data that could be used for pre-training a large language model to achieve better understanding of historical English and historical world knowledge. The dataset could also be added to the external database of a retrieval-augmented language model to make historical information - ranging from interpretations of political events to minutiae about the lives of people's ancestors - more widely accessible. Furthermore, structured article texts facilitate using transformer-based methods for popular social science applications like topic classification, detection of reproduced content, and news story clustering. Finally, American Stories provides a massive silver quality dataset for innovating multimodal layout analysis models and other multimodal applications.

paragraphs: Historical newspaper scans contain complicated page layouts, so converting them into text requires more than recognizing individual letters. Existing collections can mix together articles, headlines, captions, and advertisements. American Stories addresses this problem by extracting complete articles while preserving the distinctions between different regions of a newspaper page.

The researchers built a deep learning pipeline and applied it to nearly 20 million scans from the Library of Congress’s Chronicling America collection. The pipeline detects layout regions, evaluates legibility, performs custom optical character recognition, and connects article text distributed across multiple boxes. Efficient architectures originally designed for mobile phones make processing this large collection feasible.

The resulting structured texts could support language model training on historical English or provide historical material for retrieval-based systems. They also make article classification, reproduced-content detection, and story clustering more accessible to transformer methods. These are potential uses rather than reported improvements to particular language models. The collection additionally provides large-scale, automatically produced training material for research on document layout and multimodal analysis.
summary.tldr: American Stories turns nearly 20 million historical newspaper scans into structured article texts for language and document research.

title: American Stories: A Large-Scale Structured Text Dataset of Historical U.S. Newspapers

abstract: While neural networks (NNs) have a large potential as autonomous controllers for Cyber-Physical Systems, verifying the safety of neural network based control systems (NNCSs) poses significant challenges for the practical use of NNs— especially when safety is needed for unbounded time horizons. One reason for this is the intractability of analyzing NNs, ODEs and hybrid systems. To this end, we introduce VerSAILLE (Verifiably Safe AI via Logically Linked Envelopes): The first general approach that allows reusing control theory literature for NNCS verification. By joining forces, we can exploit the efficiency of NN verification tools while retaining the rigor of differential dynamic logic (dL). Based on a provably safe control envelope in dL, we derive a specification for the NN which is proven with NN verification tools. We show that a proof of the NN’s adherence to the specification is then mirrored by a dL proof on the infinite-time safety of the NNCS.The NN verification properties resulting from hybrid systems typically contain nonlinear arithmetic over formulas with arbitrary logical structure while efficient NN verification tools merely support linear constraints. To overcome this divide, we present Mosaic: An efficient, sound and complete verification approach for polynomial real arithmetic properties on piece-wise linear NNs. Mosaic partitions complex NN verification queries into simple queries and lifts off-the-shelf linear constraint tools to the nonlinear setting in a completeness-preserving manner by combining approximation with exact reasoning for counterexample regions. In our evaluation we demonstrate the versatility of VerSAILLE and Mosaic: We prove infinite-time safety on the classical Vertical Airborne Collision Avoidance NNCS verification benchmark for some scenarios while (exhaustively) enumerating counterexample regions in unsafe scenarios. We also show that our approach significantly outperforms the State-of-the-Art tools in closed-loop NNV

paragraphs: Proving a neural controller safe indefinitely requires reasoning about both the network and the physical system it controls. VerSAILLE connects these tasks through a control envelope already proved safe in differential dynamic logic. From that envelope, it derives a specification for the neural network. Proving that the network satisfies this specification yields a corresponding infinite-time safety proof for the controlled system.

A technical obstacle is that these specifications can contain nonlinear arithmetic and complex logical structure, whereas efficient neural-network verification tools often support only linear constraints. The paper introduces Mosaic to bridge that gap. For polynomial real-arithmetic properties of piecewise-linear networks, Mosaic provides sound and complete verification by splitting queries and combining approximation with exact reasoning about counterexample regions.

On the Vertical Airborne Collision Avoidance benchmark, the approach proves infinite-time safety for some scenarios and exhaustively enumerates counterexample regions in unsafe ones. It also substantially outperforms evaluated closed-loop verification tools. The safety conclusion remains tied to the proved envelope and verified network specification; the method establishes that connection rather than assuming every tested controller is safe.
summary.tldr: VerSAILLE links neural-network specifications to infinite-time control safety proofs, while Mosaic verifies the nonlinear properties needed for that link.

title: Provably Safe Neural Network Controllers via Differential Dynamic Logic

abstract: The pretraining data of today's strongest language models remains opaque, even when their parameters are open-sourced.In particular, little is known about the proportions of different domains, languages, or code represented in the data. While a long line of membership inference attacks aim to identify training examples on an instance level, they do not extend easily to *global* statistics about the corpus. In this work, we tackle a task which we call *data mixture inference*, which aims to uncover the distributional make-up of the pretraining data. We introduce a novel attack based on a previously overlooked source of information — byte-pair encoding (BPE) tokenizers, used by the vast majority of modern language models. Our key insight is that the ordered vocabulary learned by a BPE tokenizer naturally reveals information about the token frequencies in its training data: the first token is the most common byte pair, the second is the most common pair after merging the first token, and so on. Given a tokenizer's merge list along with data samples for each category of interest (e.g., different natural languages), we formulate a linear program that solves for the relative proportion of each category in the tokenizer's training set. Importantly, to the extent to which tokenizer training data is representative of the pretraining data, we indirectly learn about the pretraining data. In controlled experiments, we show that our attack can recover mixture ratios with high precision for tokenizers trained on known mixtures of natural languages, programming languages, and data sources. We then apply our approach to off-the-shelf tokenizers released alongside recent LMs. We confirm much publicly disclosed information about these models, and also make several new inferences: GPT-4o is much more multilingual than its predecessors, training on 10x more non-English data than GPT-3.5, Llama 3 and Claude are trained on predominantly code, and many recent models are trained on 7-16% books. We hope our work sheds light on current design practices for pretraining data, and inspires continued research into data mixture inference for LMs.

This paper studies data mixture inference: estimating those overall proportions instead of identifying individual training examples. Its information source is the byte-pair encoding tokenizer released with a model.

A tokenizer's ordered merge list reflects which byte pairs were frequent as its vocabulary was constructed. Given that list and sample data from categories of interest, the authors formulate a linear program to estimate the categories' relative proportions in the tokenizer's training set. Extending those estimates to model pretraining depends on how representative the tokenizer's data is of the model's data.

Applied to released tokenizers, the method confirms some disclosed information and produces additional inferences about multilingual data, code, and books. Those are indirect corpus estimates subject to the representativeness condition. The work shows that tokenizer construction can expose aggregate information even when the underlying pretraining corpus remains undisclosed.
summary.tldr: BPE merge lists can reveal tokenizer training mixtures and, when representative, support indirect estimates of a language model's pretraining composition.

title: Data Mixture Inference Attack: BPE Tokenizers Reveal Training Data Compositions

abstract: The sim-to-real gap, which represents the disparity between training and testing environments, poses a significant challenge in reinforcement learning (RL). A promising approach to addressing this challenge is distributionally robust RL, often framed as a robust Markov decision process (RMDP). In this framework, the objective is to find a robust policy that achieves good performance under the worst-case scenario among all environments within a pre-specified uncertainty set centered around the training environment. Unlike previous work, which relies on a generative model or a pre-collected offline dataset enjoying good coverage of the deployment environment, we tackle robust RL via interactive data collection, where the learner interacts with the training environment only and refines the policy through trial and error. In this robust RL paradigm, two main challenges emerge: managing distributional robustness while striking a balance between exploration and exploitation during data collection. Initially, we establish that sample-efficient learning without additional assumptions is unattainable owing to the curse of support shift; i.e., the potential disjointedness of the distributional supports between the training and testing environments. To circumvent such a hardness result, we introduce the vanishing minimal value assumption to RMDPs with a total-variation (TV) distance robust set, postulating that the minimal value of the optimal robust value function is zero. We prove that such an assumption effectively eliminates the support shift issue for RMDPs with a TV distance robust set, and present an algorithm with a provable sample complexity guarantee. Our work makes the initial step to uncovering the inherent difficulty of robust RL via interactive data collection and sufficient conditions for designing a sample-efficient algorithm accompanied by sharp sample complexity analysis.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning policy may perform poorly when deployment differs from training. Distributionally robust learning addresses this by optimizing performance in the worst environment within a specified uncertainty set. This paper studies how to learn such a policy when the agent can collect data only by interacting with the training environment.

The authors establish a fundamental obstacle: sample-efficient learning is impossible in general without additional assumptions. The issue is support shift, where deployment may involve outcomes that training interactions cannot reveal. The learner must therefore manage more than the usual exploration problem; some relevant deployment behavior may lie outside what it can observe.

For uncertainty sets defined using total-variation distance, the authors introduce a sufficient condition: the smallest value of the optimal robust value function is zero. They prove that this condition removes the support-shift obstacle in that setting and give an algorithm with a sample-complexity guarantee. The contribution identifies both a general hardness result and a specific assumption under which efficient interactive robust learning becomes possible.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes a barrier to interactive robust reinforcement learning and a sufficient condition that enables sample-efficient learning.

title: Distributionally Robust Reinforcement Learning with Interactive Data Collection: Fundamental Hardness and Near-Optimal Algorithms

abstract: We present AROMA (Attentive Reduced Order Model with Attention), a framework designed to enhance the modeling of partial differential equations (PDEs) using local neural fields. Our flexible encoder-decoder architecture can obtain smooth latent representations of spatial physical fields from a variety of data types, including irregular-grid inputs and point clouds. This versatility eliminates the need for patching and allows efficient processing of diverse geometries. The sequential nature of our latent representation can be interpreted spatially and permits the use of a conditional transformer for modeling the temporal dynamics of PDEs. By employing a diffusion-based formulation, we achieve greater stability and enable longer rollouts compared to conventional MSE training. AROMA's superior performance in simulating 1D and 2D equations underscores the efficacy of our approach in capturing complex dynamical behaviors.

paragraphs: AROMA models physical systems described by partial differential equations using a compact representation that retains spatial meaning. Its encoder and decoder use local neural fields to represent physical quantities across space. They can handle irregular grids and point clouds, allowing the framework to work with different geometries without first dividing the input into patches.

The resulting latent representation is smooth and arranged as a sequence whose elements can be interpreted spatially. This gives a conditional transformer a structured representation on which to model changes over time. The approach therefore connects flexible spatial encoding with temporal prediction, keeping spatial organization available after the original physical field has been compressed.

AROMA uses a diffusion-based formulation for modeling these dynamics. The authors report greater stability and longer successive predictions than conventional training based on mean squared error. Experiments on one- and two-dimensional equations show superior simulation performance. These results connect the framework's spatial representation and temporal formulation to its ability to reproduce complex dynamics over longer rollouts.
summary.tldr: AROMA combines spatially interpretable local neural fields with diffusion-based temporal modeling to improve PDE simulation stability and rollout length.

title: AROMA: Preserving Spatial Structure for Latent PDE Modeling with Local Neural Fields

abstract: The brain prepares for learning even before interacting with the environment, by refining and optimizing its structures through spontaneous neural activity that resembles random noise. However, the mechanism of such a process has yet to be understood, and it is unclear whether this process can benefit the algorithm of machine learning. Here, we study this issue using a neural network with a feedback alignment algorithm, demonstrating that pretraining neural networks with random noise increases the learning efficiency as well as generalization abilities without weight transport. First, we found that random noise training modifies forward weights to match backward synaptic feedback, which is necessary for teaching errors by feedback alignment. As a result, a network with pre-aligned weights learns notably faster and reaches higher accuracy than a network without random noise training, even comparable to the backpropagation algorithm. We also found that the effective dimensionality of weights decreases in a network pretrained with random noise. This pre-regularization allows the network to learn simple solutions of a low rank, reducing the generalization error during subsequent training. This also enables the network to robustly generalize a novel, out-of-distribution dataset. Lastly, we confirmed that random noise pretraining reduces the amount of meta-loss, enhancing the network ability to adapt to various tasks. Overall, our results suggest that random noise training with feedback alignment offers a straightforward yet effective method of pretraining that facilitates quick and reliable learning without weight transport.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether random-noise pre-training can prepare a neural network for later learning. Inspired by spontaneous neural activity, the authors study networks trained with feedback alignment, an approach that teaches through backward feedback without weight transport. The biological motivation frames the question, while the reported findings concern the studied learning algorithm.

Noise pre-training changes forward weights so they align with backward feedback, preparing the network to use teaching errors. The resulting networks learn faster and reach higher accuracy than networks without this preparation, with performance reported as comparable to backpropagation. The authors also find that noise pre-training lowers the effective dimensionality of the weights.

That reduced dimensionality acts as pre-regularization: subsequent training learns simpler, low-rank solutions with lower generalization error. The study also reports robust generalization to a novel out-of-distribution dataset and reduced meta-loss, indicating improved adaptation across tasks. Together, the results suggest that noise can serve as useful preparation for feedback-alignment learning before task-specific training begins.
summary.tldr: Random-noise pre-training improves feedback-alignment learning by aligning forward weights with feedback and encouraging simpler subsequent solutions.

title: Pretraining with Random Noise for Fast and Robust Learning without Weight Transport

abstract: It has repeatedly been observed that loss minimization by stochastic gradient descent (SGD) leads to heavy-tailed distributions of neural network parameters. Here, we analyze a continuous diffusion approximation of SGD, called homogenized stochastic gradient descent (hSGD), and show in a regularized linear regression framework that it leads to an asymptotically heavy-tailed parameter distribution, even though local gradient noise is Gaussian. We give explicit upper and lower bounds on the tail-index of the resulting parameter distribution and validate these bounds in numerical experiments. Moreover, the explicit form of these bounds enables us to quantify the interplay between optimization hyperparameters and the tail-index. Doing so, we contribute to the ongoing discussion on links between heavy tails and the generalization performance of neural networks as well as the ability of SGD to avoid suboptimal local minima.

paragraphs: Neural-network parameters trained with stochastic gradient descent have repeatedly been observed to follow heavy-tailed distributions. Such distributions allow unusually large parameter values more readily than a Gaussian distribution would. The paper investigates how this behavior can arise from the training dynamics themselves, even when the local noise is Gaussian.

The analysis studies homogenized stochastic gradient descent, a continuous diffusion approximation to SGD, within regularized linear regression. In this setting, the authors show that the parameter distribution becomes heavy-tailed asymptotically. The result distinguishes the distribution of local gradient noise from the distribution produced by the evolving optimization process.

The authors derive explicit upper and lower bounds on the tail index, which describes the heaviness of the resulting tails, and validate those bounds numerically. Their formulas also quantify how optimization hyperparameters interact with that index. This contributes a concrete theoretical mechanism to discussions about heavy tails, generalization, and escaping poor local minima, without establishing those broader benefits for neural networks in general.
summary.tldr: A diffusion approximation to SGD develops heavy-tailed parameter distributions in regularized linear regression despite Gaussian local gradient noise.

title: Emergence of heavy tails in homogenized stochastic gradient descent

abstract: Recent advancements in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have enabled complex multimodal tasks by processing text and image data simultaneously, significantly enhancing the field of artificial intelligence. However, these models often exhibit biases that can skew outputs towards societal stereotypes, thus necessitating debiasing strategies. Existing debiasing methods focus narrowly on specific modalities or tasks, and require extensive retraining. To address these limitations, this paper introduces Selective Feature Imputation for Debiasing (SFID), a novel methodology that integrates feature pruning and low confidence imputation (LCI) to effectively reduce biases in VLMs. SFID is versatile, maintaining the semantic integrity of outputs and costly effective by eliminating the need for retraining. Our experimental results demonstrate SFID's effectiveness across various VLMs tasks including zero-shot classification, text-to-image retrieval, image captioning, and text-to-image generation, by significantly reducing gender biases without compromising performance. This approach not only enhances the fairness of VLMs applications but also preserves their efficiency and utility across diverse scenarios.

This approach not only enhances the fairness of VLMs applications but also preserves their efficiency and utility across diverse scenarios.

paragraphs: Models that process both images and text can reproduce societal stereotypes in their outputs. Addressing these biases becomes difficult when a correction only works for one task or one type of input, or requires expensive retraining. This paper proposes a shared debiasing approach that can operate across several uses of vision-language models.

The method, Selective Feature Imputation for Debiasing, combines feature pruning with a procedure called low confidence imputation. It intervenes in the model's features, removing selected information and using imputation as part of the correction. The intended balance is to reduce biased behavior while retaining the meaning needed to perform the original task. The approach does not require retraining.

The experiments cover zero-shot classification, text-to-image retrieval, image captioning, and text-to-image generation. Across these evaluated tasks, the authors report significant reductions in gender bias without a loss of task performance. These results support the usefulness of a feature-based intervention across different multimodal applications. Its practical appeal comes from combining the reported bias reductions with preserved utility and avoiding the cost of training the models again.
summary.tldr: SFID reduces gender bias across several vision-language tasks through feature pruning and imputation without retraining.

title: A Unified Debiasing Approach for Vision-Language Models across Modalities and Tasks

abstract: Recently, prompt learning has emerged as the state-of-the-art (SOTA) for fair text-to-image (T2I) generation. Specifically, this approach leverages readily available reference images to learn inclusive prompts for each target Sensitive Attribute (tSA), allowing for fair image generation. In this work, we first reveal that this prompt learning-based approach results in degraded sample quality. Our analysis shows that the approach's training objective--which aims to align the embedding differences of learned prompts and reference images-- could be sub-optimal, resulting in distortion of the learned prompts and degraded generated images. To further substantiate this claim, **as our major contribution**, we deep dive into the denoising subnetwork of the T2I model to track down the effect of these learned prompts by analyzing the cross-attention maps. In our analysis, we propose a novel prompt switching analysis: I2H and H2I. Furthermore, we propose new quantitative characterization of cross-attention maps. Our analysis reveals abnormalities in the early denoising steps, perpetuating improper global structure that results in degradation in the generated samples. Building on insights from our analysis, we propose two ideas: (i) *Prompt Queuing* and (ii) *Attention Amplification* to address the quality issue. Extensive experimental results on a wide range of tSAs show that our proposed method outperforms SOTA approach's image generation quality, while achieving competitive fairness. More resources at FairQueue Project site: https://sutd-visual-computing-group.github.io/FairQueue

paragraphs: Prompt learning for fair text-to-image generation uses reference images to learn inclusive prompts for target sensitive attributes. This paper finds that the approach can degrade image quality. The authors suggest that its objective, which aligns differences between prompt and image embeddings, may distort the learned prompts.

The main contribution is an investigation of how those prompts affect the model's denoising process. The authors introduce two prompt-switching analyses, I2H and H2I, and quantitative descriptions of cross-attention maps. These analyses locate abnormalities in early denoising steps, where problems in global image structure can arise and persist into the generated result.

Across experiments covering a wide range of sensitive attributes, it improves image quality over the state-of-the-art approach while maintaining competitive fairness. The result matters because evaluating fair generation also requires attention to the visual effects of the intervention. Here, examining intermediate attention behavior provides the basis for improving that balance.
summary.tldr: FairQueue traces quality degradation in fairness-oriented prompt learning to early denoising behavior and improves image quality while retaining competitive fairness.

title: FairQueue: Rethinking Prompt Learning for Fair Text-to-Image Generation

abstract: We introduce a novel capacity measure 2sED for statistical models based on the effective dimension. The new quantity provably bounds the generalization error under mild assumptions on the model. Furthermore, simulations on standard data sets and popular model architectures show that 2sED correlates well with the training error. For Markovian models, we show how to efficiently approximate 2sED from below through a layerwise iterative approach, which allows us to tackle deep learning models with a large number of parameters. Simulation results suggest that the approximation is good for different prominent models and data sets.

paragraphs: The paper introduces 2sED, a measure of statistical model capacity built on effective dimension. Its purpose is to characterize model complexity in a way that connects to learning behavior. Under mild assumptions on the model, the authors prove that this quantity bounds generalization error, giving it a theoretical connection to performance beyond training data.

The authors also examine the measure through simulations using standard datasets and popular architectures. They find that 2sED correlates well with training error. This is a separate finding from the generalization bound: one is an empirical relationship with fitting the observed data, while the other is a mathematical guarantee under stated assumptions.

Computing complexity measures can become difficult for networks with many parameters. For Markovian models, the paper develops an iterative, layer-by-layer approximation that approaches 2sED from below. Simulations suggest this approximation is good across several prominent models and datasets. Together, these results offer both a theoretically grounded capacity measure and a practical route to estimating it for large deep-learning models.
summary.tldr: 2sED is a model-capacity measure with a conditional generalization bound and a scalable lower approximation for Markovian models.

title: A two-scale Complexity Measure for Deep Learning Models

abstract: The goal of *generalized* few-shot semantic segmentation (GFSS) is to recognize *novel-class* objects through training with a few annotated examples and the *base-class* model that learned the knowledge about the base classes.Unlike the classic few-shot semantic segmentation, GFSS aims to classify pixels into both base and novel classes, meaning it is a more practical setting.Current GFSS methods rely on several techniques such as using combinations of customized modules, carefully designed loss functions, meta-learning, and transductive learning.However, we found that a simple rule and standard supervised learning substantially improve the GFSS performance.In this paper, we propose a simple yet effective method for GFSS that does not use the techniques mentioned above.Also, we theoretically show that our method perfectly maintains the segmentation performance of the base-class model over most of the base classes.Through numerical experiments, we demonstrated the effectiveness of our method.It improved in novel-class segmentation performance in the $1$-shot scenario by $6.1$% on the PASCAL-$5^i$ dataset, $4.7$% on the PASCAL-$10^i$ dataset, and $1.0$% on the COCO-$20^i$ dataset.Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/IBM/BCM.

paragraphs: Generalized few-shot semantic segmentation asks a model to label image pixels belonging to both familiar categories and new categories learned from very few annotated examples. This makes adding new knowledge only part of the problem: the model must also retain its ability to recognize categories it already learned.

The paper proposes a method built around a simple rule and standard supervised learning. It avoids the customized modules, specially designed losses, meta-learning, and transductive learning used by existing approaches. The authors also provide a theoretical result showing that their method perfectly preserves the original model's segmentation performance for most base classes. That qualification matters: the stated preservation result does not cover every base class.

Experiments support the method's effectiveness. In the one-shot setting, the authors report novel-class segmentation improvements of 6.1% on PASCAL-5i, 4.7% on PASCAL-10i, and 1.0% on COCO-20i. Together, the theoretical and experimental findings show that a comparatively simple learning procedure can improve recognition of new categories while retaining substantial existing capability.
summary.tldr: A simple supervised method improves few-shot segmentation of new categories and theoretically preserves performance for most previously learned categories.

title: A Surprisingly Simple Approach to Generalized Few-Shot Semantic Segmentation

abstract: Despite alleviating the dependence on dense annotations inherent to fully supervised methods, weakly supervised point cloud semantic segmentation suffers from inadequate supervision signals. In response to this challenge, we introduce a novel perspective that imparts auxiliary constraints by regulating the feature space under weak supervision. Our initial investigation identifies which distributions accurately characterize the feature space, subsequently leveraging this priori to guide the alignment of the weakly supervised embeddings. Specifically, we analyze the superiority of the mixture of von Mises-Fisher distributions (moVMF) among several common distribution candidates. Accordingly, we develop a Distribution Guidance Network (DGNet), which comprises a weakly supervised learning branch and a distribution alignment branch. Leveraging reliable clustering initialization derived from the weakly supervised learning branch, the distribution alignment branch alternately updates the parameters of the moVMF and the network, ensuring alignment with the moVMF-defined latent space. Extensive experiments validate the rationality and effectiveness of our distribution choice and network design. Consequently, DGNet achieves state-of-the-art performance under multiple datasets and various weakly supervised settings.

paragraphs: Assigning semantic categories to points in a 3D point cloud normally requires extensive annotation. Weak supervision reduces that burden, but leaves the model with fewer signals about how to organize its learned representations. This paper adds guidance by constraining the distribution of those representations, rather than relying only on the available labels.

The authors compare several candidate distributions and identify a mixture of von Mises-Fisher distributions as particularly suitable for the feature space they study. Their Distribution Guidance Network has two branches: one learns from weak supervision, while the other aligns features with the selected distribution. Clustering information from the first branch provides a reliable initialization for the second.

The alignment branch alternates between updating the distribution parameters and updating the network. This lets the distribution model and learned features adjust together. Experiments support both the distribution choice and the architecture, with reported state-of-the-art performance across multiple datasets and weak supervision settings. The findings show how feature organization can supply useful additional constraints when direct annotation is sparse.
summary.tldr: DGNet improves weakly supervised point-cloud segmentation by aligning learned features with a fitted mixture distribution.

title: Distribution Guidance Network for Weakly Supervised Point Cloud Semantic Segmentation

abstract: Perceptual learning refers to the practices through which participants learn to improve their performance in perceiving sensory stimuli. Two seemingly conflicting phenomena of specificity and transfer have been widely observed in perceptual learning. Here, we propose a dual-learning model to reconcile these two phenomena. The model consists of two learning processes. One is task-based learning, which is fast and enables the brain to adapt to a task rapidly by using existing feature representations. The other is feature-based learning, which is slow and enables the brain to improve feature representations to match the statistical change of the environment. Associated with different training paradigms, the interactions between these two learning processes induce the rich phenomena of perceptual learning. Specifically, in the training paradigm where the same stimulus condition is presented excessively, feature-based learning is triggered, which incurs specificity, while in the paradigm where the stimulus condition varies during the training, task-based learning dominates to induce the transfer effect. As the number of training sessions under the same stimulus condition increases, a transition from transfer to specificity occurs. We demonstrate that the dual-learning model can account for both the specificity and transfer phenomena observed in classical psychophysical experiments. We hope that this study gives us insight into understanding how the brain balances the accomplishment of a new task and the consumption of learning effort.

paragraphs: Perceptual practice sometimes improves performance only under the trained conditions, while other training allows improvements to transfer. This paper proposes a dual-learning model to explain both patterns. Its central idea is that learning to perform a task and changing the sensory features used for that task operate on different timescales.

The fast process adapts task performance using feature representations that already exist. The slower process changes those representations to match shifts in environmental statistics. According to the model, repeatedly presenting the same stimulus condition triggers feature learning and produces specificity. When stimulus conditions vary during training, task learning dominates and produces transfer.

The interaction also explains a transition from transfer to specificity as training under a single condition accumulates. The authors show that the model can account for both effects observed in classical psychophysical experiments. This offers a unified interpretation of apparently conflicting learning outcomes through differences in training conditions and duration. The broader proposal is that perceptual learning balances adapting to a task with the effort of modifying representations.
summary.tldr: A model combining fast task learning and slow feature learning explains both transfer and specificity in perceptual practice.

title: To Learn or Not to Learn, That is the Question — A Feature-Task Dual Learning Model of Perceptual Learning

abstract: Deep learning-based feature matching has shown great superiority for point cloud registration in the absence of pose priors. Although coarse-to-fine matching approaches are prevalent, the coarse matching of existing methods is typically sparse and loose without consideration of geometric consistency, which makes the subsequent fine matching rely on ineffective optimal transport and hypothesis-and-selection methods for consistency. Therefore, these methods are neither efficient nor scalable for real-time applications such as odometry in robotics. To address these issues, we design a consistency-aware spot-guided Transformer (CAST), which incorporates a spot-guided cross-attention module to avoid interfering with irrelevant areas, and a consistency-aware self-attention module to enhance matching capabilities with geometrically consistent correspondences. Furthermore, a lightweight fine matching module for both sparse keypoints and dense features can estimate the transformation accurately. Extensive experiments on both outdoor LiDAR point cloud datasets and indoor RGBD point cloud datasets demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art accuracy, efficiency, and robustness.

paragraphs: Point cloud registration aligns two collections of 3D points describing a scene. CAST addresses this task without requiring prior knowledge of their relative pose. The paper targets a weakness in coarse-to-fine matching: early correspondences can be sparse and geometrically inconsistent, leaving later stages with substantial work to recover a coherent alignment.

CAST introduces two attention mechanisms that address this problem during feature matching. Spot-guided cross-attention focuses comparisons on relevant regions across the point clouds, reducing interference from unrelated areas. Consistency-aware self-attention strengthens correspondences that agree geometrically. Together, these components make geometric agreement part of the matching process before the final alignment is estimated.

A lightweight fine-matching module then estimates the transformation using either sparse keypoints or dense features. Experiments on outdoor LiDAR and indoor RGBD datasets report state-of-the-art accuracy, efficiency, and robustness. These findings support the approach across both sensing settings and connect its early consistency checks to the practical need for efficient registration in applications such as robotic odometry.
summary.tldr: CAST improves point cloud alignment by directing attention toward relevant regions and geometrically consistent matches.

title: A Consistency-Aware Spot-Guided Transformer for Versatile and Hierarchical Point Cloud Registration

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently showcased remarkable capabilities, spanning a wide range of tasks and applications, including those in the medical domain. Models like GPT-4 excel in medical question answering but may face challenges in the lack of interpretability when handling complex tasks in real clinical settings. We thus introduce the diagnostic reasoning dataset for clinical notes (DiReCT), aiming at evaluating the reasoning ability and interpretability of LLMs compared to human doctors. It contains 511 clinical notes, each meticulously annotated by physicians, detailing the diagnostic reasoning process from observations in a clinical note to the final diagnosis. Additionally, a diagnostic knowledge graph is provided to offer essential knowledge for reasoning, which may not be covered in the training data of existing LLMs. Evaluations of leading LLMs on DiReCT bring out a significant gap between their reasoning ability and that of human doctors, highlighting the critical need for models that can reason effectively in real-world clinical scenarios.

Additionally, a diagnostic knowledge graph is provided to offer essential knowledge for reasoning, which may not be covered in the training data of existing LLMs. Evaluations of leading LLMs on DiReCT bring out a significant gap between their reasoning ability and that of human doctors, highlighting the critical need for models that can reason effectively in real-world clinical scenarios.

paragraphs: DiReCT is a dataset designed to evaluate how language models reason from clinical notes to diagnoses. The motivation is that strong performance on medical questions does not by itself establish interpretable reasoning on complex clinical records. The paper makes the reasoning process an explicit object of evaluation, allowing comparison with the diagnostic reasoning supplied by physicians.

The dataset contains 511 clinical notes annotated by doctors. Each annotation traces how observations in a note support the final diagnosis, giving evaluators more to examine than the diagnosis alone. The authors also provide a diagnostic knowledge graph containing information relevant to the reasoning task. That resource addresses the possibility that some necessary knowledge was absent from a model’s training data.

Evaluations of leading language models reveal a substantial gap between their reasoning and that of human doctors on DiReCT. The finding identifies a specific challenge for medical language models: connecting clinical evidence to a diagnosis through an interpretable reasoning process. The paper contributes both the annotated evaluation material and supporting knowledge needed to study that challenge.
summary.tldr: DiReCT provides physician-annotated clinical reasoning examples and reveals a substantial reasoning gap between evaluated language models and human doctors.

title: DiReCT: Diagnostic Reasoning for Clinical Notes via Large Language Models

abstract: Traditional information theory provides a valuable foundation for Reinforcement Learning (RL), particularly through representation learning and entropy maximiza tion for agent exploration. However, existing methods primarily concentrate on modeling the uncertainty associated with RL’s random variables, neglecting the in herent structure within the state and action spaces. In this paper, we propose a novel Structural Information principles-based Effective Exploration framework, namely SI2E. Structural mutual information between two variables is defined to address the single-variable limitation in structural information, and an innovative embedding principle is presented to capture dynamics-relevant state-action representations. The SI2E analyzes value differences in the agent’s policy between state-action pairs and minimizes structural entropy to derive the hierarchical state-action struc ture, referred to as the encoding tree. Under this tree structure, value-conditional structural entropy is defined and maximized to design an intrinsic reward mechanism that avoids redundant transitions and promotes enhanced coverage in the state-action space. Theoretical connections are established between SI2E and classical information-theoretic methodologies, highlighting our framework’s rationality and advantage. Comprehensive evaluations in the MiniGrid, MetaWorld, and DeepMind Control Suite benchmarks demonstrate that SI2E significantly outperforms state-of-the-art exploration baselines regarding final performance and sample efficiency, with maximum improvements of 37.63% and 60.25%, respectively.

They report significant improvements over state-of-the-art exploration baselines in final performance and sample efficiency, with maximum gains of 37.63% and 60.25%, respectively. These are maximum reported improvements, supporting the usefulness of structured exploration in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: SI2E organizes state-action pairs into a hierarchy and uses structural entropy to reward exploration, improving performance and sample efficiency in reported benchmarks.

title: Effective Exploration Based on the Structural Information Principles

abstract: Classical worst-case optimization theory neither explains the success of optimization in machine learning, nor does it help with step size selection. In this paper we demonstrate the viability and advantages of replacing the classical 'convex function' framework with a 'random function' framework. With complexity $\mathcal{O}(n^3d^3)$, where $n$ is the number of steps and $d$ the number of dimensions, Bayesian optimization with gradients has not been viable in large dimension so far. By bridging the gap between Bayesian optimization (i.e. random function optimization theory) and classical optimization we establish viability. Specifically, we use a 'stochastic Taylor approximation' to rediscover gradient descent, which is scalable in high dimension due to $\mathcal{O}(nd)$ complexity. This rediscovery yields a specific step size schedule we call Random Function Descent (RFD). The advantage of this random function framework is that RFD is scale invariant and that it provides a theoretical foundation for common step size heuristics such as gradient clipping and gradual learning rate warmup.

paragraphs: Random Function Descent approaches optimization by treating the objective as a random function. The authors propose this framework as a way to explain optimization behavior in machine learning and guide step-size selection. Their starting point is a connection between Bayesian optimization, which reasons about uncertain functions, and classical gradient-based optimization.

Gradient-informed Bayesian optimization has a stated computational complexity of O(n³d³), where n is the number of steps and d is the dimension. The paper uses a stochastic Taylor approximation to recover gradient descent with O(nd) complexity. This approximation makes the random-function perspective computationally viable in high dimensions and yields a specific step-size schedule called Random Function Descent.

The resulting method is scale invariant. The framework also supplies a theoretical basis for familiar practices such as gradient clipping and gradually increasing the learning rate during warmup. Its contribution is therefore both computational and explanatory: it derives a scalable optimization procedure while connecting its step-size behavior to heuristics already used in training.
summary.tldr: Random Function Descent derives a scalable, scale-invariant gradient-descent schedule from random-function modeling and helps explain clipping and warmup.

title: Random Function Descent

abstract: Combinatorial optimization problems are widespread but inherently challenging due to their discrete nature. The primary limitation of existing methods is that they can only access a small fraction of the solution space at each iteration, resulting in limited efficiency for searching the global optimal. To overcome this challenge, diverging from conventional efforts of expanding the solver's search scope, we focus on enabling information to actively propagate to the solver through heat diffusion. By transforming the target function while preserving its optima, heat diffusion facilitates information flow from distant regions to the solver, providing more efficient navigation. Utilizing heat diffusion, we propose a framework for solving general combinatorial optimization problems. The proposed methodology demonstrates superior performance across a range of the most challenging and widely encountered combinatorial optimizations. Echoing recent advancements in harnessing thermodynamics for generative artificial intelligence, our study further reveals its significant potential in advancing combinatorial optimization.
