paragraphs: Understanding an activity from the participant's viewpoint and from an outside observer's viewpoint requires connecting information across perspectives. A model that understands either video individually may still struggle to relate them. EgoExoBench creates a dedicated evaluation of this ability in multimodal large language models, focusing on first-person and third-person video understanding.

Built from publicly available datasets, the benchmark contains more than 7,300 question–answer pairs across eleven subtasks. These are organized around three challenges: aligning meaning across perspectives, associating viewpoints, and reasoning about time. This structure separates different demands of cross-view understanding rather than treating performance on individual videos as evidence that a model can integrate their perspectives.

The authors evaluate thirteen leading multimodal models. Although the models perform strongly on single-view tasks, they struggle with semantic alignment, view association, and temporal dynamics in the combined setting. The results identify a gap between understanding an isolated perspective and connecting perspectives. The benchmark is intended to support research on embodied agents and assistants that need this broader form of video understanding.
summary.tldr: EgoExoBench reveals that strong single-view video understanding does not reliably translate into reasoning across first-person and third-person perspectives.

title: EgoExoBench: A Benchmark for First- and Third-person View Video Understanding in MLLMs

abstract: Part of the success of diffusion models stems from their ability to perform iterative refinement, i.e., repeatedly correcting outputs during generation. However, modern masked discrete diffusion lacks this capability: when a token is generated, it cannot be updated again, even when it introduces an error. Here, we address this limitation by introducing the remasking diffusion model (ReMDM) sampler, a method that can be applied to pretrained masked diffusion models in a principled way and that is derived from a discrete diffusion model with a custom remasking backward process. Most interestingly, ReMDM endows discrete diffusion with a form of inference-time compute scaling. By increasing the number of sampling steps, ReMDM generates natural language outputs that approach the quality of autoregressive models, whereas when the computation budget is limited, ReMDM better maintains quality. ReMDM also improves sample quality of masked diffusion models for discretized images, and in scientific domains such as molecule design, ReMDM facilitates diffusion guidance and pushes the Pareto frontier of controllability relative to classical masking and uniform noise diffusion. When applied to large pretrained diffusion language models, ReMDM boosts the model’s performance on downstream tasks requiring factual knowledge grasp and reasoning ability.

paragraphs: Masked discrete diffusion generates outputs by filling masked positions, but the models discussed here cannot revise a token once it has been generated. That prevents later steps from correcting an earlier mistake. ReMDM introduces a sampler that allows remasking, restoring a form of iterative refinement to this generation process.

The sampler is derived from a discrete diffusion model with a specially designed remasking backward process and can be applied to pretrained masked diffusion models. Increasing its sampling steps lets natural-language output quality approach that of autoregressive models. When computation is limited, the method also better preserves quality, making the sampling procedure a way to adjust the tradeoff between generation effort and output quality.

The reported benefits extend beyond language generation. ReMDM improves samples for discretized images and supports guidance in molecule design, advancing the controllability tradeoff relative to classical masking and uniform-noise diffusion. Applied to large pretrained diffusion language models, it also improves downstream tasks involving factual knowledge and reasoning. These findings connect revisable outputs with useful inference-time computation.
summary.tldr: ReMDM lets pretrained masked diffusion models revise generated tokens, improving sample quality and enabling useful scaling with additional inference steps.

title: Remasking Discrete Diffusion Models with Inference-Time Scaling

abstract: Diffusion models are increasingly deployed in real-world text-to-image services. These models, however, encode implicit assumptions about the world based on web-scraped image-caption pairs used during training. Over time, such assumptions may become outdated, incorrect, or socially biased--leading to failures where the generated images misalign with users' expectations or evolving societal norms. Identifying and fixing such failures is challenging and, thus, a valuable asset for service providers, as failures often emerge post-deployment and demand specialized expertise and resources to resolve them. In this work, we introduce $\textit{SURE}$, the first end‑to‑end framework that $\textbf{S}$ec$\textbf{U}$rely $\textbf{RE}$pairs failures flagged by users of diffusion-based services. $\textit{SURE}$ enables the service provider to securely collaborate with an external third-party specialized in model repairing (i.e., Model Repair Institute) without compromising the confidentiality of user feedback, the service provider’s proprietary model, or the Model Repair Institute’s proprietary repairing knowledge. To achieve the best possible efficiency, we propose a co-design of a model editing algorithm with a customized two-party cryptographic protocol. Our experiments show that $\textit{SURE}$ is highly practical: $\textit{SURE}$ securely and effectively repairs all 32 layers of {Stable Diffusion v1.4} in under 17 seconds (four orders of magnitude more efficient than a general baseline). Our results demonstrate that practical, secure model repair is attainable for large-scale, modern diffusion services.

summary.tldr: SURE combines model editing with customized cryptography to repair user-flagged diffusion-model failures while protecting each participant's confidential information.

title: Pin the Tail on the Model: Blindfolded Repair of User-Flagged Failures in Text-to-Image Services

abstract: The field of embodied AI (EAI) is rapidly advancing. Unlike virtual AI, EAI systems can exist in, learn from, reason about, and act in the physical world. With recent advances in AI and hardware research and design, EAI systems are becoming increasingly capable across an expanding set of operational domains. While EAI systems can offer many benefits, they also pose significant short- and long-term risks, including physical harm, surveillance, and societal disruption. These risks require urgent attention from policymakers, as existing policies for industrial robots and autonomous vehicles are insufficient to manage the full range of concerns EAI systems present. To address this issue, this paper makes three contributions. First, we provide a taxonomy of the physical, informational, economic, and social risks EAI systems pose. Second, we analyze policies in the US, UK, and EU to assess how existing frameworks address these risks and to identify critical gaps. We conclude by offering policy recommendations for the safe and beneficial deployment of EAI systems, such as mandatory testing and certification schemes, clarified liability frameworks, and strategies to manage EAI’s potentially transformative economic and societal impacts.

The contribution is a policy framework for anticipating and governing deployment, grounded in a structured risk analysis and comparison of existing approaches.
summary.tldr: The paper maps embodied AI risks, identifies gaps in US, UK, and EU policies, and recommends stronger testing, liability, and societal planning.

title: Emerging Risks from Embodied AI Require Urgent Policy Action

abstract: Contrastive learning has shown effectiveness in improving sequential recommendation models. However, existing methods still face challenges in generating high-quality contrastive pairs: they either rely on random perturbations that corrupt user preference patterns or depend on sparse collaborative data that generates unreliable contrastive pairs. Furthermore, existing approaches typically require predefined selection rules that impose strong assumptions, limiting the model's ability to autonomously learn optimal contrastive pairs. To address these limitations, we propose a novel approach named Semantic Retrieval Augmented Contrastive Learning (SRA-CL). SRA-CL leverages the semantic understanding and reasoning capabilities of LLMs to generate expressive embeddings that capture both user preferences and item characteristics. These semantic embeddings enable the construction of candidate pools for inter-user and intra-user contrastive learning through semantic-based retrieval. To further enhance the quality of the contrastive samples, we introduce a learnable sample synthesizer that optimizes the contrastive sample generation process during model training. SRA-CL adopts a plug-and-play design, enabling seamless integration with existing sequential recommendation architectures. Extensive experiments on four public datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and model-agnostic nature of our approach. Our code is available at https://github.com/ziqiangcui/SRA-CL

paragraphs: Sequential recommenders learn from the order of a user's interactions. Contrastive learning can strengthen these models, but its usefulness depends on constructing meaningful training pairs. Randomly altering histories can damage preference patterns, while sparse collaborative data can produce unreliable pairings. Fixed rules for selecting pairs also constrain what the training process can discover.

SRA-CL uses language models to produce semantic embeddings that describe user preferences and item characteristics. Retrieval with these embeddings builds candidate pools for contrastive learning both across users and within a user's data. A learnable sample synthesizer then optimizes how contrastive samples are generated during training, allowing sample construction to adapt beyond predefined selection rules.

The approach is designed as a component that can be added to existing sequential recommendation architectures. Experiments on four public datasets support its effectiveness and compatibility with different models. The contribution connects semantic retrieval with trainable sample generation: richer candidate pools provide the starting material, and the synthesizer learns how to turn that material into useful contrastive supervision.
summary.tldr: SRA-CL combines language-model semantic retrieval with a learned sample synthesizer to improve contrastive training for sequential recommendation.

title: Semantic Retrieval Augmented Contrastive Learning for Sequential Recommendation

abstract: Trees and the associated shortest-path tree metrics provide a powerful framework for representing hierarchical and combinatorial structures in data. Given an arbitrary metric space, its deviation from a tree metric can be quantified by Gromov’s $\delta$-hyperbolicity. Nonetheless, designing algorithms that bridge an arbitrary metric to its closest tree metric is still a vivid subject of interest, as most common approaches are either heuristical and lack guarantees, or perform moderately well. In this work, we introduce a novel differentiable optimization framework, coined DeltaZero, that solves this problem. Our method leverages a smooth surrogate for Gromov’s $\delta$-hyperbolicity which enables a gradient-based optimization, with a tractable complexity. The corresponding optimization procedure is derived from a problem with better worst case guarantees than existing bounds, and is justified statistically. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our method consistently achieves state-of-the-art distortion.

Nonetheless, designing algorithms that bridge an arbitrary metric to its closest tree metric is still a vivid subject of interest, as most common approaches are either heuristical and lack guarantees, or perform moderately well. In this work, we introduce a novel differentiable optimization framework, coined DeltaZero, that solves this problem. paragraphs: Tree metrics describe distances as shortest paths through a tree, making them useful for representing hierarchical and combinatorial relationships. Real datasets can have distance structures that do not fit a tree exactly. The challenge is to find a tree-based representation that changes those distances as little as possible.

DeltaZero addresses this problem through differentiable optimization. Its central ingredient is a smooth substitute for Gromov hyperbolicity, a quantity that measures departure from tree-like distances. Smoothing this quantity makes it usable with gradient-based optimization while keeping the computation tractable. This supplies a direct optimization route for moving between an arbitrary metric and a tree metric.

The authors derive their procedure from a problem with improved worst-case guarantees relative to existing bounds and provide a statistical justification. On synthetic and real-world datasets, they report consistently leading distortion results. Here, distortion captures how much the resulting representation alters the original distances, so the reported improvements indicate better preservation of the relationships encoded by those distances.
summary.tldr: DeltaZero uses a differentiable measure of tree-likeness to optimize tree metrics with strong guarantees and low empirical distortion.

title: Bridging Arbitrary and Tree Metrics via Differentiable Gromov Hyperbolicity

abstract: Shapley values have emerged as a critical tool for explaining which features impact the decisions made by machine learning models. However, computing exact Shapley values is difficult, generally requiring an exponential (in the feature dimension) number of model evaluations. To address this, many model-agnostic randomized estimators have been developed, the most influential and widely used being the KernelSHAP method (Lundberg & Lee, 2017). While related estimators such as unbiased KernelSHAP (Covert & Lee, 2021) and LeverageSHAP (Musco & Witter, 2025) are known to satisfy theoretical guarantees, bounds for KernelSHAP have remained elusive. We describe a broad and unified framework that encompasses KernelSHAP and related estimators constructed using both with and without replacement sampling strategies. We then prove strong non-asymptotic theoretical guarantees that apply to all estimators from our framework. This provides, to the best of our knowledge, the first theoretical guarantees for KernelSHAP and sheds further light on tradeoffs between existing estimators. Through comprehensive benchmarking on small and medium dimensional datasets for Decision-Tree models, we validate our approach against exact Shapley values, consistently achieving low mean squared error with modest sample sizes. Furthermore, we make specific implementation improvements to enable scalability of our methods to high-dimensional datasets. Our methods, tested on datasets such MNIST and CIFAR10, provide consistently better results compared to the KernelSHAP library.
originalAbstract: Shapley values have emerged as a critical tool for explaining which features impact the decisions made by machine learning models. However, computing exact Shapley values is difficult, generally requiring an exponential (in the feature dimension) number of model evaluations. To address this, many model-agnostic randomized estimators have been developed, the most influential and widely used being the KernelSHAP method (Lundberg & Lee, 2017). While related estimators such as unbiased KernelSHAP (Covert & Lee, 2021) and LeverageSHAP (Musco & Witter, 2025) are known to satisfy theoretical guarantees, bounds for KernelSHAP have remained elusive. We describe a broad and unified framework that encompasses KernelSHAP and related estimators constructed using both with and without replacement sampling strategies. We then prove strong non-asymptotic theoretical guarantees that apply to all estimators from our framework. This provides, to the best of our knowledge, the first theoretical guarantees for KernelSHAP and sheds further light on tradeoffs between existing estimators. Through comprehensive benchmarking on small and medium dimensional datasets for Decision-Tree models, we validate our approach against exact Shapley values, consistently achieving low mean squared error with modest sample sizes. Furthermore, we make specific implementation improvements to enable scalability of our methods to high-dimensional datasets. Our methods, tested on datasets such MNIST and CIFAR10, provide consistently better results compared to the KernelSHAP library.

paragraphs: Shapley values describe how features contribute to a model’s decisions, but calculating them exactly generally requires exponentially many model evaluations as the number of features grows. Randomized estimators make this more manageable. The paper addresses a theoretical gap surrounding KernelSHAP, a widely used estimator whose guarantees had remained unresolved even though related methods already had established bounds.

The authors develop a common framework covering KernelSHAP and related estimators, including approaches that sample with or without replacement. They prove guarantees for finite sample sizes across this framework. This provides what they describe as the first theoretical guarantees for KernelSHAP, while making tradeoffs between estimators easier to analyze within the same mathematical setting.

Experiments on small and medium dimensional datasets compare estimates against exact Shapley values for decision trees, finding low mean squared error with modest sample counts. Separate implementation improvements support higher dimensional datasets. Tests on MNIST and CIFAR10 report consistently better results than the KernelSHAP library, connecting the theoretical framework to practical estimation improvements.
summary.tldr: A unified framework supplies finite-sample guarantees for KernelSHAP and related estimators, alongside practical improvements for estimating feature contributions.

title: A Unified Framework for Provably Efficient Algorithms to Estimate Shapley Values

abstract: In this paper, we propose a simple but effective solution to the structured labeling problem: a fixed-point model. Recently, layered models with sequential classifiers/regressors have gained an increasing amount of interests for structural prediction. Here, we design an algorithm with a new perspective on layered models; we aim to find a fixed-point function with the structured labels being both the output and the input. Our approach alleviates the burden in learning multiple/different classifiers in different layers. We devise a training strategy for our method and provide justifications for the fixed-point function to be a contraction mapping. The learned function captures rich contextual information and is easy to train and test. On several widely used benchmark datasets, the proposed method observes significant improvement in both performance and efficiency over many state-of-the-art algorithms.

paragraphs: Structured labeling requires predictions that capture relationships among labels. Layered approaches address this by passing information through sequences of classifiers or regressors, but learning multiple different models across layers creates an additional burden. This paper proposes a fixed-point model as a simpler way to capture the contextual information needed for structured prediction.

The key idea is to learn a function that takes structured labels as input and also produces structured labels as output. The desired labeling is represented through a fixed point of that function. The paper develops a training strategy and provides justifications for the function to be a contraction mapping, giving mathematical support to the proposed fixed-point formulation.

The learned function captures rich context while being easy to train and evaluate, according to the paper. Experiments on several widely used benchmarks report significant improvements in both predictive performance and efficiency over many compared methods. These findings support organizing structured labeling around a learned fixed-point function while reducing the burden of training separate models for different layers.
summary.tldr: A learned fixed-point function captures label context and improves structured-labeling performance and efficiency on several benchmarks.

title: Fixed-Point Model For Structured Labeling

abstract: In this paper, we propose to address the problem of domain adaptation for sequence labeling tasks via distributed representation learning by using a log-bilinear language adaptation model. The proposed neural probabilistic language model simultaneously models two different but related data distributions in the source and target domains based on induced distributed representations, which encode both generalizable and domain-specific latent features. We then use the learned dense real-valued representation as augmenting features for natural language processing systems. We empirically evaluate the proposed learning technique on WSJ and MEDLINE domains with POS tagging systems, and on WSJ and Brown corpora with syntactic chunking and name entity recognition systems. Our primary results show that the proposed domain adaptation method outperforms a number comparison methods for cross domain sequence labeling tasks.

We then use the learned dense real-valued representation as augmenting features for natural language processing systems. Our primary results show that the proposed domain adaptation method outperforms a number comparison methods for cross domain sequence labeling tasks.

paragraphs: The paper addresses domain adaptation for sequence labeling: using language-processing systems across different data domains. Its approach learns distributed representations that can supply useful information to these systems. The representations are designed to encode both latent features that generalize between domains and features specific to an individual domain.

A log-bilinear neural probabilistic language adaptation model jointly represents the two related distributions in the source and target domains. The resulting dense, real-valued representations are added as features to language-processing systems. This makes the learned representation the mechanism for adaptation, connecting joint modeling of the domains to the information available for sequence-labeling decisions.

The empirical evaluation covers part-of-speech tagging on WSJ and MEDLINE, and syntactic chunking and named-entity recognition on WSJ and Brown corpora. The primary results outperform several comparison methods on cross-domain labeling tasks. These findings support using representations that retain domain-specific information while also learning information that can transfer between the source and target.
summary.tldr: A joint language model learns transferable and domain-specific features that improve cross-domain sequence labeling in the reported evaluations.

title: Domain Adaptation for Sequence Labeling Tasks with a Probabilistic Language Adaptation Model

abstract: Starting from a multivariate data set, we study several techniques to isolate affine combinations of the variables with a maximum amount of mean reversion, while constraining the variance to be larger than a given threshold. We show that many of the optimization problems arising in this context can be solved exactly using semidefinite programming and some variant of the \mathcalS-lemma. In finance, these methods are used to isolate statistical arbitrage opportunities, i.e. mean reverting portfolios with enough variance to overcome market friction. In a more general setting, mean reversion and its generalizations are also used as a proxy for stationarity, while variance simply measures signal strength.

paragraphs: The paper asks how to combine several measured variables into a signal that strongly tends to return toward its mean. It searches over affine combinations, which allow weighted sums together with an offset. Alongside maximizing mean reversion, it requires the resulting signal’s variance to stay above a chosen threshold.

That variance constraint captures a practical tradeoff. A signal may show desirable mean-reverting behavior but fluctuate too little to be useful. In the financial application described by the authors, the goal is to identify mean-reverting portfolios with enough variation to overcome market friction. More generally, mean reversion and related properties serve as proxies for stationarity, while variance represents signal strength.

The authors study several formulations and show that many of the resulting optimization problems can be solved exactly through semidefinite programming and a variant of the S-lemma. The significance is computational: the search for combinations satisfying both temporal behavior and minimum strength can, in these cases, be handled by exact optimization methods. The stated exactness applies to many of the studied problems, rather than every possible formulation.
summary.tldr: The paper finds strongly mean-reverting variable combinations with minimum variance, solving many formulations exactly through semidefinite programming.

title: Mean Reversion with a Variance Threshold

abstract: We propose a novel method for clustering data which is grounded in information-theoretic principles and requires no parametric assumptions. Previous attempts to use information theory to define clusters in an assumption-free way are based on maximizing mutual information between data and cluster labels. We demonstrate that this intuition suffers from a fundamental conceptual flaw that causes clustering performance to deteriorate as the amount of data increases. Instead, we return to the axiomatic foundations of information theory to define a meaningful clustering measure based on the notion of consistency under coarse-graining for finite data.
originalAbstract: We propose a novel method for clustering data which is grounded in information-theoretic principles and requires no parametric assumptions. Previous attempts to use information theory to define clusters in an assumption-free way are based on maximizing mutual information between data and cluster labels. We demonstrate that this intuition suffers from a fundamental conceptual flaw that causes clustering performance to deteriorate as the amount of data increases. Instead, we return to the axiomatic foundations of information theory to define a meaningful clustering measure based on the notion of consistency under coarse-graining for finite data.

paragraphs: The paper asks how information theory can define meaningful clusters without parametric assumptions. Earlier approaches pursue this goal by maximizing mutual information between the observations and their assigned cluster labels. The authors argue that this appealing objective contains a fundamental conceptual problem.

They demonstrate that the flaw can cause clustering performance to worsen as the amount of data grows. This makes the issue more than a question of optimizing the objective effectively: it challenges whether the objective captures the intended notion of clustering. The analysis motivates revisiting the principles used to define the measure itself.

The proposed alternative draws on information theory's axiomatic foundations and uses consistency under coarse-graining for finite data. Coarse-graining concerns describing information at a less detailed level, so consistency across such descriptions becomes a guiding requirement. The contribution is a new nonparametric clustering method grounded in that requirement, together with a conceptual explanation of why the earlier mutual-information intuition can fail.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies a flaw in mutual-information clustering and proposes a measure based on finite-data consistency under coarse-graining.

title: Demystifying Information-Theoretic Clustering

abstract: Unsupervised feature learning is the task of using unlabeled examples for building a representation of objects as vectors. This task has been extensively studied in recent years, mainly in the context of unsupervised pre-training of neural networks. Recently, (Coates et al., 2011) conducted extensive experiments, comparing the accuracy of a linear classifier that has been trained using features learnt by several unsupervised feature learning methods. Surprisingly, the best performing method was the simplest feature learning approach that was based on applying the K-means clustering algorithm after a whitening of the data. The goal of this work is to shed light on the success of K-means with whitening for the task of unsupervised feature learning. Our main result is a close connection between K-means and ICA (Independent Component Analysis). Specifically, we show that K-means and similar clustering algorithms can be used to recover the ICA mixing matrix or its inverse, the ICA filters. It is well known that the independent components found by ICA form useful features for classification (Le et al., 2012; 2011; 2010), hence the connection between K-mean and ICA explains the empirical success of K-means as a feature learner. Moreover, our analysis underscores the significance of the whitening operation, as was also observed in the experiments reported in (Coates et al., 2011). Finally, our analysis leads to a better initialization of K-means for the task of feature learning.

paragraphs: The paper investigates why a simple unsupervised feature-learning recipe—whitening data and then applying K-means—had performed so well in earlier classification experiments. The broader task is to use unlabeled examples to construct useful vector representations. The authors seek a theoretical explanation for the success of this clustering-based approach.

Their central result links K-means with independent component analysis, or ICA. In the sparse independent-component setting identified by the title, K-means and related clustering methods can recover the ICA mixing matrix or its inverse, the ICA filters. This connects the representation produced through clustering to components already known to provide useful classification features.

Beyond explaining a successful recipe, the theory leads to an improved initialization for K-means feature learning. The contribution is therefore both an account of why clustering can uncover useful features and a way to improve how that clustering begins.
summary.tldr: A connection between K-means and ICA under sparse independent components explains the usefulness of whitening-based feature learning and suggests better initialization.

title: K-means recovers ICA filters when independent components are sparse

abstract: We present a batch reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm that provides probabilistic guarantees about the quality of each policy that it proposes, and which has no hyper-parameter that requires expert tuning. Specifically, the user may select any performance lower-bound and confidence level and our algorithm will ensure that the probability that it returns a policy with performance below the lower bound is at most the specified confidence level. We then propose an incremental algorithm that executes our policy improvement algorithm repeatedly to generate multiple policy improvements. We show the viability of our approach with a simple 4 x 4 gridworld and the standard mountain car problem, as well as with a digital marketing application that uses real world data.
originalAbstract: We present a batch reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm that provides probabilistic guarantees about the quality of each policy that it proposes, and which has no hyper-parameter that requires expert tuning. Specifically, the user may select any performance lower-bound and confidence level and our algorithm will ensure that the probability that it returns a policy with performance below the lower bound is at most the specified confidence level. We then propose an incremental algorithm that executes our policy improvement algorithm repeatedly to generate multiple policy improvements. We show the viability of our approach with a simple 4 x 4 gridworld and the standard mountain car problem, as well as with a digital marketing application that uses real world data.

paragraphs: A policy-improvement method needs to address more than whether a proposed policy looks promising on available data. This paper develops a batch reinforcement learning algorithm that attaches a probabilistic performance guarantee to each policy it proposes. The user specifies a performance floor and a confidence setting rather than relying on expert-tuned hyperparameters.

More precisely, the algorithm bounds the probability that it returns a policy whose performance falls below the selected floor. The abstract defines that failure-probability bound using the user's specified confidence level. This gives the user a direct way to express an acceptable performance requirement together with a bound on the chance of violating it.

The authors also build an incremental procedure that repeatedly applies the policy-improvement algorithm to generate multiple improvements. They demonstrate viability on a small gridworld, mountain car, and a digital-marketing application using real data. These examples support the practicality of the approach, while the central contribution is the explicit probabilistic connection between proposed policies and a user-chosen performance requirement.
summary.tldr: A batch RL algorithm proposes policies with user-specified probabilistic performance guarantees and supports repeated policy improvement.

title: High Confidence Policy Improvement

abstract: We consider a variant of the stochastic multi-armed bandit problem, where multiple players simultaneously choose from the same set of arms and may collide, receiving no reward. This setting has been motivated by problems arising in cognitive radio networks, and is especially challenging under the realistic assumption that communication between players is limited. We provide a communication-free algorithm (Musical Chairs) which attains constant regret with high probability, as well as a sublinear-regret, communication-free algorithm (Dynamic Musical Chairs) for the more difficult setting of players dynamically entering and leaving throughout the game. Moreover, both algorithms do not require prior knowledge of the number of players. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first communication-free algorithms with these types of formal guarantees.

We provide a communication-free algorithm (Musical Chairs) which attains constant regret with high probability, as well as a sublinear-regret, communication-free algorithm (Dynamic Musical Chairs) for the more difficult setting of players dynamically entering and leaving throughout the game. paragraphs: In a multi-player bandit problem, several players repeatedly choose among the same options while learning which ones offer good rewards. Here, players who collide on an option receive no reward. This adds a coordination problem to learning: an individually attractive choice can become unproductive when another player chooses it at the same time.

Motivated by cognitive radio networks, the paper focuses on learning without communication between players. Its Musical Chairs algorithm achieves constant regret with high probability in the setting considered. Regret measures accumulated reward shortfall, so this guarantee describes strong control of the cost of learning and avoiding collisions, subject to the stated probability qualification.

The authors also develop Dynamic Musical Chairs for a population in which players can enter and leave during play. That algorithm provides sublinear regret without communication, a different guarantee for the more difficult changing-population setting. Neither algorithm requires advance knowledge of the number of players. The contribution shows that formal coordination guarantees are possible even without explicit messages or a known player count.
summary.tldr: Musical Chairs algorithms learn to share bandit options without communication or a known player count, with guarantees for fixed and changing populations.

title: Multi-Player Bandits – a Musical Chairs Approach

abstract: We propose a stochastic variance reduced optimization algorithm for solving a class of large-scale nonconvex optimization problems with cardinality constraints, and provide sufficient conditions under which the proposed algorithm enjoys strong linear convergence guarantees and optimal estimation accuracy in high dimensions. Numerical experiments demonstrate the efficiency of our method in terms of both parameter estimation and computational performance.
originalAbstract: We propose a stochastic variance reduced optimization algorithm for solving a class of large-scale nonconvex optimization problems with cardinality constraints, and provide sufficient conditions under which the proposed algorithm enjoys strong linear convergence guarantees and optimal estimation accuracy in high dimensions. Numerical experiments demonstrate the efficiency of our method in terms of both parameter estimation and computational performance.

paragraphs: The paper addresses large-scale nonconvex optimization with cardinality constraints. These constraints restrict how many components of a solution can be nonzero, making sparsity an explicit requirement of the optimization problem. The authors propose a stochastic variance-reduced algorithm for a class of problems with this structure.

The theoretical contribution gives sufficient conditions under which the algorithm has strong linear convergence guarantees and optimal estimation accuracy in high dimensions. These concern two different aspects of the solution: how quickly the optimization procedure converges and how accurately it estimates the desired parameters. Both claims are tied to the conditions established for the analyzed problem class.

Numerical experiments demonstrate efficiency in parameter estimation and computational performance. The paper therefore connects sparse solution requirements with a stochastic optimization approach and evaluates both statistical and computational behavior. Its stated findings support the method for the covered class of nonconvex sparse-learning problems, with the convergence and accuracy guarantees resting on sufficient conditions rather than on nonconvexity or sparsity alone.
summary.tldr: A variance-reduced stochastic algorithm offers linear convergence and optimal high-dimensional estimation accuracy under sufficient conditions for sparse nonconvex problems.

title: Stochastic Variance Reduced Optimization for Nonconvex Sparse Learning

abstract: We learn recurrent neural network optimizers trained on simple synthetic functions by gradient descent. We show that these learned optimizers exhibit a remarkable degree of transfer in that they can be used to efficiently optimize a broad range of derivative-free black-box functions, including Gaussian process bandits, simple control objectives, global optimization benchmarks and hyper-parameter tuning tasks. Up to the training horizon, the learned optimizers learn to trade-off exploration and exploitation, and compare favourably with heavily engineered Bayesian optimization packages for hyper-parameter tuning.
originalAbstract: We learn recurrent neural network optimizers trained on simple synthetic functions by gradient descent. We show that these learned optimizers exhibit a remarkable degree of transfer in that they can be used to efficiently optimize a broad range of derivative-free black-box functions, including Gaussian process bandits, simple control objectives, global optimization benchmarks and hyper-parameter tuning tasks. Up to the training horizon, the learned optimizers learn to trade-off exploration and exploitation, and compare favourably with heavily engineered Bayesian optimization packages for hyper-parameter tuning.

paragraphs: This paper trains a recurrent neural network to act as an optimizer. Gradient descent is used to train the optimizer on simple synthetic functions. After training, the learned optimizer can tackle derivative-free black-box objectives, where it must search using function evaluations rather than derivatives of the objective being optimized.

The authors report transfer across several kinds of problems: Gaussian process bandits, simple control objectives, global optimization benchmarks, and hyperparameter tuning. This transfer is the central result. Training on synthetic functions produces a search procedure that can be used efficiently on a broader collection of objectives than those used to teach it.

Up to the training horizon, the learned optimizers develop a tradeoff between exploring uncertain possibilities and exploiting promising ones. They also compare favorably with heavily engineered Bayesian optimization packages on hyperparameter tuning. The horizon qualification matters: the stated finding about learned exploration and exploitation applies over that span. The work shows that useful optimization behavior can itself be acquired through training.
summary.tldr: Recurrent optimizers trained on synthetic functions transfer to diverse derivative-free tasks and learn exploration–exploitation tradeoffs up to their training horizon.

title: Learning to Learn without Gradient Descent by Gradient Descent

abstract: Most existing sequence labelling models rely on a fixed decomposition of a target sequence into a sequence of basic units. These methods suffer from two major drawbacks: $1$) the set of basic units is fixed, such as the set of words, characters or phonemes in speech recognition, and $2$) the decomposition of target sequences is fixed. These drawbacks usually result in sub-optimal performance of modeling sequences. In this paper, we extend the popular CTC loss criterion to alleviate these limitations, and propose a new loss function called Gram-CTC . While preserving the advantages of CTC, Gram-CTC automatically learns the best set of basic units (grams), as well as the most suitable decomposition of target sequences. Unlike CTC, Gram-CTC allows the model to output variable number of characters at each time step, which enables the model to capture longer term dependency and improves the computational efficiency. We demonstrate that the proposed Gram-CTC improves CTC in terms of both performance and efficiency on the large vocabulary speech recognition task at multiple scales of data, and that with Gram-CTC we can outperform the state-of-the-art on a standard speech benchmark.

These drawbacks usually result in sub-optimal performance of modeling sequences. In this paper, we extend the popular CTC loss criterion to alleviate these limitations, and propose a new loss function called Gram-CTC . While preserving the advantages of CTC, Gram-CTC automatically learns the best set of basic units (grams), as well as the most suitable decomposition of target sequences. paragraphs: Sequence-labeling systems often begin with a fixed vocabulary of basic units and a fixed way to divide target sequences into them. In speech recognition, those units might be characters, words, or phonemes. This paper argues that fixing both choices can restrict modeling performance and proposes learning them through the loss function.

Gram-CTC extends the CTC criterion so that the model can learn useful units, called grams, and suitable decompositions of target sequences. It preserves the advantages of CTC while allowing different numbers of characters to be emitted at a time step. This flexibility enables the model to capture longer-term dependencies and improves computational efficiency.

The authors evaluate Gram-CTC on large-vocabulary speech recognition across multiple data scales. They report improvements over CTC in both predictive performance and efficiency, as well as results exceeding the state of the art on a standard speech benchmark. These findings support treating unit selection and target decomposition as learnable parts of sequence modeling.
summary.tldr: Gram-CTC learns output units and target decompositions, improving reported speech-recognition performance and efficiency over CTC.

title: Gram-CTC: Automatic Unit Selection and Target Decomposition for Sequence Labelling

abstract: Many popular dimensionality reduction procedures have out-of-sample extensions, which allow a practitioner to apply a learned embedding to observations not seen in the initial training sample. In this work, we consider the problem of obtaining an out-of-sample extension for the adjacency spectral embedding, a procedure for embedding the vertices of a graph into Euclidean space. We present two different approaches to this problem, one based on a least-squares objective and the other based on a maximum-likelihood formulation. We show that if the graph of interest is drawn according to a certain latent position model called a random dot product graph, then both of these out-of-sample extensions estimate the true latent position of the out-of-sample vertex with the same error rate. Further, we prove a central limit theorem for the least-squares-based extension, showing that the estimate is asymptotically normal about the truth in the large-graph limit.

In this work, we consider the problem of obtaining an out-of-sample extension for the adjacency spectral embedding, a procedure for embedding the vertices of a graph into Euclidean space. We present two different approaches to this problem, one based on a least-squares objective and the other based on a maximum-likelihood formulation. We show that if the graph of interest is drawn according to a certain latent position model called a random dot product graph, then both of these out-of-sample extensions estimate the true latent position of the out-of-sample vertex with the same error rate. Further, we prove a central limit theorem for the least-squares-based extension, showing that the estimate is asymptotically normal about the truth in the large-graph limit.

paragraphs: Adjacency spectral embedding represents graph vertices as points in Euclidean space. This paper asks how to extend such a representation to a vertex that was not included in the original embedding. The goal parallels out-of-sample extensions in other dimensionality-reduction methods: use an existing learned representation to position a new observation.

The authors propose two approaches, one based on least squares and another on maximum likelihood. Under a random dot product graph model, both methods estimate the new vertex’s true latent position with the same error rate. This comparison gives a theoretical basis for two different estimation objectives within the specified graph model.

For the least-squares extension, the paper additionally proves a central limit theorem. As the graph becomes large, the estimate is asymptotically normal around the true latent position. This describes the form of estimation uncertainty beyond its rate alone. Together, the results establish both error-rate guarantees for the two extensions and a more detailed large-graph characterization for the least-squares approach.
summary.tldr: Two out-of-sample graph embedding methods achieve the same latent-position error rate under a random dot product graph model.

title: Out-of-sample extension of graph adjacency spectral embedding

abstract: Word embedding is a useful approach to capture co-occurrence structures in large text corpora. However, in addition to the text data itself, we often have additional covariates associated with individual corpus documents—e.g. the demographic of the author, time and venue of publication—and we would like the embedding to naturally capture this information. We propose CoVeR, a new tensor decomposition model for vector embeddings with covariates. CoVeR jointly learns a base embedding for all the words as well as a weighted diagonal matrix to model how each covariate affects the base embedding. To obtain author or venue-specific embedding, for example, we can then simply multiply the base embedding by the associated transformation matrix. The main advantages of our approach are data efficiency and interpretability of the covariate transformation. Our experiments demonstrate that our joint model learns substantially better covariate-specific embeddings compared to the standard approach of learning a separate embedding for each covariate using only the relevant subset of data, as well as other related methods. Furthermore, CoVeR encourages the embeddings to be “topic-aligned” in that the dimensions have specific independent meanings. This allows our covariate-specific embeddings to be compared by topic, enabling downstream differential analysis. We empirically evaluate the benefits of our algorithm on datasets, and demonstrate how it can be used to address many natural questions about covariate effects.

paragraphs: CoVeR learns word representations that account for document information such as author demographics, publication time, or venue. These covariates can influence word co-occurrence patterns. The goal is to capture their effects while sharing information across the corpus, instead of learning each covariate-specific representation entirely from its own subset of documents.

The model uses tensor decomposition to jointly learn a common word embedding and a diagonal transformation for each covariate. Multiplying the common embedding by a covariate’s matrix produces its corresponding representation. Because the transformation weights individual dimensions, it offers an interpretable description of how that covariate changes the shared representation.

Experiments find substantially better covariate-specific embeddings than separately trained embeddings and other related methods. CoVeR also encourages dimensions with independent topic meanings, allowing representations to be compared topic by topic. This supports differential analysis: examining how the same shared topics vary across covariates. The reported results demonstrate both the benefits of joint learning and applications to questions about covariate effects.
summary.tldr: CoVeR shares a base word embedding across covariates and learns interpretable transformations that improve covariate-specific representations.

title: CoVeR: Learning Covariate-Specific Vector Representations with Tensor Decompositions

abstract: We study the estimation of the mutual information I(X;T_$\ell$) between the input X to a deep neural network (DNN) and the output vector T_$\ell$ of its $\ell$-th hidden layer (an “internal representation”). Focusing on feedforward networks with fixed weights and noisy internal representations, we develop a rigorous framework for accurate estimation of I(X;T_$\ell$). By relating I(X;T_$\ell$) to information transmission over additive white Gaussian noise channels, we reveal that compression, i.e. reduction in I(X;T_$\ell$) over the course of training, is driven by progressive geometric clustering of the representations of samples from the same class. Experimental results verify this connection. Finally, we shift focus to purely deterministic DNNs, where I(X;T_$\ell$) is provably vacuous, and show that nevertheless, these models also cluster inputs belonging to the same class. The binning-based approximation of I(X;T_$\ell$) employed in past works to measure compression is identified as a measure of clustering, thus clarifying that these experiments were in fact tracking the same clustering phenomenon. Leveraging the clustering perspective, we provide new evidence that compression and generalization may not be causally related and discuss potential future research ideas.

The analysis relates this information measurement to transmission through an additive white Gaussian noise channel.

Within that framework, the authors connect decreasing mutual information during training to geometric clustering: representations of examples from the same class progressively gather together. Experiments verify this connection. This gives the measured compression a concrete geometric interpretation, relating an abstract information quantity to how samples are arranged in representation space.

summary.tldr: The paper connects measured information compression to representation clustering and questions whether compression causally explains generalization.

title: Estimating Information Flow in Deep Neural Networks

abstract: We study Imitation Learning (IL) from Observations alone (ILFO) in large-scale MDPs. While most IL algorithms rely on an expert to directly provide actions to the learner, in this setting the expert only supplies sequences of observations. We design a new model-free algorithm for ILFO, Forward Adversarial Imitation Learning (FAIL), which learns a sequence of time-dependent policies by minimizing an Integral Probability Metric between the observation distributions of the expert policy and the learner. FAIL provably learns a near-optimal policy with a number of samples that is polynomial in all relevant parameters but independent of the number of unique observations. The resulting theory extends the domain of provably sample efficient learning algorithms beyond existing results that typically only consider tabular RL settings or settings that require access to a near-optimal reset distribution. We also demonstrate the efficacy ofFAIL on multiple OpenAI Gym control tasks.

paragraphs: Learning from an expert is harder when demonstrations show observations but omit the actions that produced them. This paper studies that setting in large-scale Markov decision processes. It introduces Forward Adversarial Imitation Learning, or FAIL, a model-free algorithm that learns from the expert’s observation sequences.

FAIL learns a sequence of policies that can differ across time. Its objective minimizes an Integral Probability Metric between the observation distributions produced by the learner and the expert. This gives the learner a distribution-level target even though the demonstrations do not directly specify which actions to imitate.

The authors prove that FAIL learns a near-optimal policy with a sample requirement polynomial in the relevant parameters and independent of the number of distinct observations. The result extends provable sample efficiency beyond earlier work typically restricted to tabular settings or access to a near-optimal reset distribution. Experiments on several OpenAI Gym control tasks also demonstrate effectiveness, linking the theoretical approach to practical control evaluations.
summary.tldr: FAIL learns from expert observations without action labels and provides a near-optimality guarantee with sample complexity independent of observation count.

title: Provably Efficient Imitation Learning from Observation Alone

abstract: Consider a setting with $N$ independent individuals, each with an unknown parameter, $p_i \in [0, 1]$ drawn from some unknown distribution $P^\star$. After observing the outcomes of $t$ independent Bernoulli trials, i.e., $X_i \sim \text{Binomial}(t, p_i)$ per individual, our objective is to accurately estimate $P^\star$ in the sparse regime, namely when $t \ll N$. This problem arises in numerous domains, including the social sciences, psychology, health-care, and biology, where the size of the population under study is usually large yet the number of observations per individual is often limited. Our main result shows that, in this sparse regime where $t \ll N$, the maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) is both statistically minimax optimal and efficiently computable. Precisely, for sufficiently large $N$, the MLE achieves the information theoretic optimal error bound of $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{t})$ for $t < c\log{N}$, with regards to the earth mover’s distance (between the estimated and true distributions). More generally, in an exponentially large interval of $t$ beyond $c \log{N}$, the MLE achieves the minimax error bound of $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{t\log N}})$. In contrast, regardless of how large $N$ is, the naive "plug-in" estimator for this problem only achieves the sub-optimal error of $\Theta(\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}})$. Empirically, we also demonstrate the MLE performs well on both synthetic as well as real datasets.

paragraphs: This paper estimates the distribution of success probabilities across a population when each individual has only a few observations. Each of N independent individuals has a probability drawn from an unknown distribution, and contributes t independent Bernoulli trials. The target is the population distribution, particularly when t is much smaller than N.

The authors prove that maximum likelihood estimation is efficiently computable and minimax optimal in this sparse setting. Over an exponentially large interval of t beyond that threshold, it achieves order 1/sqrt(t log N).

The comparison is with a naive plug-in estimator, whose error remains of order 1/sqrt(t) regardless of population size. Thus, estimating the distribution through maximum likelihood can use a large population more effectively than simply collecting individual estimates into a distribution. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets also demonstrate good performance, complementing the stated optimality guarantees.
summary.tldr: Maximum likelihood efficiently achieves optimal distribution-estimation rates when many individuals each provide few Bernoulli observations.

title: Maximum Likelihood Estimation for Learning Populations of Parameters

abstract: We propose Dirichlet Simplex Nest, a class of probabilistic models suitable for a variety of data types, and develop fast and provably accurate inference algorithms by accounting for the model’s convex geometry and low dimensional simplicial structure. By exploiting the connection to Voronoi tessellation and properties of Dirichlet distribution, the proposed inference algorithm is shown to achieve consistency and strong error bound guarantees on a range of model settings and data distributions. The effectiveness of our model and the learning algorithm is demonstrated by simulations and by analyses of text and financial data.

paragraphs: Dirichlet Simplex Nest is a family of probabilistic models designed to accommodate different kinds of data. The paper develops inference algorithms that take advantage of the models' geometry, particularly their convex structure and low-dimensional simplicial organization. The central idea is that this structure can guide learning, making geometric properties a source of computational and statistical benefits.

The inference approach uses a connection to Voronoi tessellation together with properties of the Dirichlet distribution. These ingredients support algorithms described as both fast and provably accurate. For a range of model settings and data distributions, the authors establish consistency and strong error bounds, giving theoretical support for the accuracy of the inferred model as well as its computational appeal.

The paper demonstrates the model and learning procedure through simulations and analyses of text and financial data. These examples illustrate applicability across different data domains. The combined contribution is a probabilistic model class and a geometrically informed inference method, with guarantees that apply across the stated range of settings.
summary.tldr: Dirichlet Simplex Nest uses low-dimensional convex geometry to enable fast inference with consistency and error guarantees across a range of settings.

title: Dirichlet Simplex Nest and Geometric Inference

abstract: Recent work on policy learning from observational data has highlighted the importance of efficient policy evaluation and has proposed reductions to weighted (cost-sensitive) classification. But, efficient policy evaluation need not yield efficient estimation of policy parameters. We consider the estimation problem given by a weighted surrogate-loss classification with any score function, either direct, inverse-propensity-weighted, or doubly robust. We show that, under a correct specification assumption, the weighted classification formulation need not be efficient for policy parameters. We draw a contrast to actual (possibly weighted) binary classification, where correct specification implies a parametric model, while for policy learning it only implies a semi-parametric model. In light of this, we instead propose an estimation approach based on generalized method of moments, which is efficient for the policy parameters. We propose a particular method based on recent developments on solving moment problems using neural networks and demonstrate the efficiency and regret benefits of this method empirically.

paragraphs: Learning a decision policy from observational data is often converted into a weighted classification problem. This paper examines a distinction within that strategy: accurately and efficiently evaluating a policy does not automatically make the estimation of its parameters statistically efficient. Here, efficiency concerns how effectively the estimator uses available information.

The analysis covers surrogate-loss classification with direct, inverse-propensity-weighted, or doubly robust scores. Even under correct specification, the weighted classification formulation need not estimate policy parameters efficiently. The authors explain this through a difference from ordinary binary classification: correct specification gives a parametric model there, but only a semiparametric model in the policy-learning setting.

To address the resulting gap, the paper proposes estimation through the generalized method of moments and establishes efficiency for policy parameters. It also develops a particular implementation using neural-network methods for solving moment problems. Experiments demonstrate benefits in both estimation efficiency and regret. The result clarifies why a strong policy-evaluation ingredient may still need a different estimation procedure to produce an efficient learned policy.
summary.tldr: Weighted classification can inefficiently estimate policy parameters even under correct specification; a moment-based alternative addresses this gap.

title: Efficient Policy Learning from Surrogate-Loss Classification Reductions

abstract: Spectral clustering (SC) is a popular clustering technique to find strongly connected communities on a graph. SC can be used in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to implement pooling operations that aggregate nodes belonging to the same cluster. However, the eigendecomposition of the Laplacian is expensive and, since clustering results are graph-specific, pooling methods based on SC must perform a new optimization for each new sample. In this paper, we propose a graph clustering approach that addresses these limitations of SC. We formulate a continuous relaxation of the normalized minCUT problem and train a GNN to compute cluster assignments that minimize this objective. Our GNN-based implementation is differentiable, does not require to compute the spectral decomposition, and learns a clustering function that can be quickly evaluated on out-of-sample graphs. From the proposed clustering method, we design a graph pooling operator that overcomes some important limitations of state-of-the-art graph pooling techniques and achieves the best performance in several supervised and unsupervised tasks.

paragraphs: Graph pooling combines nodes into larger units, allowing a graph neural network to work with a coarser representation. Spectral clustering offers a way to group strongly connected nodes, but its Laplacian eigendecomposition is expensive. Its graph-specific results also mean that a new graph requires a new clustering optimization.

This paper replaces that repeated procedure with a learned clustering function. The authors formulate a continuous relaxation of normalized minCUT and train a graph neural network to produce cluster assignments that minimize the objective. The implementation is differentiable and avoids spectral decomposition, while the learned function can be evaluated quickly on previously unseen graphs.

The authors use this clustering method to construct a graph pooling operator. They report that it addresses important limitations of existing pooling techniques and achieves the best performance in several supervised and unsupervised tasks. The approach connects a graph-partitioning objective to trainable pooling, so the structure used to aggregate nodes can be learned and reused across graph samples.
summary.tldr: A GNN learns differentiable minCUT-based clustering for graph pooling, avoiding eigendecomposition and transferring quickly to unseen graphs.

title: Spectral Clustering with Graph Neural Networks for Graph Pooling

abstract: In many applications areas—lending, education, and online recommenders, for example—fairness and equity concerns emerge when a machine learning system interacts with a dynamically changing environment to produce both immediate and long-term effects for individuals and demographic groups. We discuss causal directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) as a unifying framework for the recent literature on fairness in such dynamical systems. We show that this formulation affords several new directions of inquiry to the modeler, where sound causal assumptions can be expressed and manipulated. We emphasize the importance of computing interventional quantities in the dynamical fairness setting, and show how causal assumptions enable simulation (when environment dynamics are known) and estimation by adjustment (when dynamics are unknown) of intervention on short- and long-term outcomes, at both the group and individual levels.

paragraphs: A machine learning decision can affect both an immediate outcome and the environment in which later decisions occur. This makes fairness in lending, education, and recommendation a question about effects over time as well as effects at one moment. The paper develops causal directed acyclic graphs as a common framework for studying these interacting consequences.

The framework gives modelers a way to state and manipulate causal assumptions explicitly. Its emphasis is on interventional quantities: outcomes associated with changing how a system acts. That focus connects fairness questions to the effects of interventions on individuals and demographic groups, over both short and long horizons.

The authors explain two routes for evaluating these effects. When the environment's dynamics are known, causal assumptions enable simulation; when the dynamics are unknown, they enable estimation through adjustment. The contribution is a unified language for existing work and further investigation. Its conclusions depend on sound causal assumptions, making those assumptions part of the fairness analysis rather than leaving them implicit.
summary.tldr: Causal graphs organize fairness questions about interventions and their short- and long-term effects on individuals and groups.

title: Causal Modeling for Fairness In Dynamical Systems

abstract: The evolution of a deep neural network trained by the gradient descent in the overparametrization regime can be described by its neural tangent kernel (NTK) \cite{jacot2018neural, du2018gradient1,du2018gradient2,arora2019fine}. It was observed \cite{arora2019exact} that there is a performance gap between the kernel regression using the limiting NTK and the deep neural networks. We study the dynamic of neural networks of finite width and derive an infinite hierarchy of differential equations, the neural tangent hierarchy (NTH). We prove that the NTH hierarchy truncated at the level $p\geq 2$ approximates the dynamic of the NTK up to arbitrary precision under certain conditions on the neural network width and the data set dimension. The assumptions needed for these approximations become weaker as $p$ increases. Finally, NTH can be viewed as higher order extensions of NTK. In particular, the NTH truncated at $p=2$ recovers the NTK dynamics.

paragraphs: The neural tangent kernel provides a way to describe gradient-descent training in overparameterized networks. However, prediction using the limiting kernel can perform differently from an actual deep network. This paper studies finite-width learning dynamics to develop a richer mathematical description beyond that limiting kernel account.

The authors derive an infinite collection of linked differential equations called the neural tangent hierarchy. Successive levels provide higher-order extensions of the neural tangent kernel description. Truncating the hierarchy at level two recovers NTK dynamics, placing the familiar kernel model inside a broader family of descriptions rather than treating it as an isolated approximation.

The main approximation result is conditional on network width and dataset dimension. Under the required conditions, a hierarchy truncated at a level of at least two can approximate NTK dynamics to arbitrary precision. The assumptions become weaker as the truncation level increases. This establishes a controlled framework for studying finite-width effects and clarifies how adding higher-order dynamics can extend the reach of kernel-based analysis.
summary.tldr: The neural tangent hierarchy extends NTK analysis with higher-order equations that approximate finite-width training dynamics under stated conditions.

title: Dynamics of Deep Neural Networks and Neural Tangent Hierarchy

abstract: We introduce a new approach for comparing reinforcement learning policies, using Wasserstein distances (WDs) in a newly defined latent behavioral space. We show that by utilizing the dual formulation of the WD, we can learn score functions over policy behaviors that can in turn be used to lead policy optimization towards (or away from) (un)desired behaviors. Combined with smoothed WDs, the dual formulation allows us to devise efficient algorithms that take stochastic gradient descent steps through WD regularizers. We incorporate these regularizers into two novel on-policy algorithms, Behavior-Guided Policy Gradient and Behavior-Guided Evolution Strategies, which we demonstrate can outperform existing methods in a variety of challenging environments. We also provide an open source demo.

Combined with smoothed WDs, the dual formulation allows us to devise efficient algorithms that take stochastic gradient descent steps through WD regularizers. paragraphs: The paper proposes comparing reinforcement learning policies through their behaviors in a newly defined latent space. Wasserstein distance supplies the measure of difference between those behaviors. This gives policy optimization a way to account explicitly for behavioral similarity or separation when deciding how to improve a policy.

Using the dual formulation of Wasserstein distance, the method learns functions that assign scores to behaviors. Those scores can steer optimization toward desired behavior or away from undesired behavior. The authors combine this formulation with smoothed Wasserstein distances to build efficient algorithms that take stochastic gradient steps through the resulting regularization terms.

The framework leads to two on-policy methods: Behavior-Guided Policy Gradient and Behavior-Guided Evolution Strategies. Experiments show that these methods can outperform existing approaches across a variety of challenging environments. The contribution is both a comparison mechanism and a way to use that comparison during learning. Behavioral distance becomes an actionable training signal, with the reported performance advantages established empirically in the evaluated environments.
summary.tldr: Learned Wasserstein-based behavior scores guide policy optimization toward desired behaviors and away from undesired ones.

title: Learning to Score Behaviors for Guided Policy Optimization

abstract: Graph-based approaches are empirically shown to be very successful for the nearest neighbor search (NNS). However, there has been very little research on their theoretical guarantees. We fill this gap and rigorously analyze the performance of graph-based NNS algorithms, specifically focusing on the low-dimensional ($d \ll \log n$) regime. In addition to the basic greedy algorithm on nearest neighbor graphs, we also analyze the most successful heuristics commonly used in practice: speeding up via adding shortcut edges and improving accuracy via maintaining a dynamic list of candidates. We believe that our theoretical insights supported by experimental analysis are an important step towards understanding the limits and benefits of graph-based NNS algorithms.

We fill this gap and rigorously analyze the performance of graph-based NNS algorithms, specifically focusing on the low-dimensional ($d \ll \log n$) regime. In addition to the basic greedy algorithm on nearest neighbor graphs, we also analyze the most successful heuristics commonly used in practice: speeding up via adding shortcut edges and improving accuracy via maintaining a dynamic list of candidates. We believe that our theoretical insights supported by experimental analysis are an important step towards understanding the limits and benefits of graph-based NNS algorithms.

paragraphs: Nearest-neighbor search finds data points close to a query. Graph-based methods have been successful empirically, but their practical success has had relatively little theoretical support. This paper develops rigorous analysis to help explain the performance of these methods and the effects of commonly used search heuristics.

The analysis focuses on low-dimensional data, specifically when dimension d is much smaller than log n, where n is the number of points. It examines a basic greedy search on nearest-neighbor graphs as well as two practical modifications. Shortcut edges aim to accelerate movement through the graph, while a changing list of candidate points is used to improve search accuracy.

The authors support their theoretical investigation with experimental analysis. By considering both the basic algorithm and practical modifications, the work connects mathematical understanding with choices made in working search systems. Its stated dimensional regime is important to interpreting the contribution: the analysis offers insight into benefits and limits of graph search within that setting, rather than claiming a general guarantee across all dimensions.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes graph-based nearest-neighbor search and common speed and accuracy heuristics in a low-dimensional regime.

title: Graph-based Nearest Neighbor Search: From Practice to Theory

abstract: Stochastic gradient descent without replacement sampling is widely used in practice for model training. However, the vast majority of SGD analyses assumes data is sampled with replacement, and when the function minimized is strongly convex, an $\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{T}\right)$ rate can be established when SGD is run for $T$ iterations. A recent line of breakthrough works on SGD without replacement (SGDo) established an $\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{n}{T^2}\right)$ convergence rate when the function minimized is strongly convex and is a sum of $n$ smooth functions, and an $\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{T^2}+\frac{n^3}{T^3}\right)$ rate for sums of quadratics. On the other hand, the tightest known lower bound postulates an $\Omega\left(\frac{1}{T^2}+\frac{n^2}{T^3}\right)$ rate, leaving open the possibility of better SGDo convergence rates in the general case. In this paper, we close this gap and show that SGD without replacement achieves a rate of $\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{T^2}+\frac{n^2}{T^3}\right)$ when the sum of the functions is a quadratic, and offer a new lower bound of $\Omega\left(\frac{n}{T^2}\right)$ for strongly convex functions that are sums of smooth functions.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient descent is often implemented without replacement, so examples are not repeatedly sampled within the same pass. Much of its theory instead analyzes sampling with replacement. This paper sharpens the convergence guarantees for the practical sampling scheme, focusing on strongly convex objectives formed by summing n smooth functions over T iterations.

Earlier results left a gap between the fastest proven convergence and the limits suggested by lower bounds. When the summed objective is quadratic, the authors establish an upper bound of order 1/T² + n²/T³. This matches the stated lower bound and improves the previous quadratic result, whose second term involved n³ rather than n².

For the broader class of strongly convex sums of smooth functions, the paper proves a lower bound of order n/T², matching the existing upper rate. The two results distinguish the quadratic setting from the general smooth setting. They explain which convergence improvements are achievable within these classes and where the known guarantees already reach the theoretical limit.
summary.tldr: Matching upper and lower bounds resolve convergence-rate gaps for SGD without replacement in quadratic and general strongly convex settings.

title: Closing the convergence gap of SGD without replacement

abstract: The gradient noise of SGD is considered to play a central role in the observed strong generalization abilities of deep learning. While past studies confirm that the magnitude and the covariance structure of gradient noise are critical for regularization, it remains unclear whether or not the class of noise distributions is important. In this work we provide negative results by showing that noises in classes different from the SGD noise can also effectively regularize gradient descent. Our finding is based on a novel observation on the structure of the SGD noise: it is the multiplication of the gradient matrix and a sampling noise that arises from the mini-batch sampling procedure. Moreover, the sampling noises unify two kinds of gradient regularizing noises that belong to the Gaussian class: the one using (scaled) Fisher as covariance and the one using the gradient covariance of SGD as covariance. Finally, thanks to the flexibility of choosing noise class, an algorithm is proposed to perform noisy gradient descent that generalizes well, the variant of which even benefits large batch SGD training without hurting generalization.
