Our finding is based on a novel observation on the structure of the SGD noise: it is the multiplication of the gradient matrix and a sampling noise that arises from the mini-batch sampling procedure. Moreover, the sampling noises unify two kinds of gradient regularizing noises that belong to the Gaussian class: the one using (scaled) Fisher as covariance and the one using the gradient covariance of SGD as covariance. Finally, thanks to the flexibility of choosing noise class, an algorithm is proposed to perform noisy gradient descent that generalizes well, the variant of which even benefits large batch SGD training without hurting generalization.

paragraphs: Noise in stochastic gradient descent is thought to contribute to its ability to generalize. Earlier findings emphasize the importance of noise magnitude and covariance structure. This paper asks whether effective regularization also requires the particular distribution class of SGD's noise, and finds that other classes can work.

The analysis starts by expressing SGD noise as a gradient matrix multiplied by sampling noise from minibatch selection. This separates the gradients from the randomness used to sample them. The sampling-noise view also unifies two Gaussian regularization approaches: one based on a scaled Fisher covariance and another based on SGD's gradient covariance.

Using the flexibility to choose a noise class, the authors propose a noisy gradient-descent algorithm that generalizes well. A variant also benefits large-batch SGD without harming generalization in the reported findings. The contribution challenges the necessity of reproducing SGD's noise distribution class, while retaining the importance of how noise interacts with gradients. It supplies both an organizing explanation and an algorithmic use of that explanation.
summary.tldr: Noise from distribution classes different from SGD's can still regularize gradient descent effectively, motivating alternative noisy optimization methods.

title: On the Noisy Gradient Descent that Generalizes as SGD

abstract: Many machine learning problems can be formulated as minimax problems such as Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), AUC maximization and robust estimation, to mention but a few. A substantial amount of studies are devoted to studying the convergence behavior of their stochastic gradient-type algorithms. In contrast, there is relatively little work on understanding their generalization, i.e., how the learning models built from training examples would behave on test examples. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive generalization analysis of stochastic gradient methods for minimax problems under both convex-concave and nonconvex-nonconcave cases through the lens of algorithmic stability. We establish a quantitative connection between stability and several generalization measures both in expectation and with high probability. For the convex-concave setting, our stability analysis shows that stochastic gradient descent ascent attains optimal generalization bounds for both smooth and nonsmooth minimax problems. We also establish generalization bounds for both weakly-convex-weakly-concave and gradient-dominated problems. We report preliminary experimental results to verify our theory.

Understanding whether optimization converges does not by itself explain performance on new examples. This paper studies that generalization question for stochastic gradient methods through algorithmic stability: how sensitive learning is to changes in its training data.

The authors establish quantitative relationships between stability and several measures of generalization. Their results include guarantees in expectation and with high probability, and cover both convex-concave and nonconvex-nonconcave problems. This provides a framework for connecting properties of the learning algorithm to the gap between training behavior and test behavior.

For convex-concave problems, the analysis yields optimal generalization bounds for stochastic gradient descent ascent in both smooth and nonsmooth settings. The paper also derives bounds for weakly-convex-weakly-concave and gradient-dominated problems. Preliminary experiments support the theory. The contribution broadens the analysis of minimax optimization from finding solutions on training data to understanding when those learned solutions generalize.
summary.tldr: A stability analysis establishes generalization guarantees for stochastic minimax learning, including optimal bounds in convex-concave settings.

title: Stability and Generalization of Stochastic Gradient Methods for Minimax Problems

abstract: Interacting agent and particle systems are extensively used to model complex phenomena in science and engineering. We consider the problem of learning interaction kernels in these dynamical systems constrained to evolve on Riemannian manifolds from given trajectory data. The models we consider are based on interaction kernels depending on pairwise Riemannian distances between agents, with agents interacting locally along the direction of the shortest geodesic connecting them. We show that our estimators converge at a rate that is independent of the dimension of the state space, and derive bounds on the trajectory estimation error, on the manifold, between the observed and estimated dynamics. We demonstrate the performance of our estimator on two classical first order interacting systems: Opinion Dynamics and a Predator-Swarm system, with each system constrained on two prototypical manifolds, the $2$-dimensional sphere and the Poincaré disk model of hyperbolic space.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to infer interaction rules from trajectories of agents whose motion is constrained to a curved geometric space. These rules, called interaction kernels, describe how agents influence one another. Accounting for the geometry matters because both the distance between agents and the direction of their interaction are defined on the manifold.

The models assume that interactions depend on pairwise Riemannian distances and act locally along the shortest geodesic connecting the agents. Within this model class, the authors construct estimators and prove a convergence rate independent of the dimension of the state space. They also bound the discrepancy between trajectories produced by the estimated and observed dynamics.

The estimator is demonstrated on opinion dynamics and a predator-swarm system, each placed on a sphere and on the Poincaré disk representation of hyperbolic space. The contribution combines geometry-aware learning with theoretical control of both interaction estimation and trajectory error. Its dimension-independent rate concerns the specified interaction model rather than every possible dynamical system on a manifold.
summary.tldr: The paper learns distance-based interaction rules on manifolds with dimension-independent convergence rates and bounds on trajectory estimation error.

title: Learning Interaction Kernels for Agent Systems on Riemannian Manifolds

abstract: Deep neural networks have been shown to be susceptible to adversarial attacks. This lack of adversarial robustness is even more pronounced when models are compressed in order to meet hardware limitations. Hence, if adversarial robustness is an issue, training of sparsely connected networks necessitates considering adversarially robust sparse learning. Motivated by the efficient and stable computational function of the brain in the presence of a highly dynamic synaptic connectivity structure, we propose an intrinsically sparse rewiring approach to train neural networks with state-of-the-art robust learning objectives under high sparsity. Importantly, in contrast to previously proposed pruning techniques, our approach satisfies global connectivity constraints throughout robust optimization, i.e., it does not require dense pre-training followed by pruning. Based on a Bayesian posterior sampling principle, a network rewiring process simultaneously learns the sparse connectivity structure and the robustness-accuracy trade-off based on the adversarial learning objective. Although our networks are sparsely connected throughout the whole training process, our experimental benchmark evaluations show that their performance is superior to recently proposed robustness-aware network pruning methods which start from densely connected networks.

paragraphs: Compressing a neural network can make adversarial robustness harder to maintain. This paper addresses training networks with few connections while explicitly optimizing robustness. Its approach keeps the network sparse throughout training, avoiding the need to first train a dense network and then prune connections to reach the desired connectivity budget.

The method uses a rewiring process motivated by Bayesian posterior sampling. It jointly learns which connections to retain and the tradeoff between accuracy and robustness under an adversarial learning objective. Global connectivity constraints remain satisfied throughout optimization, so sparsity governs the training process itself rather than appearing only in the final model.

Benchmark experiments show performance superior to recently proposed robustness-aware pruning methods that begin with dense networks. The result is especially relevant to the paper’s focus on high sparsity: it demonstrates that the evaluated robust-learning objectives can work with dynamically changing sparse connectivity. The contribution combines a constrained network structure with learned rewiring, supporting adversarially robust training without dense pretraining in the reported comparisons.
summary.tldr: Bayesian connectivity sampling trains adversarially robust networks while keeping them sparse throughout optimization.

title: Training Adversarially Robust Sparse Networks via Bayesian Connectivity Sampling

abstract: Sparsifying deep neural networks is of paramount interest in many areas, especially when those networks have to be implemented on low-memory devices. In this article, we propose a new formulation of the problem of generating sparse weights for a pre-trained neural network. By leveraging the properties of standard nonlinear activation functions, we show that the problem is equivalent to an approximate subdifferential inclusion problem. The accuracy of the approximation controls the sparsity. We show that the proposed approach is valid for a broad class of activation functions (ReLU, sigmoid, softmax). We propose an iterative optimization algorithm to induce sparsity whose convergence is guaranteed. Because of the algorithm flexibility, the sparsity can be ensured from partial training data in a minibatch manner. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, we perform experiments on various networks in different applicative contexts: image classification, speech recognition, natural language processing, and time-series forecasting.

paragraphs: Making a pretrained network's weights sparse is useful when deployment memory is limited. This paper gives a new mathematical formulation of that task. Instead of treating sparsity only as a direct search over weights to remove, it uses properties of the network's activation functions to express the problem in another optimization form.

The authors show an equivalence to an approximate subdifferential inclusion problem, with the accuracy of the approximation controlling sparsity. The formulation applies to a broad class of activation functions, including ReLU, sigmoid, and softmax. This makes the activation's mathematical structure part of the sparsification method and provides an explicit connection between approximation and sparse weights.

They propose an iterative optimization algorithm with a convergence guarantee. Its flexibility also allows sparsity to be induced using partial training data in minibatches. Experiments cover image classification, speech recognition, natural language processing, and time-series forecasting. These evaluations demonstrate the approach across several application contexts, while the central contribution is a convergent optimization framework for sparsifying existing networks.
summary.tldr: The paper reformulates pretrained-network sparsification as approximate subdifferential inclusion and develops a convergent minibatch-compatible algorithm.

title: Sparsifying Networks via Subdifferential Inclusion

abstract: We consider the problem of learning fair policies in (deep) cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL). We formalize it in a principled way as the problem of optimizing a welfare function that explicitly encodes two important aspects of fairness: efficiency and equity. We provide a theoretical analysis of the convergence of policy gradient for this problem. As a solution method, we propose a novel neural network architecture, which is composed of two sub-networks specifically designed for taking into account these two aspects of fairness. In experiments, we demonstrate the importance of the two sub-networks for fair optimization. Our overall approach is general as it can accommodate any (sub)differentiable welfare function. Therefore, it is compatible with various notions of fairness that have been proposed in the literature (e.g., lexicographic maximin, generalized Gini social welfare function, proportional fairness). Our method is generic and can be implemented in various MARL settings: centralized training and decentralized execution, or fully decentralized. Finally, we experimentally validate our approach in various domains and show that it can perform much better than previous methods, both in terms of efficiency and equity.

paragraphs: Cooperating agents need to consider both how well they perform together and how fairly the benefits are distributed. This paper expresses that goal through a welfare function that explicitly captures efficiency and equity. Doing so makes fairness part of the learning objective, giving the agents a mathematical criterion for balancing overall outcomes with their distribution.

The authors analyze convergence of policy-gradient learning for this objective and propose a neural architecture containing two subnetworks designed around efficiency and equity. Their experiments demonstrate the importance of both components. The framework accepts any differentiable or subdifferentiable welfare function, allowing it to accommodate different established notions of fairness, including proportional fairness and generalized Gini welfare.

The method supports centralized training with decentralized execution as well as fully decentralized learning. Experiments across several domains show that it can substantially improve both efficiency and equity over previous methods. The contribution is a general way to connect a chosen definition of social welfare to the architecture and optimization used by cooperating reinforcement-learning agents.
summary.tldr: A welfare-based learning objective and two-part neural architecture help cooperative agents improve both efficiency and equity.

title: Learning Fair Policies in Decentralized Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: In spite of the high performance and reliability of deep learning algorithms in a wide range of everyday applications, many investigations tend to show that a lot of models exhibit biases, discriminating against specific subgroups of the population (e.g. gender, ethnicity). This urges the practitioner to develop fair systems with a uniform/comparable performance across sensitive groups. In this work, we investigate the gender bias of deep Face Recognition networks. In order to measure this bias, we introduce two new metrics, BFAR and BFRR, that better reflect the inherent deployment needs of Face Recognition systems. Motivated by geometric considerations, we mitigate gender bias through a new post-processing methodology which transforms the deep embeddings of a pre-trained model to give more representation power to discriminated subgroups. It consists in training a shallow neural network by minimizing a Fair von Mises-Fisher loss whose hyperparameters account for the intra-class variance of each gender. Interestingly, we empirically observe that these hyperparameters are correlated with our fairness metrics. In fact, extensive numerical experiments on a variety of datasets show that a careful selection significantly reduces gender bias.

paragraphs: A face recognition model can perform well overall while treating gender groups unevenly. This paper addresses both measuring that disparity and reducing it. The authors introduce two metrics, BFAR and BFRR, intended to reflect the deployment needs of face recognition systems more closely.

Their mitigation method transforms the embeddings produced by a pretrained recognition network. A shallow neural network learns this transformation using a Fair von Mises-Fisher loss, motivated by the geometry of the representations. Its hyperparameters account for within-class variability for each gender, with the aim of giving disadvantaged subgroups more expressive representations.

Experiments across several datasets show that carefully selecting these hyperparameters significantly reduces gender bias. The authors also observe an empirical correlation between the hyperparameters and their fairness metrics. This links the representation adjustment to the disparities the metrics measure, making parameter selection a substantive part of the approach. The stated outcome is reduced bias through post-processing pretrained embeddings, with improvements demonstrated empirically.
summary.tldr: A shallow transformation of pretrained face embeddings reduces measured gender bias through a carefully tuned Fair von Mises-Fisher loss.

title: Mitigating Gender Bias in Face Recognition using the von Mises-Fisher Mixture Model

abstract: Human can extrapolate well, generalize daily knowledge into unseen scenarios, raise and answer counterfactual questions. To imitate this ability via generative models, previous works have extensively studied explicitly encoding Structural Causal Models (SCMs) into architectures of generator networks. This methodology, however, limits the flexibility of the generator as they must be carefully crafted to follow the causal graph, and demands a ground truth SCM with strong ignorability assumption as prior, which is a nontrivial assumption in many real scenarios. Thus, many current causal GAN methods fail to generate high fidelity counterfactual results as they cannot easily leverage state-of-the-art generative models. In this paper, we propose to study counterfactual synthesis from a new perspective of knowledge extrapolation, where a given knowledge dimension of the data distribution is extrapolated, but the remaining knowledge is kept indistinguishable from the original distribution. We show that an adversarial game with a closed-form discriminator can be used to address the knowledge extrapolation problem, and a novel principal knowledge descent method can efficiently estimate the extrapolated distribution through the adversarial game. Our method enjoys both elegant theoretical guarantees and superior performance in many scenarios.

paragraphs: Counterfactual generation asks how data might look under a change to some aspect of the world. Earlier causal GAN approaches encode structural causal models directly into generator architectures. The paper identifies difficulties with that approach: it restricts architectural flexibility and requires a ground-truth causal model with a strong ignorability assumption.

The authors instead formulate knowledge extrapolation as changing one specified knowledge dimension of a data distribution while keeping the remaining knowledge indistinguishable from the original distribution. This defines the desired change at the distribution level. It provides a different perspective on counterfactual synthesis from carefully constructing a generator to follow a supplied causal graph.

The paper shows that an adversarial game with a closed-form discriminator can address this extrapolation problem. It introduces principal knowledge descent to estimate the extrapolated distribution efficiently through that game. The authors report theoretical guarantees and superior performance across multiple scenarios. The contribution is a principled formulation and estimation method for controlled extrapolation, motivated by the flexibility and fidelity challenges of earlier causal generators.
summary.tldr: An adversarial formulation changes a chosen knowledge dimension while preserving the rest of a distribution, with principal knowledge descent estimating the extrapolated result.

title: Principled Knowledge Extrapolation with GANs

abstract: Gaussian smoothing (GS) is a derivative-free optimization (DFO) algorithm that estimates the gradient of an objective using perturbations of the current parameters sampled from a standard normal distribution. We generalize it to sampling perturbations from a larger family of distributions. Based on an analysis of DFO for non-convex functions, we propose to choose a distribution for perturbations that minimizes the mean squared error (MSE) of the gradient estimate. We derive three such distributions with provably smaller MSE than Gaussian smoothing. We conduct evaluations of the three sampling distributions on linear regression, reinforcement learning, and DFO benchmarks in order to validate our claims. Our proposal improves on GS with the same computational complexity, and are competitive with and usually outperform Guided ES and Orthogonal ES, two computationally more expensive algorithms that adapt the covariance matrix of normally distributed perturbations.

paragraphs: Gaussian smoothing supports optimization when derivatives are unavailable by perturbing the current parameters and using objective evaluations to estimate a gradient. Its usual perturbations come from a standard normal distribution. This paper asks whether changing that sampling distribution can improve the gradient estimate while retaining the same computational complexity.

The authors analyze derivative-free optimization of nonconvex functions and choose perturbation distributions according to the mean squared error of the resulting gradient estimate. They derive three distributions with provably smaller estimation error than Gaussian smoothing. This makes the perturbation distribution an explicit part of the optimization design, with a mathematical criterion for choosing it.

Evaluations cover linear regression, reinforcement learning, and derivative-free optimization benchmarks. The proposed distributions improve on Gaussian smoothing without increasing computational complexity. They are also competitive with, and usually outperform, Guided ES and Orthogonal ES in the reported evaluations. Those alternatives adapt the covariance of Gaussian perturbations at greater computational cost, making the results evidence that changing the sampling family itself can be useful.
summary.tldr: Three alternative perturbation distributions reduce gradient-estimation error and improve random-search optimization at Gaussian smoothing’s computational complexity.

title: Generalizing Gaussian Smoothing for Random Search

abstract: To deal with ambiguities in partial label learning (PLL), state-of-the-art strategies implement disambiguations by identifying the ground-truth label directly from the candidate label set. However, these approaches usually take the label that incurs a minimal loss as the ground-truth label or use the weight to represent which label has a high likelihood to be the ground-truth label. Little work has been done to investigate from the perspective of how a candidate label changing a predictive model. In this paper, inspired by influence function, we develop a novel PLL framework called Partial Label Learning via Label Influence Function (PLL-IF). Moreover, we implement the framework with two specific representative models, an SVM model and a neural network model, which are called PLL-IF+SVM and PLL-IF+NN method respectively. Extensive experiments conducted on various datasets demonstrate the superiorities of the proposed methods in terms of prediction accuracy, which in turn validates the effectiveness of the proposed PLL-IF framework.

paragraphs: In partial label learning, an example comes with a set of candidate labels whose ambiguity must be resolved during training. Existing approaches commonly favor the candidate with the smallest loss or assign weights representing how likely each candidate is to be correct. This paper investigates another source of information: how a candidate label affects the predictive model.

Inspired by influence functions, the authors develop the PLL-IF framework. The central change in perspective is to consider a label through its influence on the model, bringing the consequences of a candidate choice into the disambiguation process. This supplies a different basis for handling uncertain labels than relying solely on their current loss or likelihood weights.

The framework is implemented with both a support vector machine and a neural network, producing PLL-IF+SVM and PLL-IF+NN. Experiments across various datasets report superior prediction accuracy for the proposed methods. These results support the effectiveness of the influence-based perspective in the evaluated settings and demonstrate its use with two distinct predictive model families.
summary.tldr: PLL-IF resolves candidate-label ambiguity by considering labels' influence on the predictive model, with reported accuracy improvements.

title: Partial Label Learning via Label Influence Function

abstract: Uncertainty quantification of predictive models is crucial in decision-making problems. Conformal prediction is a general and theoretically sound answer. However, it requires exchangeable data, excluding time series. While recent works tackled this issue, we argue that Adaptive Conformal Inference (ACI, Gibbs & Cand{è}s, 2021), developed for distribution-shift time series, is a good procedure for time series with general dependency. We theoretically analyse the impact of the learning rate on its efficiency in the exchangeable and auto-regressive case. We propose a parameter-free method, AgACI, that adaptively builds upon ACI based on online expert aggregation. We lead extensive fair simulations against competing methods that advocate for ACI’s use in time series. We conduct a real case study: electricity price forecasting. The proposed aggregation algorithm provides efficient prediction intervals for day-ahead forecasting. All the code and data to reproduce the experiments are made available on GitHub.

paragraphs: Prediction intervals express uncertainty by giving a range around a forecast. Standard conformal prediction relies on exchangeability, an assumption that does not accommodate general time-series dependence. This paper investigates Adaptive Conformal Inference, or ACI, as a useful procedure for dependent time series beyond the distribution-shift setting that originally motivated it.

The authors theoretically examine how ACI’s learning rate affects efficiency in exchangeable and autoregressive cases. This matters because an adaptation procedure’s behavior depends on how quickly it responds to new observations. They then introduce AgACI, a parameter-free method that uses online expert aggregation to adaptively combine ACI procedures, addressing the choice of adaptation settings through aggregation.

Simulation comparisons support the use of ACI for time series, and an electricity-price forecasting study evaluates the proposed aggregation method in practice. AgACI produces efficient intervals for day-ahead forecasts in that study. Together, the theoretical analysis and empirical results support adaptive conformal methods for this setting, while keeping the theoretical conclusions tied to the cases actually analyzed.
summary.tldr: AgACI aggregates adaptive conformal procedures to produce time-series prediction intervals without manually selecting an adaptation parameter.

title: Adaptive Conformal Predictions for Time Series

abstract: Optimal transport (OT) has gained popularity due to its various applications in fields such as machine learning, statistics, and signal processing. However, the balanced mass requirement limits its performance in practical problems. To address these limitations, variants of the OT problem, including unbalanced OT, Optimal partial transport (OPT), and Hellinger Kantorovich (HK), have been proposed. In this paper, we propose the Linear optimal partial transport (LOPT) embedding, which extends the (local) linearization technique on OT and HK to the OPT problem. The proposed embedding allows for faster computation of OPT distance between pairs of positive measures. Besides our theoretical contributions, we demonstrate the LOPT embedding technique in point-cloud interpolation and PCA analysis. Our code is available at https://github.com/Baio0/LinearOPT.

paragraphs: Optimal transport compares collections of mass by reasoning about how that mass can be moved between them. Its balanced formulation imposes a mass requirement that can restrict practical use. Optimal partial transport is among the variants developed to address that restriction. This paper focuses on making comparisons under this partial-transport formulation faster to compute.

The proposed Linear Optimal Partial Transport embedding, or LOPT, extends a local linearization approach previously applied to optimal transport and Hellinger–Kantorovich formulations. The contribution is to bring that representation strategy to optimal partial transport. The embedding enables faster computation of OPT distances between pairs of positive measures, the mathematical objects representing the mass being compared.

Alongside theoretical contributions, the authors demonstrate the embedding in point-cloud interpolation and principal component analysis. These examples connect the distance-computation method to constructing intermediate point configurations and analyzing variation in data. The paper’s practical significance lies in making partial-transport geometry more accessible to such computations, while the approach itself is specifically grounded in a local linearization technique.
summary.tldr: LOPT extends local transport linearization to optimal partial transport, enabling faster distance computation and applications to point-cloud interpolation and PCA.

title: Linear optimal partial transport embedding

abstract: Integral to recent successes in deep reinforcement learning has been a class of temporal difference methods that use infrequently updated target values for policy evaluation in a Markov Decision Process. Yet a complete theoretical explanation for the effectiveness of target networks remains elusive. In this work, we provide an analysis of this popular class of algorithms, to finally answer the question: “why do target networks stabilise TD learning”? To do so, we formalise the notion of a partially fitted policy evaluation method, which describes the use of target networks and bridges the gap between fitted methods and semigradient temporal difference algorithms. Using this framework we are able to uniquely characterise the so-called deadly triad–the use of TD updates with (nonlinear) function approximation and off-policy data–which often leads to nonconvergent algorithms.This insight leads us to conclude that the use of target networks can mitigate the effects of poor conditioning in the Jacobian of the TD update. Instead, we show that under mild regularity con- ditions and a well tuned target network update frequency, convergence can be guaranteed even in the extremely challenging off-policy sampling and nonlinear function approximation setting.

paragraphs: Temporal-difference learning often uses target values that are updated less frequently than the model being trained. This practice has helped deep reinforcement learning succeed, but its stabilizing effect has lacked a complete theoretical explanation. The paper develops a framework for analyzing target networks during policy evaluation.

The authors formalize partially fitted policy evaluation, connecting fitted methods with semigradient temporal-difference algorithms. This framework characterizes the deadly triad: temporal-difference updates combined with function approximation and off-policy data, a combination that often causes nonconvergence. The analysis identifies poor conditioning in the Jacobian of the update as something target networks can mitigate.

The resulting convergence guarantee requires mild regularity conditions and a well-tuned target-network update frequency. Under those conditions, convergence can hold even with nonlinear function approximation and off-policy sampling. The result therefore explains a mechanism behind stabilization and specifies conditions under which it is guaranteed. It does not claim that simply adding a target network makes every temporal-difference procedure converge regardless of its update schedule.
summary.tldr: Target networks can mitigate poorly conditioned temporal-difference updates, with convergence guaranteed under regularity conditions and a suitably tuned update frequency.

title: Why Target Networks Stabilise Temporal Difference Methods

abstract: This work studies the combinatorial optimization problem of finding an optimal core tensor shape, also called multilinear rank, for a size-constrained Tucker decomposition. We give an algorithm with provable approximation guarantees for its reconstruction error via connections to higher-order singular values. Specifically, we introduce a novel Tucker packing problem, which we prove is NP-hard, and give a polynomial-time approximation scheme based on a reduction to the 2-dimensional knapsack problem with a matroid constraint. We also generalize our techniques to tree tensor network decompositions. We implement our algorithm using an integer programming solver, and show that its solution quality is competitive with (and sometimes better than) the greedy algorithm that uses the true Tucker decomposition loss at each step, while also running up to 1000x faster.

paragraphs: A Tucker decomposition represents a multidimensional array using a smaller core and associated factors. Under a size budget, choosing the core's dimensions is itself an optimization problem: different shapes allocate representational capacity differently and can produce different reconstruction errors. This paper studies how to choose that shape, also called the multilinear rank.

The authors connect reconstruction quality to higher-order singular values and introduce a related Tucker packing problem. They prove that this packing problem is NP-hard, then provide a polynomial-time approximation scheme through a connection to a two-dimensional knapsack problem with a matroid constraint. Their approach gives provable approximation guarantees for reconstruction error and extends to tree tensor network decompositions.

For practical evaluation, they implement their algorithm with an integer programming solver. Its solution quality is competitive with, and sometimes better than, a greedy method that evaluates the actual Tucker decomposition loss at each step. Reported speedups reach 1000 times. This suggests that selecting core shapes through the proposed optimization formulation can substantially reduce computation while retaining strong reconstruction quality in the evaluated cases.
summary.tldr: An approximation approach selects tensor decomposition core shapes with reconstruction guarantees and reported speedups of up to 1000 times.

title: Approximately Optimal Core Shapes for Tensor Decompositions

abstract: Crowdsourcing has emerged as an effective platform for labeling large amounts of data in a cost- and time-efficient manner. Most previous work has focused on designing an efficient algorithm to recover only the ground-truth labels of the data. In this paper, we consider multi-choice crowdsourcing tasks with the goal of recovering not only the ground truth, but also the most confusing answer and the confusion probability. The most confusing answer provides useful information about the task by revealing the most plausible answer other than the ground truth and how plausible it is. To theoretically analyze such scenarios, we propose a model in which there are the top two plausible answers for each task, distinguished from the rest of the choices. Task difficulty is quantified by the probability of confusion between the top two, and worker reliability is quantified by the probability of giving an answer among the top two. Under this model, we propose a two-stage inference algorithm to infer both the top two answers and the confusion probability. We show that our algorithm achieves the minimax optimal convergence rate. We conduct both synthetic and real data experiments and demonstrate that our algorithm outperforms other recent algorithms. We also show the applicability of our algorithms in inferring the difficulty of tasks and in training neural networks with top-two soft labels.

paragraphs: Crowdsourced labeling usually aims to recover the correct answer from multiple workers’ responses. This paper also seeks the strongest competing answer and the probability of confusing it with the correct one. Those additional outputs describe ambiguity in a task, preserving information that a single final label would discard.

The proposed model assumes each task has two especially plausible answers, distinguished from all remaining choices. It separates task difficulty from worker reliability: difficulty concerns confusion between the top two answers, while reliability concerns the probability that a worker chooses either of them. A two-stage inference algorithm estimates the two answers and their confusion probability under this model.

The authors prove a minimax-optimal convergence rate, meaning the rate matches the best possible worst-case rate for the modeled problem. Synthetic and real-data experiments show better performance than other recent algorithms. They also demonstrate uses in estimating task difficulty and training neural networks with top-two soft labels. The contribution therefore extends label aggregation into a richer account of both the answer and its most plausible alternative.
summary.tldr: A two-stage crowdsourcing algorithm recovers the correct answer, its strongest competitor, and confusion probability with a minimax-optimal rate under a top-two model.

title: Recovering Top-Two Answers and Confusion Probability in Multi-Choice Crowdsourcing

abstract: Efficient numerical solvers for partial differential equations empower science and engineering. One commonly employed numerical solver is the preconditioned conjugate gradient (PCG) algorithm, whose performance is largely affected by the preconditioner quality. However, designing high-performing preconditioner with traditional numerical methods is highly non-trivial, often requiring problem-specific knowledge and meticulous matrix operations. We present a new method that leverages learning-based approach to obtain an approximate matrix factorization to the system matrix to be used as a preconditioner in the context of PCG solvers. Our high-level intuition comes from the shared property between preconditioners and network-based PDE solvers that excels at obtaining approximate solutions at a low computational cost. Such observation motivates us to represent preconditioners as graph neural networks (GNNs). In addition, we propose a new loss function that rewrites traditional preconditioner metrics to incorporate inductive bias from PDE data distributions, enabling effective training of high-performing preconditioners. We conduct extensive experiments to demonstrate the efficacy and generalizability of our proposed approach on solving various 2D and 3D linear second-order PDEs.

paragraphs: Numerical solvers for partial differential equations often depend on solving associated linear systems efficiently. In preconditioned conjugate gradient methods, the quality of the preconditioner strongly affects performance. Designing one by traditional numerical techniques can require substantial problem-specific expertise and careful matrix operations, motivating a learned approach.

The paper learns an approximate factorization of the system matrix for use as a preconditioner. It represents preconditioners with graph neural networks, drawing on the observation that both preconditioners and neural PDE solvers can supply approximate solutions at relatively low computational cost. The authors also introduce a loss that reformulates traditional preconditioner measures to incorporate information from the distribution of PDE data.

Experiments on various two- and three-dimensional linear second-order PDEs demonstrate effectiveness and generalizability. The approach places learning inside an established numerical solver through a component that determines its efficiency. Its training objective also makes the PDE data distribution relevant to preconditioner design, providing a route to learning useful numerical structure from examples.
summary.tldr: The method learns graph-based matrix factorizations that serve as effective preconditioners for conjugate-gradient PDE solvers.

title: Learning Preconditioners for Conjugate Gradient PDE Solvers

abstract: Molecule pretraining has quickly become the go-to schema to boost the performance of AI-based drug discovery. Naturally, molecules can be represented as 2D topological graphs or 3D geometric point clouds. Although most existing pertaining methods focus on merely the single modality, recent research has shown that maximizing the mutual information (MI) between such two modalities enhances the molecule representation ability. Meanwhile, existing molecule multi-modal pretraining approaches approximate MI based on the representation space encoded from the topology and geometry, thus resulting in the loss of critical structural information of molecules. To address this issue, we propose MoleculeSDE. MoleculeSDE leverages group symmetric (e.g., SE(3)-equivariant and reflection-antisymmetric) stochastic differential equation models to generate the 3D geometries from 2D topologies, and vice versa, directly in the input space. It not only obtains tighter MI bound but also enables prosperous downstream tasks than the previous work. By comparing with 17 pretraining baselines, we empirically verify that MoleculeSDE can learn an expressive representation with state-of-the-art performance on 26 out of 32 downstream tasks.

paragraphs: A molecule can be described through its two-dimensional connectivity or its three-dimensional geometry. Learning from both descriptions can produce stronger representations, but existing approaches compare them through encoded representations. The paper argues that this intermediate encoding can discard structural information that matters for connecting the two views.

MoleculeSDE instead learns to generate three-dimensional geometries from two-dimensional topologies and to perform the reverse transformation directly in the input space. It uses stochastic differential equation models with specified symmetry properties, including SE(3) equivariance and reflection antisymmetry. These properties make molecular symmetry part of the generative approach. The method also obtains a tighter bound on mutual information, the quantity used to connect information across the two modalities.

The authors compare MoleculeSDE with 17 pretraining baselines and report state-of-the-art performance on 26 of 32 downstream tasks. These results support the usefulness of its learned representations across the evaluated tasks. The contribution combines a stronger connection between molecular views with direct generation between those views.
summary.tldr: MoleculeSDE learns molecular representations by generating between connectivity and geometry with symmetry-aware stochastic models.

title: A Group Symmetric Stochastic Differential Equation Model for Molecule Multi-modal Pretraining

abstract: There is a growing concern that learned conditional generative models may output samples that are substantially similar to some copyrighted data $C$ that was in their training set. We give a formal definition of near access-freeness (NAF) and prove bounds on the probability that a model satisfying this definition outputs a sample similar to $C$, even if $C$ is included in its training set. Roughly speaking, a generative model $p$ is $k$-NAF if for every potentially copyrighted data $C$, the output of $p$ diverges by at most $k$-bits from the output of a model $q$ that did not access $C$ at all. We also give generative model learning algorithms, which efficiently modify the original generative model learning algorithm in a black box manner, that output generative models with strong bounds on the probability of sampling protected content. Furthermore, we provide promising experiments for both language (transformers) and image (diffusion) generative models, showing minimal degradation in output quality while ensuring strong protections against sampling protected content.

paragraphs: A generative model may produce an output substantially similar to copyrighted material in its training data. This paper develops a formal way to bound that probability, even when the material was included during training. The proposed property is called near access-freeness, or NAF.

Roughly, a model is k-NAF when its output distribution differs by at most k bits from that of a comparison model that never accessed the protected item. This comparison makes the protection relative to a model without access to that item. The authors prove probability bounds for generating similar content when the NAF condition holds.

The paper also provides algorithms that efficiently modify a generative-model learning procedure in a black-box manner to obtain strong bounds on sampling protected content. Experiments with transformer language models and diffusion image models are described as promising, with minimal loss of output quality alongside strong protection. The contribution joins a precise probabilistic definition, learning procedures designed to satisfy protective bounds, and empirical evidence about the resulting quality tradeoff.
summary.tldr: Near access-freeness bounds protected-content generation by comparing a model with one that never accessed the protected item.

title: On Provable Copyright Protection for Generative Models

abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel framework, Active Learning based Structural Inference (ALaSI), to infer the existence of directed connections from observed agents’ states over a time period in a dynamical system. With the help of deep active learning, ALaSI is competent in learning the representation of connections with a relatively small pool of prior knowledge. Moreover, based on information theory, the proposed inter- and out-of-scope message learning pipelines are remarkably beneficial to structural inference for large dynamical systems. We evaluate ALaSI on various large datasets including simulated systems and real-world networks, to demonstrate that ALaSI is able to outperform previous methods in precisely inferring the existence of connections in large systems under either supervised learning or unsupervised learning.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we propose a novel framework, Active Learning based Structural Inference (ALaSI), to infer the existence of directed connections from observed agents’ states over a time period in a dynamical system. With the help of deep active learning, ALaSI is competent in learning the representation of connections with a relatively small pool of prior knowledge. Moreover, based on information theory, the proposed inter- and out-of-scope message learning pipelines are remarkably beneficial to structural inference for large dynamical systems. We evaluate ALaSI on various large datasets including simulated systems and real-world networks, to demonstrate that ALaSI is able to outperform previous methods in precisely inferring the existence of connections in large systems under either supervised learning or unsupervised learning.

paragraphs: Observing how a system’s components change over time does not directly reveal which components are connected. This paper addresses that structural inference problem: given agents’ observed states across a time period, determine whether directed connections exist between them. Direction matters because a connection from one agent to another is a different relationship from the reverse.

The proposed framework, ALaSI, uses deep active learning to learn representations of connections with a relatively small amount of prior knowledge. It also introduces two message-learning pipelines, described as inter-scope and out-of-scope, grounded in information theory. These components are intended to make structural inference more effective for large dynamical systems.

The authors evaluate the framework on large datasets containing both simulated systems and real-world networks. They report more accurate connection inference than previous methods in both supervised and unsupervised learning settings. The contribution combines efficient use of prior knowledge with message learning for larger systems, rather than treating every connection as an isolated prediction.
summary.tldr: ALaSI combines active learning and information-theoretic message learning to infer directed connections in large dynamical systems.

title: Active Learning based Structural Inference

abstract: The task of mixture proportion estimation (MPE) is to estimate the weight of a component distribution in a mixture, given observations from both the component and mixture. Previous work on MPE adopts the irreducibility assumption, which ensures identifiablity of the mixture proportion. In this paper, we propose a more general sufficient condition that accommodates several settings of interest where irreducibility does not hold. We further present a resampling-based meta-algorithm that takes any existing MPE algorithm designed to work under irreducibility and adapts it to work under our more general condition. Our approach empirically exhibits improved estimation performance relative to baseline methods and to a recently proposed regrouping-based algorithm.

paragraphs: Mixture proportion estimation asks how much of a mixed distribution comes from a particular component, using observations from both that component and the mixture. A central issue is identifiability: whether the available distributions determine the proportion. Earlier approaches use an irreducibility assumption to ensure that this estimation target can be identified.

This paper introduces a more general sufficient condition that covers several settings where irreducibility fails. The distinction matters because relaxing that assumption expands the situations in which estimation can be justified. The contribution does not remove the need for a condition; it establishes a broader one under which the problem can be addressed.

The authors also propose a resampling-based meta-algorithm. It adapts any existing mixture-proportion estimator designed for irreducibility to operate under the new condition, providing a way to reuse established methods. Empirical comparisons show improved estimation relative to baseline methods and a recently proposed regrouping approach. The paper thus combines a broader theoretical foundation with a reusable procedure for estimation.
summary.tldr: A broader sufficient condition and a resampling procedure extend mixture proportion estimation beyond the usual irreducibility assumption.

title: Mixture Proportion Estimation Beyond Irreducibility

abstract: We focus on verifying relational properties defined over deep neural networks (DNNs) such as robustness against universal adversarial perturbations (UAP), certified worst-case hamming distance for binary string classifications, etc. Precise verification of these properties requires reasoning about multiple executions of the same DNN. However, most of the existing works in DNN verification only handle properties defined over single executions and as a result, are imprecise for relational properties. Though few recent works for relational DNN verification, capture linear dependencies between the inputs of multiple executions, they do not leverage dependencies between the outputs of hidden layers producing imprecise results. We develop a scalable relational verifier RACoon that utilizes cross-execution dependencies at all layers of the DNN gaining substantial precision over SOTA baselines on a wide range of datasets, networks, and relational properties.

paragraphs: Some neural-network properties concern several executions together. Examples include robustness against a perturbation shared across inputs and certified worst-case Hamming distance for binary-string classifications. Verifying such properties requires reasoning about relationships among executions, rather than analyzing each input-output computation independently.

The paper identifies a source of imprecision in existing verification approaches. Most focus on single executions, and even some relational methods capture only linear dependencies between inputs. They leave unused the dependencies that arise between hidden-layer outputs across executions. Those internal relationships can provide additional information for bounding the network’s possible behavior.

The authors introduce RACoon, a scalable verifier that uses cross-execution dependencies throughout all layers of a network. It achieves substantially greater precision than state-of-the-art baselines across varied datasets, networks, and relational properties. The significance is that verification can become more informative by preserving relationships inside the computation, rather than discarding them after the inputs. This targets a specific weakness in how existing methods represent multiple related executions.
summary.tldr: RACoon improves relational neural-network verification by using dependencies between multiple executions at every network layer.

title: Relational DNN Verification With Cross Executional Bound Refinement

abstract: In this paper we derive a PAC-Bayesian error bound for a class of stochastic dynamical systems with inputs, namely, for linear time-invariant stochastic state-space models (stochastic LTI systems for short). This class of systems is widely used in control engineering and econometrics, in particular, they represent a special case of recurrent neural networks. In this paper we 1) formalize the learning problem for stochastic LTI systems with inputs, 2) derive a PAC-Bayesian error bound for such systems, and 3) discuss various consequences of this error bound.
originalAbstract: In this paper we derive a PAC-Bayesian error bound for a class of stochastic dynamical systems with inputs, namely, for linear time-invariant stochastic state-space models (stochastic LTI systems for short). This class of systems is widely used in control engineering and econometrics, in particular, they represent a special case of recurrent neural networks. In this paper we 1) formalize the learning problem for stochastic LTI systems with inputs, 2) derive a PAC-Bayesian error bound for such systems, and 3) discuss various consequences of this error bound.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning for stochastic linear time-invariant state-space systems with inputs. These are dynamical models whose state evolves through linear relationships that remain fixed over time, while incorporating randomness and external inputs. The model class matters in control engineering and econometrics and also forms a special case of recurrent neural networks.

The authors first formalize the learning problem for this class of systems. They then derive a PAC-Bayesian error bound using Rényi divergence. The contribution is a theoretical result about learning error for the specified dynamical setting, connecting the system model to a framework for reasoning about the reliability of learned predictions.

The paper also discusses consequences of the bound. Its stated scope is a particular class of stochastic systems with inputs, so the connection to recurrent networks applies through that special case. The significance is the combination of a formal learning setup and an error guarantee for models used to describe evolving processes, providing a basis for analyzing learning within that class.
summary.tldr: The paper formalizes learning for stochastic LTI state-space systems with inputs and derives a PAC-Bayesian error bound using Rényi divergence.

title: PAC-Bayesian Error Bound, via Rényi Divergence, for a Class of Linear Time-Invariant State-Space Models

abstract: One major challenge in weakly supervised learning is learning from inexact supervision, ranging from partial labels (PLs) with redundant information to the extreme of unlabeled data with insufficient information. While recent work has made significant strides in specific inexact supervision contexts, supervision forms typically coexist in complex combinations. This is exemplified in semi-supervised partial label learning, where PLs act as the exclusive supervision in a semi-supervised setting. Current strategies addressing combined inexact scenarios are usually composite, which can lead to incremental solutions that essentially replicate existing methods. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to uniformly tackle both label redundancy and insufficiency, derived from a mutual information-based perspective. We design a label channel that facilitates dynamic label exchange within the candidate label sets, which identifies potential true labels and filters out likely incorrect ones, thereby minimizing error accumulation. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our method over existing state-of-the-art PL and semi-supervised learning approaches by directly integrating them. Furthermore, our extended experiments on partial-complementary label learning underscore the flexibility of our uniform treatment in managing diverse supervision scenarios.

paragraphs: Weak supervision can contain too many possible labels or no labels at all. In semi-supervised partial-label learning, the labeled portion supplies candidate sets containing ambiguity, while the remaining examples are unlabeled. The paper treats these as connected forms of inexact supervision that often coexist within the same learning problem.

The proposed approach uses a mutual-information perspective to address redundant and insufficient label information within one framework. Its central mechanism is a label channel that dynamically exchanges labels within candidate sets. This process identifies plausible true labels and removes likely incorrect alternatives, helping reduce the accumulation of errors as learning proceeds.

The value of a uniform treatment is that resolving ambiguous supervision and learning from missing supervision become parts of a common design. Experiments report better performance than directly combining existing state-of-the-art partial-label and semi-supervised methods. Additional experiments on partial-complementary label learning support the framework's flexibility across different supervision arrangements. The stated findings therefore concern both predictive performance and the ability to handle multiple forms of inexact labels.
summary.tldr: A mutual-information-based label channel jointly handles ambiguous candidate labels and unlabeled examples.

title: Learning with Partial-Label and Unlabeled Data: A Uniform Treatment for Supervision Redundancy and Insufficiency

abstract: Networked dynamical systems are widely used as formal models of real-world cascading phenomena, such as the spread of diseases and information. Prior research has addressed the problem of learning the behavior of an unknown dynamical system when the underlying network has a single layer. In this work, we study the learnability of dynamical systems over multilayer networks, which are more realistic and challenging. First, we present an efficient PAC learning algorithm with provable guarantees to show that the learner only requires a small number of training examples to infer an unknown system. We further provide a tight analysis of the Natarajan dimension which measures the model complexity. Asymptotically, our bound on the Nararajan dimension is tight for almost all multilayer graphs. The techniques and insights from our work provide the theoretical foundations for future investigations of learning problems for multilayer dynamical systems.

paragraphs: Networked dynamical systems describe cascading processes such as the spread of information or disease. Earlier learning results considered systems whose underlying network has a single layer. This paper examines multilayer networks, which offer a richer representation of such processes but make the task of inferring an unknown system more challenging.

The authors present an efficient algorithm with probably approximately correct learning guarantees. In this framework, the aim is to learn an accurate approximation with high probability from training examples. Their result shows that the unknown systems considered can be learned with a small number of examples, establishing that the added network structure remains compatible with efficient, theoretically supported learning.

The paper also analyzes the Natarajan dimension, a measure of the complexity of the model class. Its asymptotic bound is tight for almost all multilayer graphs. This complements the learning algorithm by characterizing the complexity underlying the problem, giving future studies a theoretical basis for investigating learning over multilayer dynamical systems.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes efficient PAC learning for multilayer network dynamics and tightly characterizes model complexity for almost all multilayer graphs.

title: Efficient PAC Learnability of Dynamical Systems Over Multilayer Networks

abstract: Learning from preference-based feedback has recently gained traction as a promising approach to align language models with human interests. While these aligned generative models have demonstrated impressive capabilities across various tasks, their dependence on high-quality human preference data poses a bottleneck in practical applications. Specifically, noisy (incorrect and ambiguous) preference pairs in the dataset might restrict the language models from capturing human intent accurately. While practitioners have recently proposed heuristics to mitigate the effect of noisy preferences, a complete theoretical understanding of their workings remain elusive. In this work, we aim to bridge this gap by introducing a general framework for policy optimization in the presence of random preference flips. We focus on the direct preference optimization (DPO) algorithm in particular since it assumes that preferences adhere to the Bradley-Terry-Luce (BTL) model, raising concerns about the impact of noisy data on the learned policy. We design a novel loss function, which de-bias the effect of noise on average, making a policy trained by minimizing that loss robust to the noise. Under log-linear parameterization of the policy class and assuming good feature coverage of the SFT policy, we prove that the sub-optimality gap of the proposed robust DPO (rDPO) policy compared to the optimal policy is of the order $O(\frac{1}{1-2\epsilon}\sqrt{\frac{d}{n}})$, where $\epsilon < 1/2$ is flip rate of labels, $d$ is policy parameter dimension and $n$ is size of dataset. Our experiments on IMDb sentiment generation and Anthropic’s helpful-harmless dataset shows that rDPO is robust to noise in preference labels compared to vanilla DPO and other heuristics proposed by practitioners.

summary.tldr: Robust DPO corrects preference-flip bias on average and offers conditional theoretical guarantees alongside improved empirical noise robustness.

title: Provably Robust DPO: Aligning Language Models with Noisy Feedback

abstract: We propose a new Q-learning variant, called 2RA Q-learning, that addresses some weaknesses of existing Q-learning methods in a principled manner. One such weakness is an underlying estimation bias which cannot be controlled and often results in poor performance. We propose a distributionally robust estimator for the maximum expected value term, which allows us to precisely control the level of estimation bias introduced. The distributionally robust estimator admits a closed-form solution such that the proposed algorithm has a computational cost per iteration comparable to Watkins’ Q-learning. For the tabular case, we show that 2RA Q-learning converges to the optimal policy and analyze its asymptotic mean-squared error. Lastly, we conduct numerical experiments for various settings, which corroborate our theoretical findings and indicate that 2RA Q-learning often performs better than existing methods.

paragraphs: Q-learning relies on estimates of future value, and bias in those estimates can undermine performance. The paper introduces 2RA Q-learning to give explicit control over a source of estimation bias. It changes how the maximum expected value term is estimated within the learning procedure.

The replacement is a distributionally robust estimator whose introduced bias can be precisely controlled. Although robust estimation might otherwise require extra optimization, this estimator has a closed-form solution. As a result, each iteration has a computational cost comparable to Watkins' Q-learning, making the change practical at the update level.

For the tabular setting, where values are represented explicitly, the authors prove convergence to the optimal policy and analyze asymptotic mean-squared error. Numerical experiments across various settings support the theory and indicate that 2RA often outperforms existing methods. The contribution combines control over estimation behavior with a convergence result and modest per-iteration cost; the empirical improvement is reported as frequent rather than universal.
summary.tldr: 2RA Q-learning uses a closed-form robust estimator to control estimation bias while retaining inexpensive updates and tabular convergence.

title: Regularized Q-learning through Robust Averaging

abstract: In many real-world applications, test data may commonly exhibit categorical shifts, characterized by the emergence of novel classes, as well as distribution shifts arising from feature distributions different from the ones the model was trained on. However, existing methods either discover novel classes in the open-world setting or assume domain shifts without the ability to discover novel classes. In this work, we consider a cross-domain open-world discovery setting, where the goal is to assign samples to seen classes and discover unseen classes under a domain shift. To address this challenging problem, we present CROW, a prototype-based approach that introduces a cluster-then-match strategy enabled by a well-structured representation space of foundation models. In this way, CROW discovers novel classes by robustly matching clusters with previously seen classes, followed by fine-tuning the representation space using an objective designed for cross-domain open-world discovery. Extensive experimental results on image classification benchmark datasets demonstrate that CROW outperforms alternative baselines, achieving an 8% average performance improvement across 75 experimental settings.

paragraphs: A classifier deployed in a new setting may face both unfamiliar-looking examples and entirely new categories. This paper studies those challenges together: assigning examples to previously seen classes while discovering unseen classes under a domain shift. Handling only novel categories or only changes in feature distributions leaves part of this problem unresolved.

The proposed method, CROW, uses prototypes and a cluster-then-match strategy. It starts from the structured representation space supplied by foundation models, groups examples into clusters, and matches those clusters with previously seen classes. This matching process supports discovery of novel classes while preserving a connection to categories already known to the model.

CROW then fine-tunes the representation space with an objective designed for this combined discovery setting. Across image-classification benchmarks, the authors report an average performance improvement of 8% over alternative baselines across 75 experimental settings. The results support treating recognition and discovery as linked tasks when domain changes make the relationship between examples and known classes harder to establish.
summary.tldr: CROW clusters and matches foundation-model representations to recognize known classes and discover new ones under domain shift.

title: Cross-domain Open-world Discovery

abstract: Software engineering (SE) is increasingly collaborative, with developers working together on shared complex codebases. Effective collaboration in shared environments requires participants—whether humans or AI agents—to stay on the same page as their environment evolves. When a collaborator’s understanding diverges from the current state—what we term the out-of-sync challenge—the collaborator’s actions may fail, leading to integration issues. In this work, we introduce SyncMind, a framework that systematically defines the out-of-sync problem faced by large language model (LLM) agents in collaborative software engineering (CSE). Based on SyncMind, we create SyncBench, a benchmark featuring 24,332 instances of agent out-of-sync scenarios in real-world CSE derived from 21 popular GitHub repositories with executable verification tests. Experiments on SyncBench uncover critical insights into existing LLM agents’ capabilities and limitations. Besides substantial performance gaps among agents (from Llama-3.1 agents $\leq 3.33%$ to Claude-3.5-Sonnet $\geq 28.18%$), their consistently low collaboration willingness ($\le 4.86%$) suggests fundamental limitations of existing LLM in CSE. However, when collaboration occurs, it positively correlates with out-of-sync recovery success. Minimal performance differences in agents’ resource-aware out-of-sync recoveries further reveal their significant lack of resource awareness and adaptability, shedding light on future development of resource-efficient collaborative systems. Our code and data are openly available on our project website: https://xhguo7.github.io/SyncMind/.

Acting on that outdated understanding can cause failures and integration problems. SyncMind defines this out-of-sync challenge, focusing on whether language-model agents can recover when their view of the environment no longer matches its current state.

The accompanying SyncBench contains 24,332 scenarios derived from twenty-one popular GitHub repositories, with executable tests for verification. This provides a concrete setting for measuring recovery. The evaluation also examines willingness to collaborate and how agents respond to resource considerations, extending the assessment beyond whether a code change eventually succeeds.

Collaboration willingness stays at or below 4.86%, although collaboration is positively correlated with recovery success when it occurs. Small performance differences under resource-aware recovery conditions also suggest limited resource awareness and adaptability. These findings identify coordination and adjustment to changing conditions as significant weaknesses in the evaluated agents.
summary.tldr: SyncMind and SyncBench measure how coding agents recover from outdated codebase knowledge, revealing weak collaboration and resource adaptability.

title: SyncMind: Measuring Agent Out-of-Sync Recovery in Collaborative Software Engineering

abstract: In multi-dimensional classification (MDC), the semantics of objects are characterized by multiple class variables from different dimensions. Existing MDC approaches focus on designing effective class dependency modeling strategies to enhance classification performance. However, the intercoupling of multiple class variables poses a significant challenge to the precise modeling of class dependencies. In this paper, we make the first attempt towards escaping from class dependency modeling for addressing MDC problems. Accordingly, a novel MDC approach named DCOM is proposed by decoupling the interactions of different dimensions in MDC. Specifically, DCOM endeavors to identify a latent factor that encapsulates the most salient and critical feature information. This factor will facilitate partial conditional independence among class variables conditioned on both the original feature vector and the learned latent embedding. Once the conditional independence is established, classification models can be readily induced by employing simple neural networks on each dimension. Extensive experiments conducted on benchmark data sets demonstrate that DCOM outperforms other state-of-the-art MDC approaches.

paragraphs: Multi-dimensional classification assigns several class variables to the same object, with each variable describing a different dimension. Existing approaches often improve prediction by explicitly modeling dependencies among those variables. The difficulty is that their interactions can be tightly coupled, making accurate dependency modeling challenging.

DCOM takes a different route by learning a latent factor intended to capture the most important feature information. Conditioned on both the original input and this learned embedding, the method seeks partial conditional independence among class variables. This is a qualified decoupling objective: it aims to reduce interactions through an informative representation, rather than assuming the labels were independent from the outset.

Once the relevant conditional independence is established, simple neural networks can perform classification separately for each dimension. Experiments on benchmark datasets show DCOM outperforming the compared state-of-the-art multi-dimensional classification methods. The findings support moving some of the modeling burden into a shared latent representation, making simpler per-dimension predictors effective without requiring equally elaborate explicit models of class dependencies.
summary.tldr: DCOM learns a latent representation that promotes partial conditional independence, enabling simpler classifiers for multiple output dimensions.

title: Towards Escaping from Class Dependency Modeling for Multi-Dimensional Classification

abstract: We study in this work the problem of multi-class logistic regression with one major class and multiple rare classes, which is motivated by a real application in TikTok live stream data. The model is inspired by the two-class logistic regression model of Wang (2020) but with surprising theoretical findings, which in turn motivate new estimation methods with excellent statistical and computational efficiency. Specifically, since rigorous theoretical analysis suggests that the resulting maximum likelihood estimators of different rare classes should be asymptotically independent, we consider to solve multiple pairwise two-class logistic regression problems instead of optimizing the joint log-likelihood function with computational challenge in multi-class problem, which are computationally much easier and can be conducted in a fully parallel way. To further reduce the computation cost, a subsample-based pairwise likelihood estimator is developed by down-sampling the major class. We show rigorously that the resulting estimators could be as asymptotically efficient as the global maximum likelihood estimator under appropriate regularity conditions. Extensive simulation studies are presented to support our theoretical findings and a TikTok live stream dataset is analyzed for illustration purpose.

paragraphs: This paper studies classification when one class dominates the data and several others are rare. Jointly fitting a multiclass logistic regression model can be computationally challenging in this setting. Motivated by TikTok live-stream data, the authors investigate whether simpler estimation problems can retain the statistical benefits of the full model.

Their theoretical analysis indicates that the maximum likelihood estimators for different rare classes are asymptotically independent. This motivates fitting separate two-class logistic regression problems, each pairing a rare class with the major class. The resulting problems are easier to compute and can run fully in parallel. A further variant downsamples the major class to reduce computation.

Under appropriate regularity conditions, the authors prove that the proposed estimators can match the asymptotic efficiency of the global maximum likelihood estimator. The guarantee concerns limiting statistical behavior under those conditions, rather than identical estimates in every dataset. Simulations support the theoretical findings, and analysis of TikTok live-stream data illustrates the approach in its motivating application.
summary.tldr: Separate rare-versus-majority logistic regressions can match joint estimation’s asymptotic efficiency under suitable conditions while enabling cheaper, parallel computation.

title: Pairwise Maximum Likelihood For Multi-Class Logistic Regression Model With Multiple Rare Classes

abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) has emerged as a critical technique for efficient deployment of large language models (LLMs). This work proposes NestQuant, a novel PTQ scheme for weights and activations that is based on self-similar nested lattices. Recent works have mathematically shown such quantizers to be information-theoretically optimal for low-precision matrix multiplication. We implement a practical low-complexity version of NestQuant based on Gosset lattice, making it a drop-in quantizer for any matrix multiplication step (e.g., in self-attention, MLP etc). For example, NestQuant quantizes weights, KV-cache, and activations of Llama-3-8B to 4 bits, achieving perplexity of 6.6 on wikitext2. This represents more than 55% reduction in perplexity gap with respect to unquantized model (perplexity of 6.14) compared to state-of-the-art Meta’s SpinQuant (perplexity 7.3), OstQuant (7.3) and QuaRot (8.2). Comparisons on bigger models (up to 70B) and on various LLM evaluation benchmarks confirm uniform superiority of NestQuant.

paragraphs: Post-training quantization reduces the precision used to represent a language model’s numbers, helping make deployment more efficient. NestQuant introduces a scheme for weights and activations based on self-similar nested lattices. Its starting point is prior mathematical work establishing information-theoretic optimality for this kind of quantizer in low-precision matrix multiplication.

The paper turns that foundation into a practical, low-complexity implementation based on the Gosset lattice. The resulting quantizer can be inserted into matrix multiplication steps, including those in self-attention and multilayer perceptrons. This connects a theoretically motivated quantization structure to operations used throughout language models.
