paragraphs: Dimension reduction can reveal useful structure in high-dimensional data, but removing dimensions can also discard predictive information. This paper reframes reduction as a choice about where a model is allowed to search. Learning only in a reduced space restricts the model to a corresponding parameter subspace.

Projection penalties replace that hard restriction with a preference. The model can search the full parameter space, while a penalty discourages distance from the subspace suggested by dimension reduction. This preserves access to directions outside the reduced representation while allowing the reduction to guide learning. The authors develop the framework for linear reductions and extend it to kernel-based and other nonlinear methods.

Experiments cover principal component regression and partial least squares for regression, kernel reduction for face recognition, and topic-based representations for text classification. The reported results show that projection penalties use dimension-reduction techniques more effectively and reliably. The central benefit is preserving the full search space while incorporating the structure supplied by a reduced representation.
summary.tldr: Projection penalties use reduced representations to guide learning while keeping the full parameter space available.

title: Projection Penalties: Dimension Reduction without Loss

abstract: In this paper we address the following question: “Can we approximately sample from a Bayesian posterior distribution if we are only allowed to touch a small mini-batch of data-items for every sample we generate?”. An algorithm based on the Langevin equation with stochastic gradients (SGLD) was previously proposed to solve this, but its mixing rate was slow. By leveraging the Bayesian Central Limit Theorem, we extend the SGLD algorithm so that at high mixing rates it will sample from a normal approximation of the posterior, while for slow mixing rates it will mimic the behavior of SGLD with a pre-conditioner matrix. As a bonus, the proposed algorithm is reminiscent of Fisher scoring (with stochastic gradients) and as such an efficient optimizer during burn-in.
originalAbstract: In this paper we address the following question: “Can we approximately sample from a Bayesian posterior distribution if we are only allowed to touch a small mini-batch of data-items for every sample we generate?”. An algorithm based on the Langevin equation with stochastic gradients (SGLD) was previously proposed to solve this, but its mixing rate was slow. By leveraging the Bayesian Central Limit Theorem, we extend the SGLD algorithm so that at high mixing rates it will sample from a normal approximation of the posterior, while for slow mixing rates it will mimic the behavior of SGLD with a pre-conditioner matrix. As a bonus, the proposed algorithm is reminiscent of Fisher scoring (with stochastic gradients) and as such an efficient optimizer during burn-in.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether Bayesian posterior samples can be generated while accessing only a small mini-batch of data for each sample. Stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics already addresses this computational constraint, but its slow mixing can make it difficult to move efficiently through the posterior distribution. The authors extend that approach to improve this trade-off.

Their construction uses the Bayesian Central Limit Theorem to connect sampling behavior with a normal approximation to the posterior. At high mixing rates, the algorithm samples from that approximation. At slower mixing rates, it behaves like stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics equipped with a preconditioning matrix. The two regimes therefore offer different relationships between exploration speed and the posterior distribution being approximated.

The method also resembles Fisher scoring with stochastic gradients, giving it an additional role as an efficient optimizer during burn-in. This matters because the initial movement toward a useful region and subsequent sampling are both part of posterior computation. The fast regime specifically targets a normal approximation, which is central to interpreting its sampling behavior.
summary.tldr: Stochastic gradient Fisher scoring combines mini-batch posterior sampling with fast Gaussian approximation and efficient optimization during burn-in.

title: Bayesian Posterior Sampling via Stochastic Gradient Fisher Scoring
